summary: Started the zsh prompt from scratch: a small function-based prompt with git branch and dirty marker, replacing the oh-my-zsh theme that cost 300 ms per start.
body:
The old setup loaded oh-my-zsh just for one theme, and the shell took about 300 ms to show a prompt. I wrote a new prompt in ~/.zsh/prompt.zsh using the precmd hook and the built-in vcs_info module. It shows the directory shortened to the last two parts, the git branch, and a small marker when the tree is dirty.

The first version called `git status --porcelain` on every prompt, and that was slow in a large repository. I changed it to `git diff --quiet` with `--ignore-submodules`, plus a check for untracked files that runs only when the first check is clean. That cut the cost in the big repo from about 180 ms to 40 ms.

The prompt color is red when the last command failed and dim otherwise. I used `%(?.` conditionals in PROMPT instead of a function, since that costs nothing. The right-hand side shows the duration of the last command only if it ran longer than 3 seconds, through a preexec timestamp.

One bug: the prompt broke line wrapping when I pasted escape codes without `%{ %}` around them. Long commands overwrote the start of the line until I wrapped the color codes correctly. After that, history search with the arrow keys looked right again.

I removed oh-my-zsh from .zshrc but left the folder in place for now in case I miss a plugin. Start time is down to about 60 ms measured with `time zsh -i -c exit`. Next steps are the git aliases and a proper completion setup, because compinit is now the slowest part of the start.

summary: Wrote the first set of git aliases and moved them into ~/.gitconfig, including a compact log graph and a safe force-push alias.
body:
I collected the aliases that I had been typing by hand into the [alias] section of ~/.gitconfig. The short ones are st, co, br, and ci. The more useful ones are `lg`, a one-line graph log with relative dates and decorations, and `last`, which shows the previous commit with its stat.

I spent most of the time on `pushf`, which is `push --force-with-lease`. A plain force push was something I had used a few times by mistake, and the lease version refuses if the remote has commits I have not fetched. I tested it with two clones of a scratch repository. The second clone pushed first, and pushf in the first clone was rejected with a `stale info` message, as it should be.

I also added `undo`, which is `reset --soft HEAD~1`, and `wip`, which commits everything with the message `wip` so I can switch branches fast. The wip alias worries me a bit, so I added a second alias `unwip` that undoes it only if the last message is exactly wip. It uses a shell function inside the alias with the `!` prefix.

A problem came up with quoting. The log format string contains `%` and quotes, and the alias broke until I used single quotes inside double quotes. I checked with `git config --get alias.lg` that the stored text was what I wanted.

I set `pull.rebase = true` and `init.defaultBranch = main` and `rerere.enabled = true` as well. Left for later: global ignore file, and the diff tool setting for the editor.

summary: Added a global gitignore and set the diff and merge tools in git config; macOS clutter like .DS_Store no longer shows up anywhere.
body:
Created ~/.config/git/ignore with the usual clutter: .DS_Store, *.swp, .idea, .vscode and a local .env pattern. I pointed git to it through `core.excludesfile`, though the default location is already read by git, so that line turned out to be unnecessary and I removed it again.

The next step was the tools. I set `diff.tool` and `merge.tool` to nvimdiff and wrote the command for the merge tool so that it opens four windows: local, base, remote and the merged result. I tried it on a repository with a deliberate conflict. The layout worked, but the cursor started in the wrong window. I added a `wincmd J` and a `wincmd =` to the command so the merged file sits at the bottom, and it was fine afterwards.

I also turned on `merge.conflictstyle = zdiff3`, which shows the common ancestor inside the conflict markers. It made the conflict in my test much easier to read, since I could see what each side had changed relative to the base.

I set `diff.colorMoved = default` so that moved blocks look different from added ones. The pager is delta for now, but I am not sure I like it yet. I will give it a week and look at the diffs again before I decide whether it stays in the Brewfile.

summary: First Neovim config in Lua: lazy plugin loading, a leader key, LSP for TypeScript and Python, and fuzzy finding, with start time at 45 ms.
body:
I replaced the old init.vim with a Lua config under ~/.config/nvim. The layout is init.lua for options and keymaps, and a lua/plugins folder with one file per area. The plugin manager is lazy.nvim, and nearly every plugin loads on an event, a command or a filetype.

Options first: relative numbers, no swap files, an undo file in the state directory, `ignorecase` with `smartcase`, and a split behavior that opens new windows below and to the right. The leader key is space and the local leader is comma.

For finding things I added telescope with the fzf native sorter. The keys are leader-f for files, leader-g for live grep and leader-b for buffers. Live grep needed ripgrep, which was already in the Brewfile. I noticed that telescope ignored files that were in .gitignore, which is what I want for most searches, and I added a second key with `no_ignore = true` for the rare case.

For language support I used the built-in LSP client with mason to install servers. TypeScript uses tsserver and Python uses pyright. The first problem was that pyright could not find the virtual environment of a project, so completions for installed packages were missing. I fixed that by setting `python.venvPath` per project through a small root detection function that looks for a .venv folder.

I added treesitter for highlighting and indentation. The first run compiled parsers for about a minute and then worked well. I also added a simple status line without a plugin, using a statusline string with the mode, file name, and diagnostics count.

Start time measured with `nvim --startuptime` is about 45 ms, mostly from treesitter and the colorscheme. Not yet done: formatting on save, a git signs plugin and snippets. I will do those over the next days.

summary: Added format on save to Neovim using conform.nvim with prettier and black, after the LSP formatters disagreed with the project style.
body:
The built-in LSP formatting for TypeScript used the tsserver style, which did not match the prettier settings of my projects. I added conform.nvim and mapped filetypes to formatters: prettier for JS, TS, JSON and CSS, black for Python, stylua for Lua.

Format on save is on with a timeout of 500 ms and a fallback to the LSP when no formatter is configured. A first test on a large JSON file hit the timeout and left the file unformatted, so I raised the limit to 1000 ms for that case only.

I also added a command `:FormatToggle` that turns the automatic formatting off for the current buffer, because some old files should not be touched. I tested it on a file with odd spacing, and it stayed unchanged until I called the format key by hand.

summary: Added gitsigns to Neovim with hunk keys and inline blame, and fixed a clash with the leader-h window key.
body:
Installed gitsigns.nvim and set the signs to thin bars in the sign column. The hunk keys are `]h` and `[h` to jump, leader-hs to stage a hunk and leader-hr to reset it. Inline blame is off by default and toggles with leader-tb, since it was distracting while typing.

The clash: I had already mapped leader-h to a window movement, which delayed every leader-h key by the timeout. I moved the window keys to control-h, j, k and l, which also match the tmux plan I have in mind for later. After that, the hunk keys reacted at once.

I checked staging a single hunk from a file with three changes, and `git diff --cached` showed only that one. The preview popup on leader-hp is useful too.

summary: Wrote the first tmux config: prefix on control-a, vi copy mode, mouse on, panes that open in the current directory, and a plain status bar.
body:
I wrote ~/.tmux.conf from nothing. The prefix is now control-a, since control-b is far from the hand on my keyboard, and I set `send-prefix` so that control-a twice still reaches programs that need it, such as the shell's go-to-start key.

Basic options: `mode-keys vi`, mouse on, base index 1 for windows and panes, `renumber-windows on`, history of 50000 lines and `escape-time 10`. The escape time mattered. With the default, Neovim felt slow when leaving insert mode inside tmux. After lowering it, the delay was gone.

Split keys are `|` and `-`, and both use `-c "#{pane_current_path}"` so that a new pane starts in the same directory. I unbound the old split keys. New windows follow the same rule.

For moving between panes I used control-h, j, k and l with the vim-tmux-navigator idea: a check of the pane's running command decides whether the key goes to Neovim or to tmux. I put the check into the config with an `is_vim` variable that matches the process name with a regular expression. It worked after I fixed the expression to also match `nvim` with the flags in the path.

True color was not working at first, and Neovim colors looked flat. I added `set -as terminal-features ',xterm-256color:RGB'` and set the default terminal to `tmux-256color`. The test with a 24-bit gradient script then looked smooth.

Copy mode: `v` starts a selection and `y` copies to the system clipboard through pbcopy. The status bar is simple, with the session name on the left and the time on the right, in a color close to the Neovim theme. Plugins are not used yet. Next I want a reload key and session handling.

summary: Added a reload key and a small session switcher script to tmux, and found that the fzf popup needed tmux 3.3 for display-popup.
body:
First the easy part: `prefix r` now reloads ~/.tmux.conf and prints a short message. I had been closing and reopening tmux after every change, so this saves time.

The larger part was a session switcher. I wrote a script `tmux-sessions` in ~/bin that lists sessions and also the folders under ~/code, pipes them into fzf, and then either attaches to the existing session or creates a new one named after the folder. Dots in folder names are replaced by underscores, since tmux does not accept dots in session names. I only found that after a folder called `my.site` produced `can't find session` errors.

I bound it to `prefix f` with `display-popup -E` so that the finder opens as a floating window over the current pane. On the first try the key did nothing. `tmux -V` showed 3.2, and the popup options I used need 3.3 or later. A `brew upgrade tmux` brought 3.4 and the popup worked.

Then a detail: inside the popup, fzf should not fill the terminal edges, so I set the popup to 60 percent of the width and 50 percent of the height, with a rounded border.

I also added `prefix S` to kill the current session and switch to the previous one without leaving tmux. It uses `switch-client -l` before the kill command, otherwise the client is detached.

Still open: the Brewfile does not pin the tmux version, and the script has no help text. I will add the Brewfile work next.

summary: Created the first Brewfile from `brew bundle dump` and cut it from 140 entries to the roughly 60 that I really use.
body:
Ran `brew bundle dump --file=~/dotfiles/Brewfile` and got 140 lines, most of them dependencies that had been listed as top-level formulae from old experiments.

I went through the list by hand. For each entry I ran `brew uses --installed` to see whether something else needed it, and removed the ones that were not needed and that I did not recognize. About 80 lines went away. The formulae that stayed include git, neovim, tmux, ripgrep, fd, fzf, jq, bat, and delta.

Casks went into their own block: the terminal, the browser, the password manager and a few small utilities. I added comments with a word on why for the odd ones.

The check was `brew bundle check`, which reported nothing missing, and `brew bundle cleanup` listed the 15 leftovers that I will remove next week after I make sure that nothing breaks. I did not run the cleanup with `--force` yet.

summary: Moved zsh completion setup to a cached compinit and found that nearly half of the shell start time was a repeated security check.
body:
The shell had crept back up to 190 ms. I used `zmodload zsh/zprof` at the top of .zshrc and looked at the output. The top item by far was `compinit`, with about 90 ms.

The cause was that compinit ran its full security check of every completion file on each start. I changed the call to use the dump file and to check it only once a day: a glob qualifier `(#qN.mh+24)` tests if the file .zcompdump is older than 24 hours, and only then does it run the full compinit. Otherwise it runs `compinit -C`, which skips the check.

I also compile the dump file in the background with `zcompile` when it is rebuilt, so that loading is faster.

The second item in zprof was a call to `brew --prefix` in my PATH setup, which took about 30 ms. I replaced it with a fixed path, `/opt/homebrew`, since this machine is always Apple silicon.

Result: 190 ms down to 70 ms. I left the zprof line in as a comment for next time.

One side effect: a newly installed tool does not show completions until the dump is rebuilt. I added an alias `rebuild-comp` that removes the dump and starts a new compinit. Still on the list is a lazy loader for the tools that I rarely use.

summary: Added Neovim snippets through LuaSnip and a few custom ones for TypeScript tests, after the friendly-snippets set turned out to be too noisy.
body:
I installed LuaSnip with the completion plugin, and at first loaded friendly-snippets as well. The completion menu filled with entries I never used, so I removed the package and kept only a small set of my own.

The custom snippets are in lua/snippets/typescript.lua: `desc` for a describe block, `it` for a test with an async function, and `imp` for an import with the cursor placed on the module name. Each has tab stops in the order that I fill them in.

The tab key now expands a snippet or jumps to the next stop, and falls back to a normal tab if neither is possible. I first mapped it badly, and tab inside a snippet inserted a real tab character. The cure was to check `luasnip.expand_or_jumpable()` in the mapping function before anything else.

I tried the snippets in a real test file and they saved a good amount of typing. A Python version with `def test_` and a fixture snippet is the next small thing.

summary: Fixed a Neovim problem where the LSP restarted for every file in a monorepo, by setting a single root directory from the workspace file.
body:
Opening files in the monorepo made Neovim start a new TypeScript language server for each package, and memory went over 3 GB after an hour of work. The root detection looked for the nearest package.json, and every package has one.

I changed the root function to look first for pnpm-workspace.yaml and a top-level tsconfig.base.json, and only then for the nearest package.json. With that, one server handled all packages. `:LspInfo` showed a single client attached to buffers from three packages.

There was a side effect. Go-to-definition across packages now jumped to the source files instead of the built declaration files, which is what I wanted, though only after I added the paths mapping to the base tsconfig. Before this, the jump landed in `dist/index.d.ts`.

Memory now stays at about 900 MB for the same work. I checked it with Activity Monitor after an hour of editing and running tests.

I also found that the Python server had the same trouble in a second repository with several services. For that one I set the root to the folder that has the pyproject.toml at the top, and fell back to .git. That worked on the first try.

A small cleanup came along. I moved the root helper into lua/util/root.lua and used it from the telescope config, so that file search starts at the same top folder. Before, searches inside a package only found files of that package, which confused me for a few minutes.

Still to do: a startup check that warns when two clients of the same type are running.

summary: Set up a color theme that is shared by Neovim, tmux and the terminal, with the palette stored in one Lua table and one shell file.
body:
The colors of Neovim, tmux and the terminal had drifted apart, and the tmux bar was a slightly different blue than the editor. I decided to keep one palette.

The palette lives in ~/dotfiles/theme/palette.sh as plain variables, such as `BG`, `FG`, `ACCENT` and the eight ANSI colors. A small script `theme-gen` reads it and writes two outputs: a Lua file for Neovim, and a tmux snippet that sets the status and pane border colors. The terminal profile was changed by hand from the same values, since the generator for it would be more work than the saving.

In Neovim I use the generated table to set the highlight groups on top of a base colorscheme, only for the groups I care about: normal text, comments, the cursor line, the visual selection and the diagnostics. Syntax colors still come from the base scheme.

A bug cost me some time. The tmux snippet used color names with a hash, and tmux read the hash line as a comment in one place, since I had put the value inside single quotes in the wrong spot. The status bar stayed black until I quoted it as `"#1e2030"`.

The result looks the same in all three places. Comment text was too dim in the terminal against the dark background, so I raised its brightness a little in the palette and regenerated the files.

The next step is a light variant. For this I need a second palette file and a switch, which I will do later.

summary: Wrote a bootstrap script that links the dotfiles into the home folder and installs the Brewfile, tested on a clean user account.
body:
Until now, setting up meant copying files by hand. I wrote `install.sh` in the dotfiles folder to do it in repeatable steps.

The script has four parts. First it checks for Homebrew and installs it if missing. Then it runs `brew bundle --file=Brewfile`. Third, it links the files: .zshrc, .gitconfig, .tmux.conf and the folders for nvim and git under ~/.config. Last, it prints a list of what it did.

The linking function is careful. When a target already exists and is not a link to the dotfiles, it moves the file to a `.bak` name before it creates the link, and it never overwrites an old .bak. Running the script twice makes no changes the second time, and the output says `already linked` for each entry.

To test, I created a new macOS user account and ran the script there. The first attempt failed because the account had no Xcode command line tools, and the Homebrew install stopped with a prompt that the script could not answer. I added a check with `xcode-select -p` and a clear message that tells me to run the install first.

The second run got through Homebrew but the bundle took 25 minutes, mostly from casks. The links were all correct, and zsh started without errors. The Neovim plugins installed on the first launch and the language servers followed after a `:MasonInstall` call, which I will automate later.

One mistake was that the script used `ln -s` with a relative path in one place, so a link pointed to a wrong location when I ran the script from another folder. I switched to absolute paths built from the script's own folder.

Still missing: the macOS defaults script, and the steps for the SSH setup. I will keep the notes in a README in the same folder.

summary: Wrote the macOS defaults script: Finder, Dock, keyboard repeat and screenshot settings, each as one `defaults write` line with a comment.
body:
I put the system settings I always change into ~/dotfiles/macos.sh so that a new machine gets them in one run.

Finder: show all file extensions, show the path bar and status bar, search in the current folder by default, and keep folders on top when sorting. Dock: auto-hide on, a short hide delay, no recent applications, and a smaller icon size of 42.

Keyboard: a key repeat of 2 and a delay of 15, which is faster than the slider allows in the settings app. I also turned off the press-and-hold accent popup with `ApplePressAndHoldEnabled` set to false so that holding j in Neovim repeats the key. Screenshots go to ~/Screenshots as PNG without the shadow.

At the end the script restarts Finder, Dock and SystemUIServer with `killall`, ignoring errors when a process is not running.

Testing went on the clean account again. Two settings did not take effect: the key repeat needs a logout before it works, and the Dock setting for recent applications was named differently from what I wrote, `show-recents`, not `show-recent-apps`. I fixed the name after reading the output of `defaults read com.apple.dock`.

Each line has a comment with what it does and the old value, in case I want to undo it. I also added a second script `macos-reset.sh` that is not complete but handles the Dock and Finder lines.

A question I had was whether to touch the trackpad settings. I left them out, since they differ between machines, and a wrong value there is annoying to find.

The install script now calls macos.sh at the end, but asks first. Next is the SSH part.

summary: Added fd and bat previews to the fzf setup in zsh, so that control-t shows file contents and alt-c shows a directory tree.
body:
The fzf key bindings worked but showed only names. I set `FZF_CTRL_T_OPTS` to use a preview command with bat, with a line-number style and a limit of 200 lines, so that large files do not slow the preview.

For alt-c I used `eza --tree --level=2` as the preview. I did not have eza, so I added it to the Brewfile and installed it.

I also changed the default command to `fd --type f --hidden --exclude .git`. With that, hidden files appear, and the .git folder does not clutter the list. The listing is much faster than the default find on a large folder, about 0.1 seconds against 1.5.

One bug: the preview broke with file names that contain spaces until I put `{}` in quotes in the command. A test with `my file.txt` showed the contents afterwards.

summary: Replaced the long list of shell aliases with a few functions, and removed three aliases that hid real commands and caused wrong results in scripts.
body:
Looking through .zshrc, I found about 40 aliases, and some were harmful. `alias rm='rm -i'` made scripts ask questions when they were sourced in an interactive shell, and `alias grep='grep --color=always'` put escape codes into piped output. I removed both and changed the grep one to `--color=auto`. The third was `alias ls='ls -G'`, which I replaced with eza and its icons turned off.

Some aliases were better as functions. `mkcd` creates a directory and moves into it, and `gco` is a function that runs fzf over local branches and checks out the chosen one. `take` was a duplicate of mkcd and was deleted.

I moved the aliases into ~/.zsh/aliases.zsh and the functions into ~/.zsh/functions.zsh, both sourced from .zshrc. It makes the main file about 60 lines shorter.

The shell start time did not change, still at about 70 ms.

One leftover: `alias please='sudo $(fc -ln -1)'` was kept, because I use it often. I checked each remaining alias with `type` to make sure that nothing points to a missing program.

summary: Added a light theme variant to the shared palette and a `theme` command that switches Neovim, tmux and the terminal in one step.
body:
The earlier palette work had only a dark scheme. I added palette-light.sh with the same variable names and different values, and I let theme-gen take the name of the palette as an argument.

The switch command `theme light` or `theme dark` does three things: it runs theme-gen with the right file, reloads tmux with `source-file`, and writes the name into ~/.config/theme-mode. Neovim reads that file at startup and also on the FocusGained event, so open editors follow the change after I click into them.

The terminal was the hard part. The profile cannot be changed from a script in a simple way, so I made two profiles by hand and used an escape sequence to switch the background and foreground colors on the running terminal. It works for the current window only. New windows open with the default profile, which is dark, so that has to be accepted for now.

I had a bug where tmux kept the old colors in its status bar because the generated snippet set the colors only when it was loaded the first time. I changed the file to use `set -g` without conditions, and a reload now works as expected.

The light scheme needed a darker comment color and a stronger cursor line, since the first values were almost invisible on white. I tuned them by looking at a TypeScript file and a Markdown file in each mode.

Not done: automatic switching when the system appearance changes. I might use a launch agent with a small Swift or osascript check later, but I am not sure it is worth the effort.

summary: Created a git hook setup with a global hooks folder: a pre-commit check for leftover debugger statements and large files over 2 MB.
body:
I set `core.hooksPath` to ~/.config/git/hooks so that the hooks work in every repository without copying files into each .git folder.

The first hook is pre-commit. It looks at the staged files with `git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM` and does two checks. The first greps for `debugger`, `console.log(` marked with a TODO and `breakpoint()` in the added lines only. The second stops files larger than 2 MB, since a binary went into a repository by accident last month and was a pain to remove.

Both checks print the file and the line, and the commit stops with a non-zero exit. I can skip with `--no-verify` when I really mean it.

A problem was that a global hooks path overrides the hooks of a project, for example the husky ones. A repository with its own pre-commit hook stopped running it. I solved this by letting my hook call `.git/hooks/pre-commit` at the end, if the file exists and is executable. It is simple, and it worked in the project that uses husky.

I tested the hook with three cases: a clean commit, a file with a debugger line, and a 5 MB file made with `mkfile`. All three behaved correctly.

The grep for debug lines gave a false positive in a markdown file that explains debugging, so I limited the check to code extensions: js, ts, tsx and py.

Next I want a commit-msg hook, but I will first see whether I need one.

summary: Wrote the first version of an rsync backup script for the documents and code folders, with a dry run mode and a log, tested against an external disk.
body:
Until now my backup was occasional copying in Finder. I wrote `backup.sh` in ~/bin that uses rsync to copy ~/Documents, ~/code and ~/Pictures to a folder on an external disk.

The main command uses `rsync -aH --delete --human-readable --stats` with an exclude file. The exclude list has node_modules, .venv, .cache, build outputs and `.DS_Store`. The size difference is large: ~/code is 48 GB with dependencies and about 6 GB without them.

The script first checks that the disk is mounted by testing for a marker file in the target folder. Without the check, a missing disk would make rsync write into a plain folder on the internal drive under /Volumes. I found that risk when I ran a test with the disk unplugged and the folder was created and filled. I deleted the stray 6 GB folder afterward.

There is a `--dry-run` flag that passes `-n` to rsync and prints what would change. I used it first and found that `--delete` would remove 300 files from the target that I had renamed locally, which is correct behaviour but good to see.

Each run writes a log into ~/Library/Logs/backup/ with a name that has a time stamp, and the script keeps only the last 30 logs. At the end it sends a macOS notification through osascript with the result and the number of transferred files.

The first full run took 41 minutes for about 90 GB. A second run, with only small changes, took 55 seconds.

What I want to add: snapshots with `--link-dest` so that old versions stay available, and a scheduled start. Right now `--delete` means a mistake on the source goes to the backup at once, which is a weakness I should not leave long.

summary: Added rotating snapshots to the backup script with rsync --link-dest, so each run is a full-looking folder that only stores changed files.
body:
The first backup version mirrored the source, so a deleted file was gone from the backup at the next run. I changed the script to write a new folder per run, named with the date and time, and to hard-link unchanged files to the previous snapshot through `--link-dest`.

A `latest` symlink points to the newest completed snapshot. The run first writes into a folder with the suffix `.partial` and renames it only when rsync exits with success, so a broken run never looks like a good one. The link-dest option reads from `latest`.

To check the space use, I ran two snapshots a few minutes apart with a few changed files. `du -sh` on both together was 52 GB, not 104, and the second folder alone counted as about 200 MB, since du counts the hard links only once.

Old snapshots are cleaned with a simple rule: keep all from the last 7 days, then one for each of the last 8 weeks. The function sorts the folder names and picks which to remove. I tested it on a folder of empty directories with made-up names before I trusted it on real data.

One thing I noticed was that macOS extended attributes made rsync see changes in files that had not changed. Adding `-E` did not help, and I left the default options with `--no-xattrs`, which avoided the false changes.

The next step is to run it on a schedule through launchd.

summary: Set up a launchd agent that runs the backup script every night at 02:30 and skips the run if the disk is not connected.
body:
I wrote ~/Library/LaunchAgents/local.backup.plist with a StartCalendarInterval for 02:30 each day, and loaded it with `launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u)`. Standard output and errors go into a log file in the logs folder, next to the logs of the script itself.

The agent calls backup.sh with the full path, since launchd has a minimal PATH and the first test failed with `rsync: command not found`. In that test, the Homebrew rsync was the one that I had installed for newer features, and it lives in /opt/homebrew/bin. I added the PATH to the EnvironmentVariables key in the plist.

The second issue was permissions. Run from launchd, rsync could not read ~/Documents and the log said `Operation not permitted`. In the privacy settings I gave full disk access to the rsync binary, and after that the run went through. I tested by starting the job on demand with `launchctl kickstart`.

When the disk is missing, the script now exits with code 0 and logs `disk not mounted, skipped`, instead of showing a failure notification each night when I travel. A notification only appears after three skipped nights in a row, using a small counter file.

The first scheduled run worked: the log showed 212 changed files and a duration of about 2 minutes. I will check again in a few days that the snapshots rotate as expected.

summary: Tested restoring a file and a whole folder from the newest backup snapshot, and found the restore steps worked but the log did not show which snapshot was used.
body:
After the launchd agent started running every night, I wanted to know that a restore really works, not only that the backup runs. I picked the external disk and looked at the snapshot folders made by the rsync --link-dest runs. Each one looks like a full copy of the documents and code folders.

First I restored a single file, an old notes file in the documents folder, with a plain cp from the newest snapshot. It came back with the same content and the same modification time. Then I restored the whole code folder into a temporary folder with rsync -a and compared it to the original with diff -rq. The only differences were node_modules and build folders, which the exclude list leaves out on purpose.

I also checked the disk use. Three snapshots of about 38 GB each took only 41 GB in total, which shows that the hard links work. Deleting the oldest snapshot freed just the files that no newer snapshot shared, as expected.

One gap showed up. The log says that a backup finished, but it does not say which snapshot folder it wrote, so I had to look at the folder names by hand. I added a line at the end of each run with the snapshot path and the number of changed files. I also wrote a short restore section in the backup script header with the two commands I used, so I do not have to work them out again when I need them.

Still open: a restore test for files with special permissions, and a check for what happens when the disk is unplugged during a run. The next step is the free space warning, since the disk will fill up over the coming months.

summary: Added a free space warning to the backup script that sends a macOS notification when the disk is under 15 percent free, and puts the same line in the log.
body:
This was the follow-up from the pruning change. The script now reads free space with df -k on the backup volume after each run and computes the percentage. If it is below 15, it writes a WARN line to the log and calls osascript to show a notification.

The first attempt used df -h and parsed the percent column, but that column shows the used share, and rounding made the check off by one. I switched to the kilobyte numbers and did the math in the shell. That gave the right value on the test disk, 62 percent free.

The notification did not appear when launchd ran the script, although it worked in the terminal. The launchd agent runs without a GUI session context for some commands, so osascript was silent. Using a plist key for the session type fixed it, with LimitLoadToSessionType set to Aqua. I reloaded the agent with launchctl bootout and bootstrap and forced a run to see it.

I also lowered the threshold temporarily to 90 to confirm the warning fires. It did, once, and the log line looked right. The threshold is back at 15. Nothing else is left on the backup script for now.

summary: Started the move from iTerm2 planning: listed what the iTerm2 profile does that matters, and found that only four settings are really used before trying Ghostty.
body:
I wanted to know what I would lose before moving to another terminal. I exported the iTerm2 profile as JSON and went through it by hand. Most of it is defaults. Four things matter in daily work.

First, the font and size, JetBrains Mono at 13 points with ligatures on. Second, the shared color palette, which is already in a shell file and a Lua table, so it can be reused. Third, the option key sends escape sequences, which Neovim and tmux bindings depend on. Fourth, the hotkey window that drops down with a global key.

The hotkey window is the only one without an obvious replacement. I noted that Ghostty has a quick terminal feature on macOS, but I have not checked how well it works with tmux. Other iTerm2 features I thought I used, like triggers and the profile switching by directory, turned out to be unused. I looked at the preferences history and saw I never touched them.

I also checked scroll back. iTerm2 keeps 10000 lines, but I use tmux history for that anyway. So the terminal itself only needs to be fast and render text well.

The next step is to install Ghostty through the Brewfile as a cask and write a minimal config file with these four settings. I will keep iTerm2 installed for a few weeks as a fallback. This entry is only the plan and the list, no config changed yet.

summary: Wrote a first Ghostty config with the font, palette and option key behavior, and ran it beside iTerm2 for a first test with tmux.
body:
I added the Ghostty cask to the Brewfile and installed it. The config lives in ~/.config/ghostty/config, and I linked it from the dotfiles folder through the bootstrap script, with one new line in the link list.

The config has the font family and size, the theme colors, macos-option-as-alt set to true, and a window padding of 8. The palette is generated from the shared palette file, so I added a small function to the theme command that writes a theme file for Ghostty as well. This keeps the light and dark switch working in one step.

A first test with tmux worked well. Colors matched Neovim exactly, which they did not always do in iTerm2 because of a profile color setting. True color works without any extra terminal override. Startup of a new window felt immediate.

One problem: the control-a prefix works, but the alt keys I use for the fzf directory jump printed odd characters until I set the option-as-alt value. After that it was fine.

I will use it for a day and see what else breaks.

summary: Used Ghostty for a full work session and found three problems: TERM value over SSH, the quick terminal key, and a clipboard setting that tmux needed.
body:
After the first test, I used Ghostty for everything this afternoon and wrote down what went wrong.

The first problem was SSH. Connecting to an older server printed 'unknown terminal type xterm-ghostty' and the screen was broken in vim. Ghostty sets its own TERM value, and the remote machine had no terminfo entry for it. I fixed it two ways: copied the terminfo with infocmp and tic for the servers that I use often, and added an ssh function in zsh that falls back to xterm-256color for hosts I have not prepared. The function is five lines.

The second was the quick terminal. I set the keybind to a global key with global: prefix, and macOS asked for accessibility permission. After allowing it, the drop down window works. It starts a new shell, not a tmux session, so I made it attach to a session named scratch with a command setting in the config.

The third was the clipboard. Copying in tmux copy mode did not reach the macOS clipboard. I added set-clipboard on in tmux.conf and allowed clipboard writes in Ghostty with the clipboard-write setting. After that, yank from Neovim inside tmux also reaches the system clipboard.

I also checked the memory use. Ghostty sits at about 80 MB with three windows, and iTerm2 had been at around 400 MB.

Remaining: the old iTerm2 settings I still want to compare are the bell and the tab titles. I will look at those over the next days. I also have to put the terminfo steps into the bootstrap notes so a new Mac does not hit this again.

summary: Set up tab titles and bell behavior in Ghostty so the tab shows the current tmux session and directory, and a finished long command makes a quiet sound.
body:
Two things from the iTerm2 list were left: tab titles and the bell. For titles, tmux has set-titles on and a set-titles-string of the session name and the current path. Ghostty shows that text in the tab and in the window title. I used #S and #{b:pane_current_path} to keep it short.

For the bell, I did not want a sound for every bell character, since Neovim triggers it on some errors. I set bell-features to attention only, so the Dock icon bounces once when something rings in a background window. That is enough.

I also wanted a notice when a long command ends. I wrote a small zsh hook that records the start time in preexec and in precmd checks the elapsed time. If it was more than 30 seconds, it prints a bell character. With the bell feature this makes the Dock bounce when a build finishes in another window.

I tested with sleep 35. The Dock bounced after it ended. With sleep 5 nothing happened, as intended.

The hook adds no measurable time to the prompt. I checked with zsh's zprof and it was below 1 ms.

summary: Removed iTerm2 from the Brewfile and the bootstrap script after two weeks of using only Ghostty, and kept an exported profile in an archive folder.
body:
Two weeks have passed with only Ghostty in use. I did not open iTerm2 once, which I checked with the app's last opened date in Finder.

I removed the iTerm2 cask line from the Brewfile and deleted the steps in the bootstrap script that restored its preferences. The macOS defaults script had one line for the iTerm2 prompt on quit, which I removed too.

The exported JSON profile went into an archive folder inside the dotfiles, with a short README saying it is only for reference. I do not link it anywhere.

Then I uninstalled the app with brew uninstall --cask iterm2 and removed the preferences plist. A quick run of the bootstrap script in the clean user account from before showed no errors, and Ghostty came up with the right font and colors.

The move is done. The only open item is the terminfo note for older servers.

summary: Wrote the terminfo steps for older servers into the bootstrap notes and added a helper script that copies the Ghostty entry to a host with one command.
body:
This closes the open item from the Ghostty move. I wrote a short script called sync-terminfo in the bin folder. It takes a host name, runs infocmp -x xterm-ghostty locally and pipes the result to ssh host tic -x - on the remote side.

I tested it on two servers. The first accepted it right away. On the second the home folder had no .terminfo directory, but tic created it. After that, vim and htop looked normal in Ghostty over SSH.

The zsh ssh function stays as a fallback for hosts that I do not control, where I cannot install anything. I added a comment above it that points to the helper.

The bootstrap notes now have a short section on this with the one command and the error message to look for.

summary: Replaced nvm with mise for Node: measured the shell start cost of nvm at 280 ms, installed mise, and moved the global Node and the project versions over.
body:
The shell start had crept up again, and the profile showed nvm as the cause. With zprof, sourcing nvm.sh took about 280 ms of a 420 ms start. I had tried lazy loading before, but it broke the node path for scripts, so I decided to replace it.

I added mise to the Brewfile and put eval "$(mise activate zsh)" in .zshrc. First I listed all the Node versions that I use: 18, 20 and 22. I looked through the code folder for .nvmrc files and found 14 of them. Mise reads these through the idiomatic version file setting, which I enabled with mise settings add idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools node.

Then I installed the three versions with mise install node@18 node@20 node@22 and set 22 as the global default in ~/.config/mise/config.toml. A check with mise ls showed all three and which project directories pointed at them.

Two things did not work at first. Global npm packages from nvm, like typescript-language-server and prettier, were gone since each version has its own folder. I reinstalled them with npm for the global version. And the Neovim LSP could not find node when started from the Dock, because mise only changes the path in shells. For that I added the mise shims folder to the path in .zprofile as well.

The shell start is now 140 ms in total. Mise activation itself costs about 12 ms. Opening a project with an .nvmrc switches versions at the prompt without delay.

I have not removed nvm yet. I want to run for a week and see if some script still calls it. After that I will delete the nvm folder and its lines in the dotfiles.

summary: Moved Python from pyenv to mise as well, and found that old virtualenvs broke because they pointed at the removed pyenv interpreters, so I rebuilt five of them.
body:
With Node working in mise, I did the same for Python. The goal was one tool for both and to drop pyenv from the shell start, which cost about 60 ms.

I installed Python 3.11 and 3.12 with mise and set 3.12 as the global one. Then I removed the pyenv init line from .zshrc. The first problem showed up right away: several project virtualenvs had a python symlink that pointed into ~/.pyenv/versions, and the shell reported 'bad interpreter: No such file or directory' when I ran their scripts.

I did not delete pyenv yet, so I checked which environments were affected. A small loop over the code folder looking for .venv/bin/python and testing it with readlink found five broken ones. Instead of fixing links by hand, I recreated them with python -m venv and reinstalled the packages from requirements files. Two projects had no pinned requirements, so I used pip freeze from the old environment before deleting it. That worked since the old interpreter still existed.

For new projects I switched to the uv tool for virtual environments, because it creates them quickly and uses whichever Python mise provides. I added uv to the Brewfile. A test project went from creating the environment to installed dependencies in 3 seconds instead of 25.

Black, which conform.nvim uses in Neovim, came from a pyenv global package. I moved it to a mise-managed tool with mise use -g pipx:black, and updated the conform config to find it on the path. Format on save in a Python file worked after a restart.

The shell start now measures 110 ms. Next I will remove pyenv and nvm from the Brewfile and the dotfiles once the week of testing is over. I also need to update the bootstrap script so a new Mac gets the versions from the mise config.

summary: Removed nvm and pyenv completely from the dotfiles and the machine, after a week without a single script needing them, and updated bootstrap to run mise install.
body:
The testing week is over. I searched all the dotfiles, the bin folder and the code folder for nvm and pyenv. The only hits were in two old README files and a CI note in a project, which I left alone since they are not about my machine.

From the dotfiles, I deleted the nvm block in .zshrc, which was the lazy loading function from before, and the pyenv lines in .zprofile. The Brewfile lost pyenv and pyenv-virtualenv. Then I removed the folders: rm -rf ~/.nvm and brew uninstall pyenv pyenv-virtualenv, then ~/.pyenv. That freed about 2.1 GB, mostly old Python builds.

The bootstrap script got a new step after brew bundle: mise install, which reads the global config. I put the global config file into the dotfiles folder and linked it. The tool list in it has node 22, node 20, node 18, python 3.12, python 3.11 and the black tool.

To check, I ran bootstrap in the clean test account. It took 6 minutes in total, of which Node and Python compile and download were 3. Afterwards node -v, python --version and black --version all gave the expected values in a new shell.

One warning appeared: mise said the config file was not trusted. I added mise trust to the bootstrap for the global file only.

Shell start is stable at 105 ms. The version manager move is finished.

summary: Installed Zed and tried an editor keymap that follows my Neovim keys, with vim mode and leader bindings for file search, buffers and the terminal panel.
body:
I wanted Zed available for work where a graphical editor is easier, such as reading a large diff or sharing the screen, and I wanted the muscle memory to carry over. I added the Zed cask to the Brewfile and created settings.json and keymap.json in the dotfiles, linked to ~/.config/zed.

Vim mode is on in settings with vim_mode true. For the leader I used space, as in Neovim. In keymap.json, the bindings are scoped to the context Editor && vim_mode == normal. I mapped space f f to the file finder, space f g to project search, space b b to the buffer switcher, and space e to the project panel toggle.

The Neovim keys for LSP also exist in Zed: gd for definition, gr for references, and K for hover already work in vim mode. Space r n for rename needed an explicit binding, which I added. Space c a for code actions too.

Some things do not match. Zed has no equivalent of my gitsigns hunk keys, though it has its own git panel and hunk navigation. I mapped ]h and [h to the next and previous hunk and that is close enough. The quick fix list does not exist the same way, and I will not try to imitate it.

The theme is the same shared palette. Zed themes are JSON, so I generate one from the palette file through the same theme command. The light and dark switch updates it, though Zed needs the theme name set in settings to follow it.

Format on save with prettier and black works through Zed's external formatter settings. I set the font to the same as the terminal, JetBrains Mono at 13, to avoid a visual jump.

I will use Zed this week for reading code and see which bindings I miss.

summary: Fixed the Zed theme switching so the light and dark change follows the shared theme command, by writing the theme name into settings.json with jq.
body:
After the first Zed setup, the theme command updated the theme file but Zed kept showing the old colors until I changed the name in settings by hand. That was a loose end.

The settings.json in Zed is plain JSON with comments allowed, which breaks jq when comments exist. I removed my own comments from the file and moved the notes to a README next to it.

The theme command now runs jq to set the theme key to either Palette Dark or Palette Light and writes to a temporary file, then moves it into place. Zed watches the settings file and reloads without restart, so the change shows up within a second.

I tested switching back and forth five times. Neovim, tmux, Ghostty and Zed all changed together. The slowest part was Neovim, which needs a signal to reload colors, at about 200 ms.

Done for now.

summary: Added the Zed tasks and a terminal key so tests run from the editor, and decided which work stays in Neovim and which goes to Zed.
body:
After a week with both editors, I settled on a split. Neovim stays for anything in a terminal, quick edits over SSH and long work with tmux panes. Zed is for reading large changes, browsing unfamiliar code, and when I need a window next to a browser.

To make Zed more useful I added tasks in tasks.json. One runs the test command for the current project through npm test, one runs pytest for the current file with the $ZED_FILE variable, and one starts the dev server. I bound space t t to the task spawn picker and space t r to rerun the last task.

The terminal panel in Zed opens with control-backtick. I mapped space t p to toggle it instead, so it matches my Neovim terminal key. The terminal inside Zed uses the same zsh and mise, so Node versions follow the project folder. I checked this in a project with Node 18 and node -v printed 18.

One issue was that Zed started from the Dock did not have my mise shims on the path, and its language servers failed with 'node not found'. The .zprofile entry from the Neovim fix helped here too, and after logging out and in the language server started.

I wrote the split into a short note in the dotfiles README so I remember why both exist.

summary: Created a first 1Password SSH agent setup: keys moved into the vault, the agent socket set in ssh config, and git over SSH tested against two hosts.
body:
The SSH keys had been lying in ~/.ssh as files with passphrases stored in the macOS keychain. I wanted them in 1Password so they are backed up and need a fingerprint to use.

First I turned on the SSH agent in the 1Password developer settings. Then I imported the keys. For each one I created an SSH key item by importing the private key file. There were three keys: one for my git host, one for a personal server and one old one for a work machine. The old one I did not import, since it is no longer used.

The socket path is under ~/Library/Group Containers/..., which is long, so I made a symlink at ~/.1password/agent.sock. In ~/.ssh/config I put a Host * block with IdentityAgent pointing to the symlink. I did not set IdentitiesOnly yet, which turned out to be a mistake.

When connecting to the git host, ssh offered all keys in order, and the server rejected the connection with 'Too many authentication failures' after four attempts. The fix was to add IdentitiesOnly yes and give each host an IdentityFile with the public key only. The agent then picks the matching private key. The public key files I exported from 1Password into ~/.ssh/keys.

Tests: ssh -T to the git host returned the greeting with my user name after a fingerprint prompt, and a git pull in a test repo worked. The personal server login also worked. In both cases the authorization prompt appears once and is remembered for a short time.

The bootstrap script cannot do this part automatically, since it needs the app and a sign in. I wrote it as a manual checklist in the notes. Next I want to look at signing commits with the same key, but that is a separate step.

I also removed the keychain lines from ssh config, UseKeychain and AddKeysToAgent, which no longer apply. The old private key files stay in a backup folder until I am sure all works for some weeks.

summary: Checked that the nightly backup does not copy the old private keys and the Library folder of 1Password, and added both to the exclude list.
body:
With the keys moved, I realized that the backup script still copies the code and documents folders and that a loose key file could end up in a snapshot. I looked at the exclude file used by rsync and added entries for .ssh/*, which is not in those folders anyway, but also for any file ending in .pem or id_ed25519 anywhere.

I also searched the documents folder for private key files with grep -rl 'BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY'. Two old copies turned up in a folder named old-laptop. I moved them out to the temporary backup folder that I mentioned and will delete later.

A dry run with rsync -n and --list-only after the change showed that no key pattern matches remained. The log of last night's run had 14 MB of new files, so nothing odd.

The exclude list is now 11 lines, each with a comment.

summary: Set up git commit signing with the SSH key from 1Password, so commits are signed without GPG, and found that verification needed an allowed signers file.
body:
The next step after the agent was to sign commits with the same key. I set gpg.format to ssh in ~/.gitconfig, user.signingkey to the public key text of the git host key, and commit.gpgsign to true. The program for signing is the op-ssh-sign helper that ships with 1Password, set with gpg.ssh.program to the path inside the app bundle.

A first commit worked and asked for the fingerprint. But git log --show-signature printed 'error: gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile needs to be configured and exist for ssh signature verification'. Signing worked but verification did not. I created ~/.config/git/allowed_signers with one line: my email, then the key type and the public key. Then I set gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile to this path. After that the log showed 'Good git signature for' with my email.

The git host also needs the key registered as a signing key, which is separate from the authentication key in its settings. I added it there, and the commits in a test branch showed a verified badge.

Three edge cases came up. The first was the pre-commit hook from the global hooks folder; it runs before signing, so there was no change. The second was rebases: each rewritten commit asks for the fingerprint, which is annoying for a rebase of 20 commits. The 1Password setting to remember approval for the session helps, and I set it to until the app locks. The third was that signing failed when 1Password was locked, with the message 'failed to write commit object'. That is clear enough once I know it.

The repository-specific config for work projects uses a different email. I made an includeIf block for the work folder with its own email and the same key, so the signature matches the committer address. A test commit there verified fine.

I also updated the notes with a short checklist for a new Mac: sign in, enable the agent, export public keys, run bootstrap. The old GPG key still exists but is no longer referenced anywhere, and I will revoke it later.

summary: Rebased a branch of 22 commits with signing on, which asked for a fingerprint each time, so I changed the 1Password approval to cover the session and wrote a small alias for unsigned fixups.
body:
The rebase problem I noted this morning was real. An interactive rebase of 22 commits in a project asked for approval at each commit, which means 22 prompts. I did not want to go back to unsigned commits.

The first thing I tried was the 1Password setting for the SSH agent authorization, from 'for each use' to 'until 1Password locks'. It worked: one prompt at the start and none after. I kept it, since the app locks after a few minutes of no use and when the Mac sleeps.

The second thing was fixup commits. When I use git commit --fixup and then autosquash, the temporary fixup commits are signed too, though they disappear after the squash. With the session approval this causes no prompts, so it is not a problem any more. Still, I added an alias called wip that commits with --no-gpg-sign for throwaway commits that I know will be squashed.

The third thing was to check that rebased commits keep a valid signature. Rebase creates new commits, and git signs them again with the current key when commit.gpgsign is true. I checked with git log --show-signature on the rebased branch and all 22 showed a good signature.

One more issue: the safe force-push alias from the first set of aliases uses --force-with-lease. It still works the same with signed commits, but I noticed its output was too quiet. I added a line that prints the old and new head hashes after the push.

I ran the rebase on the real branch again, and it finished in about 8 seconds including the single prompt.

summary: Went through the Zed keymap after a week of daily use, fixed four key clashes with macOS and tmux, and wrote down which Neovim keys are still missing in Zed.
body:
After a week of working mostly in Zed, I collected the keys that did not do what my hands expected. I went through keymap.json one binding at a time and tested each in a real project. Four of them needed a change.

The first clash was control-a, my tmux prefix. In the Zed terminal panel it went to the editor for a moment, so the prefix did not always reach tmux. I added a binding in the Terminal context that passes control-a straight through. The second was the leader key followed by w for window moves. It overlapped with a default pane command, so I removed the default for that context.

The third problem was alt-based keys. Zed reads the option key as a modifier, but the macOS keyboard layout turned some of them into special characters. I changed two bindings from alt to control-leader combinations. The fourth was a missing escape in the file finder, where escape closed the whole panel instead of only leaving insert mode in the search field. A context rule fixed it.

I then made a list of what Neovim still does better. Missing in Zed:
- the gitsigns hunk keys, since Zed has only partial hunk actions
- my LuaSnip snippets for TypeScript tests
- the project-wide search and replace with a preview

I copied the snippets into Zed's snippet format for TypeScript, which took about ten minutes and worked on the first try. The hunk keys I mapped to the nearest Zed actions, and they cover roughly two thirds of what I used.

The keymap file now has comments that group the bindings by purpose. I also copied it into the dotfiles folder and linked it from the bootstrap script, so a new machine gets the same keys. Next I want to see whether the search and replace gap is big enough to send that work back to Neovim.

summary: Looked into why the tmux session switcher popup was slow, found it ran fzf on a list built by a slow loop over directories, and cut the time from 900 ms to 90 ms.
body:
The session switcher I wrote early on had become slow to open. Pressing the key took nearly a second before the list showed up, which felt wrong for a popup.

I timed the script with time and then the parts separately. The fzf part was fast. The list was the problem: a shell loop went through every folder in the code directory, ran git rev-parse in each to see if it was a repository, and printed the name. With about 140 folders, that is 140 git calls.

The replacement uses fd to find .git entries with a max depth of 2 and prints their parent folders, which takes one process. I used fd -H -t d '^.git$' --max-depth 2 and stripped the suffix with sed. The result is the same list of projects. I also added the existing tmux sessions at the top of the list, marked with a star, so switching to a running session is the first choice.

A second small cost was that the script started a new zsh login shell through the popup command, which loaded .zshrc. I changed the tmux binding to call the script with sh directly, since it does not need my aliases. That saved another 60 ms.

The measurements after the change: 90 ms from the key to the visible list, compared with 900 ms before. I tried it ten times in a row and the time was stable.

One bug I introduced: folders with spaces in their name broke because the sed output was not quoted. I fixed it by using null-separated output with fd -0 and fzf --read0. Tested with a folder named 'test space' and the session was created with the right name, though tmux replaces dots and colons in names, so I also translate those to underscores.

No further change is planned. The switcher is now fast enough that I use it more than before.

summary: Reviewed the Brewfile against what is installed, removed 11 unused formulae and casks, and added a weekly list of leaves that are not in the file.
body:
It has been a while since the last Brewfile review. I ran brew bundle cleanup without --force to list what is installed but not in the file, and brew leaves to compare with the file from the other side.

The cleanup listed 9 formulae that I had installed for one-off tasks, like an image tool and two language servers I no longer use. I removed them with brew uninstall. Two casks were unused as well, a screen recorder and a markdown viewer. I checked the last used date of both apps in Finder, which was more than 6 months ago, and removed them.

In the other direction, 5 things in the file are no longer installed on the machine or were replaced, like the nvm formula's leftovers and a duplicate entry for the same tool listed as a tap and as a core formula. I deleted those lines. The file went from 71 entries to 60 net.

To catch drift in the future, I wrote a short function called brewdrift. It prints the output of brew bundle cleanup and brew leaves entries not in the Brewfile, so I can decide whether to add or remove them. I do not run it automatically, since an automatic cleanup could remove something I installed for a project.

I also checked brew bundle check, which exited 0, so everything in the file is installed.

The disk space freed was about 1.4 GB. The test of the bootstrap script in the clean account is still pending, and I will do it after the next larger change.

summary: Fixed the macOS defaults script so the key repeat setting survives a restart, by writing it with the right domain and logging out, instead of only at the first run.
body:
The fast key repeat from the defaults script was back to normal after a restart. I checked what the script wrote: defaults write NSGlobalDomain KeyRepeat -int 2 and InitialKeyRepeat -int 15. The values were in the plist, but the setting only applies after logging out, and the System Settings slider showed the old value, which seems to overwrite it when the pane is opened.

I read the plist with defaults read -g KeyRepeat and found 6, so something had overwritten it. The likely cause is that I moved the slider once in System Settings. Values of 2 and 15 are below the slider's range, so the pane replaces them when it saves.

The fix was a note in the script and a reminder not to touch the slider. I also added ApplePressAndHoldEnabled false, which I had set by hand before and not in the script, so that holding a key repeats it instead of showing accents. Then I logged out and in, and the values stayed.

I ran the whole defaults script a second time to see that it is idempotent, and it was. Each line only writes values. The Dock and Finder restarts at the end took a few seconds.

summary: Set up a second machine test of the whole setup: ran bootstrap on a fresh macOS user and fixed five problems from the new tools, so the scripts now run through without manual steps except 1Password.
body:
Since many parts have changed since the first bootstrap test, I created a new clean macOS user account and ran the whole setup there. The goal was to find everything that breaks when starting from nothing. I wrote down each failure in order.

First, bootstrap stopped at the Ghostty link because the ~/.config folder did not exist yet in the new account. The link step now runs mkdir -p for the parent folder of every target. Second, mise install failed with 'config file not trusted', although I had added the trust command. The trust call ran before the config link existed. I moved it after the links.

Third, the Zed settings link worked, but Zed was not yet installed when the theme command ran at the end, so jq failed on a missing file. The theme step now skips Zed if the settings file is not found, and prints a note. Fourth, the terminfo helper was not on the path since the bin folder is added by .zshrc, and bootstrap runs under bash. I call it with its full path now.

Fifth, the launchd agents for the backup and for linkcheck were copied but not loaded. I added launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) for each plist at the end of the script. The backup agent skips its run when the external disk is not connected, which is right for this test account.

After these fixes, I ran the script on a fresh account a second time. The total time was 9 minutes, of which the Homebrew downloads were about 5. Then linkcheck reported OK for all links, and a new Ghostty window showed the right font and colors. Neovim started in 45 ms and installed its plugins on the first run without errors.

The manual steps that remain are only signing in to 1Password and enabling its SSH agent, plus allowing accessibility for the Ghostty quick terminal. Both are in the notes as a checklist of five lines.

One thing I did not solve is the Xcode command line tools prompt, which opens a GUI dialog at the start of brew. I added a check with xcode-select -p and a message that tells to run the install and then start bootstrap again.

I deleted the test account afterwards. Next time I will repeat this after any change to bootstrap, not only after big changes.

summary: Ran the full bootstrap again on the fresh macOS test user and confirmed the five fixes from earlier hold, leaving only the 1Password step manual.
body:
This was the second pass over the fresh macOS user, started right after the first run found five problems. I deleted the test user's home folder, created it again and ran bootstrap from the beginning with nothing cached.

Homebrew installed first and the Brewfile ran through in about 11 minutes. The earlier failure with the Ghostty cask was gone, because bootstrap now taps the right source before the bundle step. mise install picked up the global Node and Python versions without a prompt after I added the trust command for the global config.

The zsh setup linked correctly and the prompt showed on the first new shell. I checked git config next. The signing settings are present, but the allowed signers file is only created when the 1Password agent is running, so signing fails quietly until the app is set up. That is the one manual step left, and I added a line about it at the top of the bootstrap output.

The macOS defaults script ran with no errors. The key repeat values were still there after I logged out and back in, which was the point of the fix from this morning. Dock and Finder settings applied as well.

I also timed the whole run: 19 minutes, of which downloads were most. I compared installed packages between the test user and my own account with brew leaves and found two differences, both tools I installed by hand and never added to the Brewfile. I added them.

Next I want to repeat this on the real new machine later and keep a short checklist of the manual parts. For now the scripts are in a good state and I stopped here. The test user stays on the machine for later runs.

summary: Wrote a short checklist for the manual parts of a new Mac setup and linked it from the bootstrap script, so the 1Password step is not forgotten.
body:
After the clean run this morning I wanted the manual steps written down in one place instead of living in my head. I created SETUP.md in the dotfiles folder with five items: sign in to 1Password, turn on the SSH agent in its settings, grant Ghostty and the terminal full disk access for the backup, connect the backup disk, and run the signers file helper.

The bootstrap script now prints the file path in its last lines, so the list shows up exactly when I need it. I considered making the script wait for 1Password and continue by itself, but the app has no reliable way to tell a script that the agent is ready, so I dropped it.

I wrote the helper for the allowed signers file as a small script that reads the public key from the agent with ssh-add -L and writes the file with my email in front. It exits with a clear message if the agent has no keys. I tested it with the agent on and off on the test user, and both paths gave the right result.

One more thing I found was that full disk access for the launchd backup job cannot be granted by a script at all, because macOS asks the user. I put it in the checklist with the exact settings path. Tomorrow nothing is planned here; the setup work is closed for now.

summary: Cut the zsh start from 190 ms to 85 ms by loading completions lazily and caching the output of the mise activation instead of running it on each start.
body:
The shell had started to feel slower than before, so I measured it with zsh -i -c exit in a loop of twenty runs. The average was 190 ms, which is not terrible but clearly more than the 60 ms I had after the move to mise.

I turned on zprof at the top of .zshrc and read the output. Two things were at the top. The first was compinit, which rebuilt its dump on every start because the dump file was older than the check allowed. The second was mise activate, which cost about 40 ms because it runs a subprocess each time.

For compinit I changed the call to check the dump only once a day, using the glob qualifier on the dump file, and to use the cached dump otherwise. That alone saved about 70 ms. For mise I tried the shims approach first, but it made the Node version in tmux panes wrong in one test, so I dropped it. Instead I kept activate but moved it behind a cache file: the output of mise activate zsh is written to a file when the mise binary changes, and the shell sources the file.

After both changes the average is 85 ms over twenty runs. I checked that cd into a project with its own Node version still switches correctly, and that tab completion for git and brew works. The cache file is rebuilt by a small function that compares the binary's modification time, and I added it to the bootstrap notes. I will measure again in a month.

summary: Added a Ghostty key binding for a split layout and checked that it does not collide with the tmux prefix.
body:
I wanted the quick two-pane layout available without going through tmux when I just open a plain window. I added two keybind lines in the Ghostty config for splitting right and down with command-d and command-shift-d.

Before keeping them I checked the tmux prefix, control-a, and the pane bindings in the tmux config. There was no overlap, because Ghostty handles command combinations itself and tmux only sees control and meta keys. I also confirmed with the key debug option that the combinations reach Ghostty and not the shell.

One small issue came up: the new splits opened in the home folder instead of the current directory. The Ghostty setting window-inherit-working-directory was off in my config, so I turned it on. The splits now follow the directory of the focused pane.

I tested it with three splits and closing them in a different order, and nothing odd happened. The config reloads with the reload key, so no restart was needed.

summary: Replaced the Neovim plugin manager config with a lockfile based setup and pinned all plugins, after an update broke the completion popup.
body:
This week an update of one completion plugin changed its default mapping and the popup stopped accepting tab. I lost about twenty minutes finding which plugin it was, because the manager had updated everything at once with no record of the previous versions.

I moved the config to lazy.nvim style loading with a lockfile that lives in the dotfiles folder, so every plugin has a commit pinned. Converting meant rewriting the plugin list into one table per plugin file, with the event or command that loads it. There were 27 plugins, and I moved them in groups of five and started Neovim after each group to catch errors early.

Startup time went from 120 ms to 48 ms, measured with --startuptime, mostly because the git and Treesitter helpers now load on file open and not at start. I restored the old completion version from the lockfile history to test the rollback, and it worked with one command.

Two plugins needed a manual fix. The file tree plugin required its setup call before a keymap that I had placed earlier, and the statusline plugin read a global that the new loader sets later. I fixed both with a small change in the order.

The lockfile is now committed with the config. The plan is to update plugins on purpose, once a week, and read the changelog of anything that touches mappings.

summary: Wrote a weekly update script for Neovim plugins that shows the lockfile diff and keeps the old lockfile as a backup before changing anything.
body:
Following the pinned plugins from two days ago, I wanted updates to be a routine and not a surprise. I wrote update-nvim in the scripts folder.

The script copies the current lockfile to a dated backup name in the archive folder, runs the headless plugin sync, and then prints the diff of the lockfile as a list of plugin names with old and new short hashes. If nothing changed, it says so and removes the backup.

I tried it for real and it updated six plugins. The diff made it easy to see that the Treesitter parser plugin was among them, so I opened Neovim and ran the health check afterwards. It reported one warning about a missing parser for a markup language that I do not use, which I ignored.

The rollback is one more command that restores the newest backup and syncs again, and I tested it once. I added a line about the script to the notes. Later I might run it from a reminder, but a manual run is fine for now.

summary: Set up tmux session restore with a small script of my own after the resurrect plugin restored panes in the wrong directories, and it now brings back layouts reliably.
body:
After a restart of the Mac last week, the resurrect plugin brought back my tmux sessions but half the panes opened in the home folder and one session lost its window names. I decided to look at what the plugin really stores before trying other plugins.

Its save files are plain text with one line per pane, including the directory, so the problem was not the saving. The restore step ran the pane start command before the directory was set when the shell took longer to start. That was a timing issue linked to my slow shell start from earlier in the month, which is better now but still a few hundred milliseconds in a new pane.

I wrote a small script, tmux-restore, which reads the same save file and creates sessions and windows with new-session and new-window using the -c option for the directory. This avoids the timing problem, because the directory is part of the creation call. Pane layouts are applied at the end with select-layout using the saved layout string.

I tested with a setup of four sessions, the biggest having three windows with splits. After a forced kill of the tmux server, the script restored everything with the right directories and names in about a second. Programs that were running are not restarted, which is what I want, apart from Neovim where I reopen the last file by hand.

A save happens every ten minutes through a tmux hook and a launchd-free approach: the status line interval runs the save script. I confirmed that it does not slow the status line, since the script exits in under 30 ms.

Remaining: I left the old plugin installed but disabled, and I will remove it after a week if the script holds up.

summary: Reworked the git aliases and config into an included file layout, with work and personal identities chosen by folder, and tested that commits carry the right email.
body:
I had a single gitconfig with my personal email and a habit of fixing the author by hand in work repositories. Twice that month a commit went out with the wrong address, so I wanted the choice to happen by folder.

The new layout has a small main gitconfig with the shared settings: aliases, pull behavior, the signing setup, the default branch name and the diff tool. At the bottom are two includeIf blocks using gitdir conditions, one for the code folder of personal projects and one for the work folder. Each included file sets user.email and the signing key reference. The work file also changes the default push behavior to be more careful.

I tested it with four repositories: two personal, one in the work folder and one in a temporary folder outside both. I ran git config user.email in each and then made a test commit and looked at the author line. All four were right, and the outside folder fell back to the personal address, which is what I decided on.

A detail that took some time was the trailing slash in the gitdir pattern. Without it the condition did not match subfolders of the work folder, and the commit in a nested repository took the personal address. With the slash and the case-insensitive variant gitdir/i the match works on the Mac file system.

I also cleaned up the aliases that were left. Two were duplicates of what the shell functions now do, so I deleted them. I kept the log alias with the graph and the one that shows the last commit stat.

Signing works in both identities, since both use the same SSH key from the agent. The allowed signers file has both email addresses now, and git log --show-signature shows good signatures for the test commits.

I added a check to the pre-commit hook setup: it warns if the author email is not one of the two known addresses. I tested the warning by setting a third address in a temporary repository. The list of known addresses is a single line in the hooks folder, so a change is easy.

The notes for bootstrap now describe the folder layout, because the includeIf paths depend on it.

summary: Found why Neovim's clipboard was empty over SSH sessions in tmux and fixed it with OSC 52 on both sides, so yanks from remote files land in the Mac clipboard.
body:
When I edited a file on a server inside tmux, yanking text in Neovim did nothing for the Mac clipboard. I could paste inside the same Neovim, but not in other apps. This had been annoying for a while and I finally sat down with it.

The path has four parts: Neovim on the server, tmux on the server, the SSH connection and Ghostty on the Mac. Ghostty supports the OSC 52 escape sequence for clipboard writes, so the idea was to make the other three pass it through. I tested the sequence by hand first with printf in a plain SSH shell, and the Mac clipboard did receive the text. So the terminal and SSH were fine.

Inside tmux the same printf failed. The cause was the tmux option set-clipboard, which was off on the server because that tmux config was an old copy.
