I wrote a one-time script that removes duplicates, keeping the latest occurrence, and drops commands shorter than three characters and lines that look like they contain tokens or passwords. The check for tokens used a pattern for long random strings and for the words key, token and secret next to an equals sign. It removed 212 lines, which I looked through by hand before accepting.

The file went from 60,000 to about 21,000 lines. I kept a copy of the original in the backup folder.

Then I set up the zsh options: hist_ignore_all_dups, hist_ignore_space, share_history and extended_history for timestamps. The size was set to 50,000 in memory and on disk. Commands starting with a space are now never stored, which is handy for one-offs with secrets.

For the search, the fzf widget on control-r was already installed through Homebrew, but the shell integration was not loaded. I enabled it and set the options to show a preview of the full command in a small window and to sort by recency, not by match score only.

I compared this with the database tool by reading its documentation and installing it on the test user. It offers per-directory filtering and exit codes in the search, which is useful. The cost is a separate database file, a background process for sync, and another thing to restore after a backup drill. For one machine the benefit is small.

I timed the shell start with fzf integration. It added 4 ms, which is fine against the 60 ms total, and the history load is about the same as before.

To get the directory filter anyway, I added a second binding, control-g, that runs the fzf search on history filtered to commands whose recorded directory matches. zsh does not store the directory, so that does not work without extra data. I dropped this idea and noted why.

I used the new search for the rest of the day and found three old commands I had been retyping for months. The decision is to keep fzf and not add the database tool. The history cleanup script is stored in the scripts folder in case I need it again.

summary: Added a tmux binding to copy the last command output through fzf, tested it with long outputs and fixed a problem with wide characters in the popup.
body:
I often copy the output of the previous command with the mouse, which is slow in tmux. I wanted a key that lets me pick lines from the pane and send them to the clipboard.

The binding opens a popup with the pane content captured by capture-pane, with the last 2,000 lines, and runs fzf in multi-select mode. The selected lines go to pbcopy. I bound it to the prefix key followed by y.

The first version broke with wide characters. Lines with box-drawing symbols from the prompt and with some CJK file names were cut in the middle of a character, because the popup width was smaller than the pane. I set the popup to 90 percent of the width and added the no-wrap option of fzf.

A second issue was the prompt lines being included, which cluttered the list. I added a filter that removes lines containing the prompt marker, using the same character that the prompt always prints.

I tested with a 5,000-line output from a test run. It captured only the last 2,000 lines as intended, which is enough in practice. The popup opened in about 80 ms.

The binding was documented in the tmux config comments next to the other bindings of the last set. It does not clash with any existing key.

summary: Reviewed what mise manages after two months, removed two unused Python versions and pinned the global Node to the current LTS line, with the project check showing no conflicts left.
body:
This was a routine look at mise, two months after the move from nvm. I ran mise ls to see all installed tools and versions.

Two Python versions had no project using them according to the project check script. I removed both with mise uninstall and freed about 900 MB. The check then reported all projects matched their version files.

The global Node was set to latest, which changed under me during an update last week and printed a warning in one project. I pinned it to the current LTS line, so a new major version will not arrive by itself. The projects keep their own version files.

I also checked the mise shims situation. The shell uses the activate hook, but Zed starts language servers without the shell environment. A Node-based server had failed once in the past because of this. I verified that Zed picks the tools from the project's folder through mise's own environment in its settings, which works at the moment.

The two projects that had conflicting version files in the first check were fixed back then, and the check still shows nothing for them.

I added the mise listing to the drift script as a short count of tools not covered by a version file. It shows one: a global CLI tool that I installed through mise on purpose. I put it in the ignore list.

The shell start is still 60 ms. Nothing more is planned for mise until the next major versions of the languages come out.

summary: Looked up why the morning report mail arrived twice and found that two launchd jobs both ran the nightly check after a copy of the plist was left in the agents folder.
body:
The report had come twice for three days. I listed the launchd agents with launchctl list and found two labels for the nightly check, one with a suffix of copy in the file name.

The copy was left from the time I tested a change to the schedule. I unloaded and deleted it. The remaining job has the right time. The next report should arrive once.

summary: Set up a weekly job that checks the 1Password CLI, Homebrew and mise for outdated tools and writes a short list instead of upgrading anything on its own.
body:
Updates had been a manual habit that I forgot for weeks, and then I had many at once. I wanted a weekly list, but no automatic upgrades, since a surprise upgrade of the terminal or the editor in the middle of work is worse than an old version.

The job runs brew outdated with the json output, mise outdated and a check of the 1Password CLI version through its own command. A small script merges the three into one list with the current and the new version and a mark for casks, since casks like Ghostty and Zed deserve a look at the release notes before updating.

I first ran brew update inside the job to get fresh data. That failed under launchd with a lock when I was using brew at the same time. I added a retry of the update after a short wait and let the job continue with the old data if the second try also fails, saying so in the output.

The list goes into the same morning report on the first day of the job's cycle, as a section that is left out if nothing is outdated. I did not make a separate mail.

A test run showed 14 outdated formulae, two casks and one mise tool. I upgraded the formulae by hand with brew upgrade and left the casks for a check of the release notes.

The job's schedule is set for the early morning on the day I usually plan the week, so the list is there at the right time. The launchd plist is in the dotfiles with the others, and I checked that the symlink script sees it. I also made sure that the drift script does not report the new agent as unknown.

One gap remains: Mac App Store apps are not covered, since the mas tool needs a signed-in session that is not available under launchd.

summary: Upgraded both outdated casks after reading their release notes and tested Ghostty and Zed against the key bindings and the font settings, with no change needed.
body:
The weekly list showed Ghostty and Zed as outdated. I read both release notes first, as planned. Ghostty had a change in how some key sequences are encoded, which hurt the session switcher in the past.

I upgraded Ghostty and tested all tmux bindings from the last set, the session switcher, the popup shell and the new copy binding. All worked. Escape delay and colors were unchanged.

Zed's update touched vim mode, so I checked the custom bindings for project grep, blame and file tree. They worked, as did the tmux task. The font and theme still match Ghostty.

summary: Investigated a complaint about the prompt freezing for a second in a large monorepo checkout and found the async git status was waiting on an untracked files scan, which is now limited.
body:
A project I work on has a very large checkout, and the prompt froze for about a second after commands there. The async git status from before should have prevented that, so I looked for what was left blocking.

I profiled the prompt with zprof and then timed the git calls by hand. git status with untracked files took 1.1 seconds in that checkout, while status without untracked files took 90 ms. The async worker was running, but the prompt waited for a result when the cache was older than a few seconds, and that was the blocking part.

The fix has two parts. First, the prompt never waits for the worker anymore. If the cache is stale it shows the old value with a small marker and redraws when the new value arrives. Second, the worker uses the untracked-files=no option when the repo is larger than a threshold. I measure the size with the number of entries in the index, using git ls-files with a count, cached per repository.

The threshold of 50,000 entries was chosen from my repos: the large one has 180,000 and the next has 9,000. The prompt then does not show the untracked marker in the big repository, which I can live with. A comment in the prompt file says so, so I do not wonder later.

I tested the redraw in zsh with the zle reset-prompt call from the worker's callback. It first caused a flicker when typing, because it redrew while a command line was half typed. I restricted the redraw to when the line buffer is empty.

After the change the prompt appeared instantly in the big checkout, and the branch and dirty marker updated within a second. In small repos nothing changed and the untracked marker still works.

I also ran the shell start time test and got the same 60 ms, since only the worker logic changed. The note of the fix is added to the notes file.

summary: Wrote a small script to export Zed settings and keymap into the dotfiles folder and made the drift script check them, after finding the live file had two settings not in the saved copy.
body:
Zed rewrites its own settings file whenever I change something in the UI, and the copy in the dotfiles had fallen behind. I had left Zed out of the drift script for that reason, but it was a gap.

I compared the live settings with the saved copy by hand first. Two differences showed up: a changed format-on-save option for one language, and the collapsed state of a panel. The first was a real setting I wanted to keep, and the second was noise.

The settings and keymap files in the config folder are now symlinks to the dotfiles copies. I checked that Zed keeps working through a symlink and it does: it writes through the link, so the dotfiles copy is always the current one. This makes an export script unnecessary, so I dropped that idea and kept it simple.

The symlink script now includes the two Zed files in its list, and the nightly check reports them if they get replaced by a normal file. This can happen if Zed saves by replacing the file, so I tested that by changing a setting in the UI and then looking at the link. The link stayed intact.

The noise setting about the panel state is stored in a separate file in Zed's own database, not in the settings, so it does not pollute the copy.

I added the Zed part to the bootstrap, so the second Mac test would link the files as well. I ran the bootstrap on the test user and the links appeared. The drift script has no check for Zed now, since the symlink makes it unnecessary.

One point to watch is that Zed updates sometimes add new keys to the settings file on startup. That will show up as a change in the dotfiles copy, which is what I want to see anyway.

summary: Did a full review of the bootstrap script on a clean test user, fixed five problems from the new scripts of the last weeks, and updated the manual steps list to match.
body:
A lot has been added since the second Mac test: the drift script, the weekly outdated list, the history setup, the tmux popup bindings and the Zed links. I wanted to know if the bootstrap still gives a working machine from nothing, so I ran it on a fresh test user.

The first problem came early. The bootstrap installed the Brewfile before the shell files were linked, and fzf's integration file was missing when zsh started, which printed an error on every new shell. I changed the order so links come after the Homebrew step and the shell loads the fzf file only if it exists.

The second problem was the history cleanup script. It was in the scripts folder but not executable, since it was copied from a backup. I set the mode and added a mode check to the symlink script for all files in the scripts folder.

The third was the launchd agents. The bootstrap loaded them with the old launchctl load command, which prints a deprecation warning on new macOS versions. I switched to bootstrap and the gui domain of the user. The weekly job then loaded correctly, and I confirmed it with launchctl print.

Fourth, the Ghostty launch script for tmux assumed the lock folder in the temp directory existed. On a fresh user it did, but the cleanup step of detached sessions failed with an error when no tmux server was running. I added a check for a running server before the cleanup.

Fifth, the key repeat setting needs a logout, and the bootstrap did not tell the user. It now prints a summary at the end of all settings that need a logout or a restart of an app. There are two: key repeat and the Dock one that needs killall, which the script does itself.

I also checked time. The whole run took 14 minutes, of which 11 were Homebrew downloads. Without the casks it would be much faster, but I did not change that.

The manual steps list is still short: sign in to 1Password, sign in to the App Store, and approve the terminal in the privacy settings for file access. The last item was new; the backup job cannot read some folders without it, and I had not listed it before. Without it, the first backup would have failed with a permission error, so I added it with a note at the top.

After the fixes I ran the bootstrap a second time on the same user to check that it is safe to repeat. It finished with no errors and changed nothing. The drift script reported zero differences afterward.

I deleted the test user. The notes file lists the five fixes in the order I found them.

summary: Wrote a plan for the next stretch of dotfiles work: what is finished, three small ideas worth doing, and a list of things to leave alone so the setup does not grow for its own sake.
body:
After the bootstrap review I took stock. The machine setup is in good shape, and each part has a script, a check and a note. The risk now is adding things just because I can.

What is finished: the shell and prompt, including the light palette and the large repo case. The editors with their shared keymap in Zed and Neovim. tmux with the new status line, window names and popup bindings. Ghostty with the tmux launch script. Mise for the tools. SSH keys and signing through 1Password. The backup with the summary file and the restore script. The nightly check and the weekly outdated list. The macOS defaults including key repeat.

Three ideas seem worth doing. The first is a restore drill again, because the backup changed with the new log layout and the last full drill was a long time ago. The second is a test of the whole setup after a major macOS update, which is due in some weeks, using the test user to find what breaks. The third is a look at the terminal font and its rendering at different sizes, since I have wanted to try another font for a while and the Ghostty config makes it easy to compare.

Things to leave alone are listed on purpose. I will not add a history database tool, since fzf is enough. I will not automate upgrades of casks, since I want to read release notes. I will not move to another prompt framework, as the small prompt of its own starts in a few milliseconds and I know every line of it. I will not sync the dotfiles to a hosting site, because the folder contains host names and the backup is enough for one person.

The order is the restore drill first, because it protects the data. The font comparison is the cheap and fun one and can fill an evening. The macOS update test waits for the update itself.

I wrote the plan into the notes file at the top and moved the older completed items below a line. The nightly report does not need a change for any of this.

One small thing from the review stays on the list: the bootstrap spends most of its time in downloads, and it would help to skip casks when asked. A flag for that is a ten-minute change, so it can be done between the larger items.

summary: Started the first of the three small ideas from the plan: a shell function that jumps to a project folder with fzf, using the folders mise and tmux already know.
body:
The plan written last week listed three small ideas, and this was the first. The goal was one command, p, that lists project folders and opens or creates a tmux session named after the folder. That fits the shorter window names decided earlier.

The folder list comes from a plain find over the two code directories, limited to depth two. It took about 40 ms, which felt slow in a popup. Caching the list in a file refreshed in the background brought it down to 8 ms.

Inside tmux the function switches the client instead of nesting a session, and outside tmux it attaches. I tested both paths, plus the case where tmux is not installed, where it only does a cd. One bug turned up: folder names with spaces broke the session name, so the name now has spaces and dots replaced by underscores.

Not done yet: a preview of the git branch in the fzf window. I will decide later whether it is worth the cost. The function lives in the zsh functions folder and the drift script now lists it.

summary: Added the project jump preview after all, showing branch and last commit, but only from the cached data, so the popup stays fast and the cache refresh stays at once per hour.
body:
This morning I left the preview open. This afternoon I tried it with a cheap version: the cache file now stores the folder, the branch and the short last commit subject, written by the background refresh.

The preview reads those columns with no git call at open time, so the popup still opens in about 9 ms. The refresh itself runs git in each folder and took 1.4 seconds for 38 folders, which is fine in the background but was too heavy to run per keystroke.

A problem showed up with folders that are not git repositories. They printed an error line into the cache, which confused the column split. I made the refresh write a dash for those.

I also checked that the refresh does not start twice when two shells open at once. A lock directory handles that. The branch data can be an hour old, and I accepted that, because the list is only for choosing a folder. The first small idea is finished.

summary: Did the second small idea: a monthly check that the Brewfile, mise and the defaults script still work on a clean user, so a broken bootstrap is noticed before a new Mac needs it.
body:
The bootstrap was last tested on a clean user about a month ago, and every new script since then widened the gap. This idea automates that test in a light form instead of a full manual run.

The new script, bootstrap-check, creates a temporary macOS user home through a HOME override, not a real user, and runs the non-interactive parts of the bootstrap in it. It covers linking the dotfiles, running brew bundle check, running mise install in dry mode, and running the defaults script in a print-only mode. It does not install anything.

The first run found three problems. The defaults script had no print-only mode, so I added one that echoes each write command. The link step failed when the target folder did not exist, which only happens on a clean home. A Brewfile line for a tap was checked in a way that needed network access.

The network issue was the awkward one. brew bundle check hit the network for one tap and made the script take 40 seconds. I set an environment flag that disables auto update, and it now takes 6 seconds.

Results go into the morning report as one line: ok, or the name of the failed step. I made it run on the first of the month through the same launchd mechanism as the weekly outdated check. I checked there is only one plist this time, after the double mail issue earlier.

To test the alarm I broke a link target on purpose, and the report line showed the failed step the next morning. Then I restored it. What remains is to see how it behaves over a few months, and I did not add anything for the manual steps, because they cannot be automated anyway.

summary: The morning report showed the bootstrap check failing on the link step, caused by a leftover test folder from my own run, and the script now cleans up after itself.
body:
The report this morning said bootstrap-check failed at the link step. I looked at the log first. The temporary home from the manual test of the alarm had not been removed, so the link step found existing files and refused to overwrite them.

The script created its temporary home with a fixed name. I changed it to use mktemp and a trap that removes the folder on exit, including after a failure. The failed run now keeps the folder only when an environment variable asks for it, for debugging.

I removed the old folder by hand and ran the script twice. Both runs reported ok and left nothing in the temp folder. The run time stayed at 6 seconds.

summary: Investigated why the shell start grew from 90 ms to 160 ms and found a new mise activation hook plus a completion rebuild on every start, both fixed to get back to about 85 ms.
body:
I noticed a short lag when opening a new tab in Ghostty and measured it with hyperfine over 30 runs of zsh -i -c exit. The median was 160 ms, while the last measurement was about 90 ms.

I used zprof to see where the time went. Two items stood out. The first was compinit, which was running a full rebuild of the completion dump on every start, about 55 ms. The second was the mise activation, which now ran a version check each time.

The compinit cause was the cleanup of weeks ago. When I removed dead functions I also moved the fpath line after compinit, so the dump never matched and was rebuilt. I moved it back before compinit and used the usual check that rebuilds the dump only once a day.

For mise, I replaced the eval of the activation output with a cached copy of that output, regenerated when the mise binary changes. That removed about 20 ms.

After both changes the median was 85 ms, with a spread of 4 ms. I ran the test again from inside tmux and got the same number.

I checked that completion still works for git, brew and mise by trying the tab key on each. One thing to watch: the cached mise output goes stale after a mise upgrade. The cache key uses the binary modification time, so it should regenerate, and I tested this by touching the file.

I added a startup time line to the health script, with a warning above 120 ms, so a regression like this one shows in the report.

summary: Added the third small idea, a quick command that shows what changed in the dotfiles since last week, and decided against a larger notes system after trying it for an hour.
body:
The third idea from the plan was a simple way to see recent changes to the configuration. Because the folder has no git history, I could not use git log. I used the backup snapshots, which keep hard-linked copies.

The new command, dotchanges, compares the current dotfiles with the snapshot from seven days ago and prints changed files with a short diff stat. It uses rsync in dry mode with itemized output, which is fast, about 0.4 seconds.

I first tried writing each change to a notes file through a zsh hook. After an hour it produced noise: every editor save was an entry. I dropped it, as the plan said to leave alone anything that grows for its own sake.

The command accepts a number of days. I tested it with 1, 7 and 30. For 30 days there was no snapshot with that exact age, so it picks the nearest older one and says which one it used.

It skips the cache files and the history file, which would show as changed every time. I added the command to the drift script help text.

With this, all three ideas from the plan are done. Next I will leave the setup alone for a while.

summary: Fixed git signing failing in a tmux popup shell because the 1Password agent socket variable was not passed in, and made the popup inherit it from the session.
body:
A commit made in the scratch popup shell failed with the error that no signing key could be reached, while the same commit in a normal pane worked. I suspected the environment first.

Inside the popup, SSH_AUTH_SOCK was empty. The popup is started by tmux run-shell style binding, which does not take the variables of the pane, only those of the tmux server at the time it started. The server had been started before the agent socket was set in my zshenv.

I looked at two options. One was to set the variable in the popup command itself. The other was to add SSH_AUTH_SOCK to update-environment in tmux.conf, so it refreshes on each attach. I chose the second, and also set it explicitly in the popup binding with the fixed socket path, because the path of the 1Password agent does not change.

After reloading the config I killed the server and reopened Ghostty, which restores the session. The popup now has the socket, and a signed test commit in a scratch repo passed. I also ran ssh-add -l inside the popup and saw the expected key.

I added a line to the health script that checks the variable inside tmux. Then I removed the test repo. The remaining oddity is that old sessions started before the fix keep the empty value until they are reattached.

summary: Replaced the old rsync exclude list of the backup with a file that is generated from the Brewfile and the cache folders, after finding 2 GB of cache in the last snapshot.
body:
While checking the backup size trend I saw that the last snapshot was 2 GB larger than the ones before. I listed the largest paths in it and found a Library cache folder from a build tool and the Homebrew download cache.

The exclude list was written by hand a long time ago. It had grown stale, with entries for tools I no longer use and none for the new ones. Keeping it by hand would repeat the problem.

I wrote a small generator, backup-excludes, that builds the exclude file from three sources: a fixed list of system caches, the cache folders of tools found through mise and brew, and an optional local list for extra entries. The backup script runs the generator before each run and writes the result next to the log.

I tested the result with rsync in dry mode, which showed the 2 GB as skipped. The dry run also showed that nothing I care about was excluded. I compared the list of included top-level folders before and after, and they were identical, except the cache ones.

One mistake: my first pattern for the Homebrew cache was too broad and matched a folder named cache inside a project. I anchored the pattern to the home path.

The real run took 3 minutes instead of 9, and the snapshot was back to the old size. The drift script now also reports when the generated list changes by more than ten lines. I kept the manual list as a fallback, but it is now only read when the generator fails. The health check reports that case.

summary: Looked at the tmux copy-mode bindings after a paste problem and found the clipboard integration worked, but the binding for selecting a word clashed with the new fzf output binding.
body:
Pasting from tmux copy mode into Zed gave an empty clipboard once. I tested it several times and could not reproduce it with the keyboard, only after a mouse selection.

The mouse path uses a different command than the keyboard one in my config. Both call pbcopy, but the mouse one had no end-of-selection handling and cancelled the selection before copying in some cases. I made both use copy-pipe-and-cancel with pbcopy.

While reading the file I saw that the word selection key was also bound in the popup for the command output copy. In copy mode the later binding won, so the word selection was dead. I moved the output binding to a prefix key table.

I tested selection by word, line and mouse, and pasted each into Zed and into the terminal. All worked.

summary: Set the Ghostty config to keep scrollback smaller and tested its memory use over a day with many tabs, which dropped from 1.4 GB to about 600 MB.
body:
Activity Monitor showed Ghostty with 1.4 GB of memory after a long working day. Most of my work happens in tmux, so the terminal scrollback was a second copy of what tmux already keeps.

I looked at the scrollback-limit setting. It was set to a high value from the iTerm2 times. I lowered it to 10 MB per surface, since tmux keeps 50000 lines for history anyway.

I opened eight tabs and ran a command that prints 200000 lines in each, once with the old setting and once with the new one. With the old one memory went up to 1.6 GB. With the new one it stayed around 650 MB.

Scrolling in tmux works as before, because tmux has its own history. I did check the case without tmux, where the limit gets hit, and found that it still holds about 8000 lines for my usual output, which is enough.

I applied the change in the saved config and the drift script shows no difference. A check on the next days will show whether the number stays there.

summary: Answered a question about why brew bundle wanted to remove a font cask, and found the font was listed only in a commented block that the cleanup had not touched.
body:
The weekly outdated check printed a line saying brew bundle cleanup would remove a font cask. I did not remember installing it by hand, so I looked.

The cask was in the installed list but not in the active part of the Brewfile. It sat in a commented block for fonts I tried when I looked at monospace options. Commented lines do not count for bundle, so it appeared as extra.

I had two choices: delete the line from the comment block and uninstall, or activate it. I did not need the font, so I uninstalled it with brew uninstall --cask and removed the line.

The other two fonts in the block were not installed, so I removed those lines too. A dry run of brew bundle cleanup now lists nothing. The JetBrains Mono entry stays active, as it is the font in use.

summary: Wrote and tested a restore drill for the backup: restored a sample of dotfiles and the SSH config into a temp folder and compared checksums, finding one file with a wrong mode.
body:
A backup is only worth anything if it restores, and I had checked the size and the log but never done a real restore since the script was written. Today I did a drill with the latest snapshot and a temporary target folder.

I picked a sample: the zsh files, the Neovim config, the tmux config, the Ghostty and Zed settings, the SSH config, and the Brewfile. I restored them with rsync from the snapshot into the temp folder.

Then I compared checksums with the live files using shasum. All matched. I also compared modes and owners with a stat loop.

One mismatch came out: the SSH config in the snapshot had mode 644, while the live file has 600. The cause was in the backup script, which used a flag set that did not preserve permissions for that path, since the folder was listed in a second rsync call with different options. I changed the second call to use the same archive flags as the first.

I ran the backup again and restored the file once more. The mode now matched. I also checked that the private key files are not in the snapshot at all, as the 1Password agent holds them. The known_hosts file is there, which is fine.

The drill took about 15 minutes. I wrote the steps into a short text file in the backup folder so they can be repeated without remembering them. A line in the health script now reports the age of the last drill. It warns after 90 days.

One gap remains: I did not test restoring on a different Mac. The new Mac setup covers that partly, since the bootstrap links files, but it does not use the snapshots. I noted this as something to try the next time I have a spare machine.

summary: Fixed the prompt showing a stale error marker after pressing Ctrl-C at an empty prompt, which kept the red mark from the last failed command.
body:
After a failed command, pressing Ctrl-C on an empty line left the red error marker in the next prompt, even though nothing had failed since. It was a small annoyance, but it made me look at the prompt twice.

The prompt reads the exit status in the precmd hook. Ctrl-C at an empty line does not run a command, so the hook saw the old status. I stored the status in a variable and reset it in a zle line-init widget, so an empty interrupted line shows the neutral marker.

I tested it with false, then Ctrl-C, then true. I also tested a real interrupted command like sleep 10 and the marker still shows 130 as it should. The light palette still looks right.

summary: Tested the Neovim config on the new Ghostty font settings and found nothing to change, though the statusline icons need the Nerd Font fallback that is already set.
body:
I checked that Neovim looks right in Ghostty after the memory and scrollback change. The question was whether the icons in the statusline and file tree still show.

They did. The Nerd Font symbols come from the fallback font setting, not from the main font, so a change of the main font would not break them. I checked this on purpose by looking at the config, since I may try another font later.

I opened the file tree, a git diff view and the diagnostics list. All icons were drawn. I also opened it inside tmux, with the same result.

No change was needed. I wrote one line in the notes about the fallback so the next font test starts there.

summary: Cleaned the zsh history of a few thousand duplicate and junk entries and set the fzf history search to ignore commands with a leading space, then checked the file size.
body:
The history file had grown to 14 MB, with many repeats of the same ls and cd lines and some commands with tokens in them that I typed by mistake.

I wrote a one-time cleanup with awk that keeps the last copy of each command and drops lines shorter than three characters. The count fell from 61000 to 23000 entries. I took a copy of the old file first and kept it in the backup folder for a week.

For the tokens I searched with grep for patterns like key and token assignments and removed those lines by hand. There were seven.

Then I set HIST_IGNORE_SPACE and made sure the fzf search widget reads the same file. A command typed with a leading space does not appear in the search now. I tested it with a harmless echo.

The file is 5 MB now, and the history search opens a little faster. I will delete the old copy next week.

summary: Prepared the move of the global git config into a base file plus a work include, so signing and aliases stay shared while the e-mail address can differ by folder.
body:
Some of my code folders need another e-mail address in commits, and until now I fixed it per repository, which I forgot more than once. The aim was to have the difference decided by folder.

Git supports includeIf with a gitdir condition. I split the global config into a base file with the aliases, the signing setup and the editor, and a second file with just the user section for the work folder. The base file includes the second one only for repositories below that folder.

I tested with git config --show-origin in a repo inside and outside the folder. Outside, the personal address came from the base file. Inside, the work address came from the include file, as wanted.

One trap appeared in the first try. The gitdir pattern needs a trailing slash to match everything below. Without it the include never applied. I found it by checking the origin output, which showed no include file.

The signing key is the same in both cases, so the 1Password helper is not affected. I made a signed commit in a scratch repo in each place and verified the signature with git log --show-signature. Both showed a good signature.

I also updated the drift script to look at both files, and the backup picks them up since they are in the same folder.

Open question: the work folder path is written as a fixed path in the base file. If I move the folder, the include breaks silently. I added a check to the health script that prints the e-mail git would use in that folder, so a mismatch shows up in the morning report.

Next I will remove the per-repository e-mail settings I set earlier. There are four, which I found with a grep over the .git/config files.

summary: Removed the four per-repository e-mail overrides and wrote a script to find stray git settings, then found two repos with an old signing key setting that also needed cleanup.
body:
After the include split from yesterday, the per-repository settings had to go, otherwise they would hide the new behavior. I started with a grep over all .git/config files below the code folders.

It found the four e-mail overrides I remembered. It also found two repos with a local user.signingkey line, set long ago before the 1Password agent. Those would have made git use an old key path that no longer exists, but both repos had commit signing off locally, so I never noticed.

To avoid doing this by hand again I wrote a small script, git-stray, that lists local settings in all repositories for a fixed set of keys: user.email, user.name, user.signingkey, commit.gpgsign, gpg.format and core.hooksPath. It prints the repository and the value.

The first run of the script printed 11 lines. Four were the e-mail overrides, two the old signing keys, and the other five were fine: they were hooks paths set by tools like a formatter.

I removed the six with git config --local --unset. Then I ran the script again and only the five hook lines remained. I wrote the hook lines into an allow list inside the script so they are not reported again.

To verify, I made a signed commit in each of the two repos with the old key line and checked the signature. Both passed, using the key from the global config. I also checked the e-mail address git reported in a work repo and a personal one.

One side effect: git-stray takes 2.5 seconds because it walks many folders. I limited the walk to depth three and skipped node_modules and the like. This reduced it to 0.6 seconds.

The script is linked into the bin folder and is part of the weekly check now. It prints nothing when all is clean, so the report stays short. I have not decided whether to run it on a new Mac too. The bootstrap has no repositories at that point, so it would be pointless.

That finishes the git config split. I do not plan more changes there, except that the signing hint from earlier still stands for the lock case.

summary: Looked at a Zed update that changed the default for inline suggestions and set it back to off in the settings, then exported the settings to the dotfiles folder.
body:
After the latest Zed update, inline suggestions appeared again while typing, even though I had turned them off in the review some weeks ago. The update had changed a default key name.

The release notes mentioned a renamed setting for the edit prediction provider. My old key was ignored. I set the new key to none.

I checked in a markdown file and a Python file that typing is not interrupted. Then I ran the export script, and the saved copy of the settings now matches the live file.

The drift script reports no differences. I will read the release notes more closely before updating Zed next time, as the weekly check lists it.

summary: Checked the weekly outdated list against what is actually used and found the pinned Homebrew formula had been fixed upstream, so the pin could go and one stale entry was dropped.
body:
The weekly job wrote its list this morning and one line was odd: the formula I pinned back during the last upgrade round showed as outdated again. I read the release notes of the newer version before touching anything. The bug that made me pin it, a crash when reading a config with an empty section, was listed as fixed.

I unpinned it, upgraded, and ran the same input that crashed before. It parsed cleanly this time. Then I checked tmux, Neovim and the commit signing flow, since those were what broke the last time something moved. All three behaved as before, and shell start stayed at about 85 ms.

The list also named a cask I no longer use, a small diff viewer that survived the earlier cleanup because a comment mentioned it. I removed it from the Brewfile and ran brew bundle cleanup in dry mode to confirm nothing else would be dropped. The weekly check now reports no outdated tools and no pins.

Next I will add a note to the weekly script output that shows pinned formulas with the reason, so a pin does not get forgotten again.

summary: Upgraded the three outdated items from the weekly list after reading the notes, and checked tmux, Neovim and the signing flow, with one Homebrew formula pinned back.
body:
With the weekly list working again, I went through the three items. One cask, Ghostty, and two formulae, tmux and neovim.

I read the release notes for each. Ghostty had a fix for a rendering issue and a changed default for one setting I do not use. The tmux release changed how the popup size is parsed, which could matter for my scratch popup. The Neovim notes had a deprecation of one API that a plugin might use.

I upgraded Ghostty and tmux first. The popup still opens at the right size, and the keys for window moving work. Then I upgraded neovim and ran checkhealth. One plugin printed a deprecation warning, the same kind of problem as earlier.

Instead of pinning the plugin, I checked and found a newer release of it fixed the call, so I updated the plugin. The warning is gone, and startup is 67 ms.

I pinned one formula back, the font tool, because its new version asked for a newer macOS than this one. The pin is in the Brewfile as a comment and with brew pin.

A signed test commit passed after all upgrades.

summary: Answered a question about how much disk the dotfiles setup and its tools use, with a short table by area, and found 6 GB of old mise installs that were safe to remove.
body:
I wanted to know why the disk was getting full and whether the setup was part of it. I measured with du over the main places: the Homebrew prefix, the mise installs, the caches, the backup folder and the dotfiles themselves.

The dotfiles are tiny, about 4 MB with the history. Homebrew was 9 GB. The backup snapshots take 3 GB, as they are hard links. The biggest surprise was the mise folder at 8 GB.

Inside it were seven Node versions and four Python versions. Only the pinned global ones and the versions named by active projects are needed. I used mise ls to see which were in use and found that five versions were not referenced anywhere.

I removed them with mise uninstall, one at a time, and ran the project check afterwards. No conflicts showed. That freed 6 GB.

I also ran brew cleanup, which removed old downloads for another 700 MB.

summary: Wrote the notes for the next Mac setup into one short file and walked through them once against the scripts, finding that two manual steps were already automated and one was missing.
body:
Since the last real setup, the scripts changed a lot, and the manual steps list was written from memory of the older flow. I decided to check it line by line against the scripts.

The list had eleven steps. Two of them, setting the key repeat and turning off the press-and-hold accent popup, are in the defaults script now, so I removed them from the list.

One step was missing: after the first login, the 1Password agent has to be switched on in its settings before the SSH config can use its socket. The bootstrap check cannot test that. Without it git signing fails with a confusing error, so I added the step with the exact setting name.

I also noticed that the order mattered. The Brewfile has to run before the mise step, as mise comes from it. The list said the reverse in one place. I fixed the order.

Then I ran the print-only modes of the scripts in sequence on the clean test home and compared the steps with the list. They agree now.

The list is nine steps long. Its length has not changed much, but each step is now needed. I put it at the top of the bootstrap readme file.

The next real test needs spare hardware, which I do not have right now.

summary: Did a quarterly review of the whole setup: startup times, backup drill, bootstrap check, drift and the weekly lists were all fine, and I wrote down what to leave alone for the next months.
body:
It was time for a review like the one in the plan from some weeks ago. I went through each area with a measurement, not only by feel.

Shell start was 86 ms with a spread of 4 ms. Neovim was 67 ms. The tmux status refresh costs about 3 ms every ten seconds. These are all inside the limits I set in the health script.

The backup ran daily without a gap, the snapshot size was stable at 3 GB, and the last restore drill is 40 days old, so the next one is due in about a month and a half. The generated exclude list had changed by two lines.

The bootstrap check passed on its last two monthly runs. The drift script reported one real change: a new Zed setting that I had made by hand. I exported it to the saved copy.

The weekly outdated list arrived every week since the fix, and the age warning stayed quiet. The git-stray script printed nothing.

Looking for problems, I found only two small ones. The tmux popup shell still keeps the old environment in sessions that were never reattached, which is cosmetic. And the p function lists a folder I no longer use, which I removed from the code folder list.

I then wrote the list of things to leave alone: no new plugin managers, no second terminal config, no theme switching by time of day, and no more shell prompt segments, since each one costs startup time.

Two ideas stay open without a date: a restore test on a second Mac, and a look at a different monospace font. The font one is only a curiosity for now, and the Nerd Font fallback note covers the technical side.

I updated the plan file with the review result and the date-free list, so the next review can compare against it.

summary: Replaced the slow nvm-style Node lookup in the Neovim LSP setup with mise shims and found two language servers still pointing at a removed Node install.
body:
The Neovim config still resolved Node through a hard-coded path from the nvm days. After the mise move this worked only by luck, because an old install was still on disk. I started by running :checkhealth and found two language servers, the TypeScript one and the JSON one, reporting a missing binary.

I traced the path to a single line in lua/lsp/init.lua that built the command from a home-folder directory. I replaced it with a lookup through `mise which node`, cached once per Neovim start so opening a file does not spawn a process each time. The cache is a plain table, not a file, so a version change in a project is seen after restarting the editor.

Then I tested three folders with different Node versions in their mise files. In each, the language server started with the version of that folder and :LspInfo showed the matching path. The Python server needed the same treatment, and it now uses the interpreter of the active mise environment instead of the system one.

Startup time of Neovim went from 61 ms to 58 ms, which is within noise. I also removed the old install that had hidden the problem, 400 MB in total, after checking nothing else referenced it with a grep over the dotfiles folder.

One thing left over is that a project opened from a tmux popup, where mise is not activated, falls back to the system Node. I wrote this in the notes file as a known limit instead of adding more shell logic. Next I want to see whether the Zed config has the same hard-coded path, since it was copied from this one.

summary: Checked the Zed config for the hard-coded Node path suspected last week and found it clean, but one language server setting pointed at a Homebrew Python.
body:
Following last week's Neovim fix, I read through the exported Zed settings for any path from the old Node setup. There was none, since Zed finds tools through the shell environment it starts in.

The Python language server setting did name a Homebrew interpreter directly. That would have ignored the mise Python of a project. I removed the line so Zed uses the environment of the folder.

I opened two projects with different Python versions and checked the version shown in the status bar. Both were right. Then I ran the export script so the saved copy matches, and the drift script reported no differences.

I did not touch the keymap. The only open point is that Zed started from the Dock does not see the mise environment, which is how macOS launches apps. Opening it from the terminal with `zed .` works, and I noted that in the manual steps list.

summary: Added a short alias and a completion for the weekly outdated list so reading it takes one command instead of finding the file.
body:
The weekly job writes its list into a cache folder, and I kept forgetting the path. I added an alias `outdated` that prints the newest list with the age of the file in the first line.

If the list is older than eight days, the alias warns that the job may not have run. I tested it by touching an old copy of the file with an earlier time.

It works in zsh and in the tmux popup shell. Nothing else changed.

summary: Tracked down why the tmux status bar showed the wrong git branch in a second window and fixed it by reading the pane path instead of the session path.
body:
The status bar showed the branch of the folder where the session was created, not of the folder in the active pane. This was visible when I kept one session and moved between two projects in different windows. The status script used `#{session_path}`, which never changes after creation.

I changed it to `#{pane_current_path}` and ran the branch lookup from there. The first version called git on every status refresh, every five seconds, and in the large monorepo checkout this took about 120 ms. That is too much for a status bar.

To fix it I reused the hourly cache of the project jump function for the branch name, and only read `.git/HEAD` directly for the current folder, which costs almost nothing. For folders that are not repositories the script prints nothing.

I tested with a normal repository, a worktree where `.git` is a file, and a folder outside any repository. The worktree case failed at first because I read `.git/HEAD` as a directory path. I added a check for the file form and followed the gitdir line in it.

The status refresh now takes under 5 ms in all three cases, measured with a simple loop of 100 runs. I reloaded the tmux config in the running session and the branch followed my pane switches.

No change was needed in the Ghostty config. I left the interval at five seconds.

summary: Looked into a Homebrew warning about a deprecated tap in the Brewfile and removed the tap after finding its two formulas were in the main repository now.
body:
The bootstrap check mail mentioned a deprecated tap. The Brewfile listed it with two formulas from it.

I looked up both formulas and found they had moved into the main Homebrew repository. I removed the tap line and changed the names to the plain form.

Then I ran `brew bundle check` and then `brew bundle cleanup` in dry-run mode. It reported that nothing was missing and nothing extra would be removed.

To be sure, I ran the bootstrap check on the clean test user. It passed, and the warning was gone. I also updated the manual notes where the tap was named.

summary: Set up commit signing checks so a commit made without the 1Password agent running fails loudly instead of leaving an unsigned commit.
body:
Last month the agent socket problem in the popup shell showed that signing can fail in a quiet way. This time I looked at the other direction: a commit that goes through unsigned.

Git was already set to sign by default, so it errors when signing fails. But a rebase of old commits with `--no-gpg-sign` in a script of mine would have made unsigned ones. I searched the dotfiles scripts and found no use of that flag.

I added a small function `signcheck` that lists the last twenty commits with their signature status using `git log --format='%h %G?'`. It prints only those that are not good. The first run showed three commits in an old test repository, which I ignored.

I added the function to the stray git settings script as an optional check. I did not add a hook, since hooks live inside each repository and would be one more thing to keep in sync.

summary: Planned and started a cleanup of the zsh functions folder, finding eleven functions that nothing used and four with the same helper copied inside.
body:
The functions folder had grown over a long time. I wanted to know which of the functions are still used before the next quarterly review.

I first counted use in the shell history. The history file has the cleaned data from a few months ago, so counts are reliable. Eleven functions had no call in the last year. Six of them were old experiments around nvm and a Docker helper I no longer use.

I did not delete them at once. I moved the eleven into an `archive/` folder that is not on the function path, so they can be fetched back in seconds. I then started a fresh shell and ran the startup timing: 84 ms, about the same as before.

The second finding was duplicated code. Four functions each contained their own copy of a small helper that checks whether a folder is a git repository. I made one shared function `_is_repo` in a file loaded first and replaced the copies.

One function broke at once because it was run in a subshell and the shared helper was not yet defined there. The fix was to autoload the helper by name instead of sourcing a file. All four then worked again in an interactive shell and in the tmux popup.

I did not yet check the scripts under `bin/`, which may call some of these functions. That is next, and I will grep for each function name before the archive is final.

summary: Grepped the bin scripts for the archived functions and found one script still calling an archived one, which I restored with a note.
body:
This morning I moved eleven unused functions into an archive folder. The remaining risk was that scripts in `bin/` or the launchd jobs called them without the shell history showing it.

I ran a grep for each archived name over the scripts, the plists and the tmux config. Ten had no match. One, a helper that formats sizes in human-readable form, was called by the disk report script.

I moved that helper back to the functions folder and added a comment line with the reason. Then I ran the disk report by hand and compared its output with the last mail. The numbers matched.

I also added the archive folder to the exclude list of the drift script so it does not report the moved files as changes. After that the drift check ran clean.

The archive stays for a month. If nothing needs it, I will delete it in the next review.

summary: Fixed the new shared repo helper being slow in the prompt by caching the result per directory for the length of one prompt draw.
body:
After the helper was shared, the prompt felt a little slower in a deep folder. I measured it with a loop and saw the repository check run three times per prompt, once for each part that needed it.

The check walked up the folder tree each time. In a path with nine levels this took about 4 ms, so 12 ms in total. Not large, but the prompt should stay near instant.

I added a variable that holds the result for the current directory, and it is reset in the precmd hook when the directory changes. Now the walk happens once per directory change.

The measured prompt time dropped to about 3 ms in the same deep folder. I tested a `cd` into a repository, out of it and into a worktree, and the prompt showed the right state each time. The shell start did not change.

summary: Wrote a small test script for the dotfiles functions with plain zsh and temp folders, and it found a bug in the branch helper with detached HEAD.
body:
After the cleanup of the functions I wanted something to catch breakage earlier than the monthly bootstrap check. I did not want a test framework, so I wrote `tests/run.zsh` that sources the functions and checks results with a tiny assert helper.

The script builds a temp folder, creates a repository with two commits, a worktree and a plain folder, and runs the functions against them. It currently has fourteen checks: the repo helper, the branch name, the size formatter, the project jump list and the status script for tmux.

The first run failed one check. In a detached HEAD state the branch helper printed the whole content of `.git/HEAD`, a long hash, instead of a short one. This is what the tmux status would show after a `git checkout` of a tag, which I had never noticed.

I changed the helper to print the first seven characters of the hash with a leading mark, so it reads like `@a1b2c3d`. The same fix was needed in the status script, which has its own copy of the logic, so I made it call the helper.

All fourteen checks pass now, and the whole run takes under a second. I added the script to the monthly bootstrap check, so the report mail shows a failure if a function breaks.

The test folder is deleted at the end of the script, and I made it use a trap so it is also removed when a check fails. I learned this from the leftover folder problem of the earlier bootstrap check.

summary: Looked at a reported double entry in the Ghostty shell integration and found that the title was set by both Ghostty and a precmd hook of mine.
body:
The tab titles in Ghostty sometimes flickered between a folder name and a command name. I first thought it was the status script of tmux, but outside tmux it happened too.

I read the Ghostty shell integration notes and saw that it sets the title itself when it is loaded. My zsh config also had an old hook from the iTerm2 time that wrote the title with an escape sequence on each prompt. Both were fighting.

I removed my hook and kept the integration. Then I checked what the title shows in four cases: at the prompt, while a command runs, in tmux and in an ssh session.

The first three were fine. In ssh the title showed the local folder, because the remote host has no integration. I accepted this, as setting it remotely would need changes on each server.

Inside tmux the title is set by tmux with `set-titles`, and I made sure the format there shows the session and window name. I tested it by opening three windows.

The change is small: one hook removed, one line changed in the tmux config. I reloaded both and ran the function tests, all fine. There was no change in startup time. I wrote the finding in the notes under terminal behaviors, because the old hook is likely to come back if I copy lines from an old backup.

summary: Prepared the macOS defaults script for a new system version by reading which keys changed and found two defaults that no longer take effect.
body:
A system update was due, so I reviewed the defaults script before it, not after. The script sets about sixty keys for the Dock, Finder, keyboard repeat and screenshots.

I first ran a dump of the current values with `defaults read` and compared it with what the script sets. Fifty-six matched. Four differed, and I checked each one.

Two of them were values I had changed by hand in System Settings and never put in the script: the trackpad tap setting and the screenshot format. I added both to the script, so a new Mac gets them.

The other two were keys the script set but that macOS now ignores or resets. One was a Dock animation key. The other was a Finder key for showing the path bar, which the system now keeps in a different place. I found this by setting the value, restarting the Finder and seeing no change.

For the path bar I found the new key by toggling the option in the Finder and reading the difference between two dumps. I replaced the old line with the new one. The Dock animation line I removed and noted why in a comment.

To test the script I ran it on the clean test user. It finished without an error, and a diff of the dump of that user against my own showed only the expected differences, such as the wallpaper and the account name.

I also noted that the script prints no warning when a key does nothing. It cannot know. So I added a short list in the notes of keys that must be checked by eye after a system update.

I will run the script again after the update and compare dumps once more.

summary: After the system update I re-ran the defaults script and the bootstrap check and found Homebrew needed new command line tools before anything else worked.
body:
The system update finished this morning. The first thing I saw was a Homebrew message asking for newer command line tools, and all `brew` commands stopped until that was done.

I installed the tools with `xcode-select --install` and let it finish, about 15 minutes. Then `brew doctor` was clean, except for one warning about an unlinked formula that I had unlinked myself on purpose.

Next I ran the defaults script and dumped the values again. Compared with the dump from before the update, three keys had changed by themselves. The system had reset the keyboard repeat rate to a slower value, and two Dock keys. The script set them back.

I then checked the other parts of the setup in order: the prompt, tmux, Neovim, Zed, Ghostty and the signing flow. All worked. The 1Password agent socket was still at the same path.

The bootstrap check on the clean user failed at the first run, because the test user also needed the tools to be present. It passed after I installed them for the whole machine, not just my user.

I added a line to the bootstrap script that checks for the command line tools at the beginning and tells the user what to do. Before, it failed later with a long error that did not say what was missing.

The weekly outdated list showed nothing new. I wrote down in the notes that the repeat rate, and two Dock keys, can be reset by a system update, and the defaults script is safe to run again.

summary: Answered a question about which shell aliases I use most, with counts from the history, and suggested dropping six that have no use in a year.
body:
The question was which aliases are worth keeping. I counted from the cleaned history file, matching only the first word of each command.

The most used were `gs` for status, `gd` for diff and `gco` for checkout, each with several thousand uses. The git aliases in the git config were used less, but `git lg` stood out with a steady count.

Six aliases had no uses at all in the last year. Four were from the old Docker work and two were shortcuts for the removed nvm commands. I listed them in a short table with the count next to each.

I did not remove them. Following the plan of the earlier review, I only suggested it. They are harmless and cost nothing at start, I measured less than 1 ms for the whole alias file.

The answer also showed that `gco` is often followed by `-b`. That would be a candidate for an alias of its own, but I left it, as a new alias for a habit that works is the kind of growth I wanted to avoid.

summary: Fixed the backup job skipping the Zed export folder because the generated exclude file matched its name against a cache pattern.
body:
While checking last night's backup log I saw that the Zed export folder in the dotfiles was missing from the snapshot. The folder is named `zed-cache-free`, which I had picked to avoid exactly this, but the exclude file still matched it.

The generator builds patterns from the cache folders it finds. One pattern was `*cache*` without an anchor, taken from a library folder name. rsync applied it to any path part, so it also hit my folder.

I changed the generator to write anchored paths relative to the home folder instead of loose patterns. Each line now starts with a slash and names the full path.

Then I ran rsync with `--dry-run --itemize-changes` and compared the list of what would be copied with the one before. The Zed folder was now in it, and nothing else had appeared or gone except two small cache files I wanted excluded anyway.

I ran the restore drill on a sample that included the Zed export, and the checksums matched. After that I ran a real backup and the size of the snapshot grew by only 40 KB.

I added a check to the generator tests: after building the file, it asserts that three named important folders are not matched by any line. This should catch the same mistake if a new cache folder appears.

The lesson is that a loose pattern is a risk for a backup and a path is not. I wrote it as a rule at the top of the generator script.

summary: Added the backup folder size and the age of the last good snapshot to the morning report so a silent backup failure shows up the next day.
body:
The missing folder this morning was found by luck from the log. The morning report mail did not mention the backup at all unless it failed in a loud way.

I added a short section to the report script. It reads the newest snapshot folder, prints its age in hours and its size, and the number of files changed since the one before.

The rule for a warning is simple: if the newest snapshot is older than 30 hours, or its size is more than 20 percent below the previous one, the line begins with a mark that I will see in the subject too.

I tested the warning cases by pointing the script at a copy of the folder with an old time stamp, and then at one with a half-size snapshot. Both triggered the mark. The normal case printed a calm line.

The report mail had no change in its length otherwise. The script runs from the same launchd job as before, so I did not add a new job. I made sure that the copied plist problem from months ago did not return by checking the agents folder: one plist, as expected.

One point I noticed is that the size check would not catch a slow shrink over many days. For that, the weekly outdated list is not the right place. I will see the numbers in the mail and decide in the next quarterly review if a trend line is useful.

summary: Reviewed the tmux config line by line, removed nine settings that are defaults now, and fixed an escape-time value that made Neovim feel slow on Esc.
body:
I read the whole tmux config, 140 lines, against the current version's documentation. The config is from the first period and has been added to over the years.

Nine settings turned out to be defaults in the current version or options that no longer exist. Among them were `utf8` flags and an old `default-terminal` workaround. I removed them one by one and reloaded after each, to see if anything changed. Nothing did.

The one real finding was `escape-time`. It was at 50 ms, set long ago for a slow ssh connection. In Neovim this gave a tiny but noticeable delay when pressing Esc to leave insert mode. I set it to 10 ms.

To measure the effect I used a key press test script that sends Esc and times the screen change. It dropped from about 60 ms to about 20 ms. Over ssh to a remote tmux, I tried 10 ms as well and saw no broken sequences, so I kept it.

I also checked `focus-events`, which Neovim needs for autoread. It was on. The truecolor setting for Ghostty was correct, and the color test showed a smooth gradient.

The key bindings I did not change. The word selection binding that clashed with the fzf output binding weeks ago is now clearly commented, with the reason next to it.

I ran the function tests, the status script check and a quick walk through windows, panes and copy mode. All worked. The config went down from 140 to 118 lines.

Next I would like to compare the config with the one on the work laptop, but that is a separate machine and I only have the notes of it, so I left it.

summary: Looked at why mise installed Python from source and took ten minutes, and fixed it by setting the precompiled build option for new versions.
body:
I ran `mise install python@latest` for a new project and it started compiling Python from source. It ran for about ten minutes and used all cores, so the fans came on.

I looked at the mise settings. The option for precompiled Python builds was not set. In the version I have, the default can differ by release, and mine fell back to compiling.

I set the option in the global mise config, canceled the running build and ran the install again. This time it downloaded a prebuilt archive and finished in 12 seconds.

I checked that the result works: `python -V`, then creating a venv and installing a small package. Both were fine. The SSL module loaded without error, which is the part that sometimes breaks with other builds.

I then went through the existing Python versions. Two were compiled the old way and one was prebuilt. I left them, since they work and a rebuild would change nothing for projects that use them.

To keep the setting after a new Mac setup, I checked that the global mise config is in the dotfiles and linked by the bootstrap script. It is, so a new machine gets it.

I added a line in the notes: if an install runs for more than a minute, stop it and check if it compiles. The bootstrap check also installs Python in the test user, so it would have been slow there too. It now takes one minute less.

summary: Investigated why the fzf file picker in Neovim missed files in ignored folders I do want, and added a per-project override instead of changing the global ignore.
body:
The picker in Neovim did not list files under a `generated/` folder, which is in a global ignore. In one project I need to open those files often.

I first checked where the ignore came from. The picker uses ripgrep with the global ignore file of git, so `generated/` was excluded for every project. Removing it globally would have made all the other projects noisy again.

The option I considered was a flag to ripgrep that includes ignored files. That would show `node_modules` too, with a huge count. I tried it in the large monorepo and the list took four seconds to appear. Not usable.

The better way was a per-project override. ripgrep reads a `.ignore` file in the project root, and entries there with an exclamation mark re-include a path. I added `!generated/` to that file in the project.

I tested it, and the files appeared, and the listing took the usual 80 ms. The folder is still not in git status, as the `.ignore` file only affects ripgrep and not git.

There was one more problem: the `.ignore` file itself showed up in git status of the project. I did not want to commit it into the repository of a team. I put it in the local exclude of that repository at `.git/info/exclude`.

I also checked that the same picker in Zed behaves the same way. Zed has its own file finder and respects `.gitignore` but not `.ignore`, so there I had to set `file_scan_exclusions` for the folder in the project settings of Zed. That worked after a restart.

This leaves two small config files per project, one for each editor. I wrote both locations into the notes with the reason.

I did not add any helper to create these files. It happens in one project only, so a script would be more work than the problem.

summary: Replaced the manual SSH config entries for three hosts with a Match block and the 1Password agent, and tested key use, forwarding and the signing path end to end.
body:
The SSH config had grown into a long list of Host entries, many with the same options repeated. I wanted to cut it down without changing how any host is reached.

I first made a copy and a list of the hosts and their effective settings, using `ssh -G host` for each. This gives the final result after all rules, so it is a good way to compare before and after.

Then I grouped hosts. Three hosts shared the same user and the same identity settings, so I replaced their separate entries with one block using a pattern. Settings that were the same for every host, like the agent socket and the keepalive, moved into a `Host *` block at the end of the file.

After the change, I ran `ssh -G` again for all twelve hosts and compared the output with a diff. Eleven were identical. One differed: a host that had an `IdentitiesOnly` setting which was in its own entry and was lost by my merge. I put it back.

Next I tested real connections to the three hosts. All logged in, and 1Password asked for approval as before. Agent forwarding to one jump host worked, and from there a `git pull` over ssh used the forwarded key.

The signing path is separate, since commits are signed with an ssh key through the same agent. I made a test commit in a scratch repository, and `git log --show-signature` reported a good signature.

I also checked the IdentityAgent path. It contains a space from the application support folder, so the quoting in the config matters. I kept the quoted form as it was.

The config went from 96 lines to 52. I saved the old one in the backup folder with a note, and I did not add it to the dotfiles repository of the folder, as it has host names that I keep out of it.

The backup restore drill includes the SSH config, so I ran it again for this file. The checksum and the mode matched.

The notes got a short paragraph on how to add a host: add it to the pattern if it fits, otherwise a single entry.

summary: Checked a Ghostty update for changes to key bindings and shell integration and found one renamed option, which I fixed in the config.
body:
A new Ghostty version was on the weekly list. I read the release notes before upgrading, as usual.

One option I use for the scrollback limit had been renamed, and the old name would print a warning at start. Everything else in my config was unchanged by the notes.

I upgraded with brew and started Ghostty. The warning appeared in the config validation output, as expected. I changed the name in the config and ran the validation command again, which was clean.

Then I tested the key bindings I use: new tab, split and the ones that pass through to tmux. All worked. The shell integration still set the title correctly, which I had checked a few weeks ago.

Memory use after an hour with many tabs was around 550 MB, similar to before. I exported nothing, since Ghostty's config is a plain file in the dotfiles folder and already linked.

The weekly list is empty again.

summary: Looked at why the zsh completion for a tool from mise was missing in new shells and fixed it by generating the file into the completion folder at install time.
body:
The completion for one tool installed with mise did not work in new shells. In the shell where I had run the install, it worked, which pointed to something temporary.

The tool prints its completion script on request and I had put a line in the zshrc that sourced it. That line ran at each start and was the cause of 25 ms of extra startup, which I saw when I measured the start with the profiler. So the completion was slow and, because of an error in the pipe order, sometimes empty.

I replaced the line with a generated file. The file lives in a completion folder of the dotfiles, and is written by a small script that I call after upgrading the tool. In the normal start, zsh only finds the file through the function path.

I tested in a new shell and tab completion listed the subcommands with their descriptions. After a restart of the terminal, it still did.

Shell start went from 112 ms back to 86 ms. This is the same kind of problem as the completion rebuild found earlier, a command running at each start that should run once.

To avoid forgetting, I added the generation step to the weekly outdated job output as a hint: when the tool is on the list, the line says to regenerate the completion after upgrading it. I did not make the job do it itself, as it should not change anything alone.

The drift script now also looks at the completion folder and warns if a generated file is older than the installed tool. I tested it by touching the file to an older time.

summary: Diagnosed a failed monthly bootstrap check as a new macOS defaults key that prompts for permission on a clean user, and made the script skip it with a note.
body:
The monthly bootstrap check mail said failed, at the defaults step. The log showed that the script stopped and waited, then timed out after two minutes.

I ran the defaults script by hand on the clean test user and watched. The step that hung was a key for the screen capture location. On the test user, macOS opened a permission dialog for the Terminal and waited for a click, which nobody gave in the unattended run.

On my own account the permission was already given, so the script had never stopped there. This is why the problem showed only on a clean user, which is the point of the check.

I had two options. One was to give the permission with a profile for the test user, which would be a big change for a small thing. The other was to detect the case. I chose the second: the script now runs this one step with a timeout of ten seconds, and when it times out it prints a clear line that says to run the step by hand after the first login.

I added the same line to the manual steps list in the notes, since a real new Mac will also need a click there. The two manual steps that were missing earlier are now three.

Then I ran the bootstrap check again from the start. It passed in four minutes, with the timeout line in the log as a warning and not an error. The check script treats that warning as acceptable, and I made it list such warnings in the mail.

I also made sure the timeout command exists on a clean macOS, since it is not part of the base system. It does not, so I used a shell function with a background process and `wait`, which works anywhere.

I tested the function with a command that sleeps for thirty seconds. It stopped after ten seconds and returned the right status. The tests for the functions folder got one more check for this.

summary: Wrote a short plan for what to do before the next Mac setup, listing the three manual steps, the open notes and what to try on the clean user once more.
body:
A new Mac may come in the next months, so I wrote down what is left. The plan is one page in the notes folder.

The first part lists the manual steps: the screen capture permission, the sign-in to 1Password with the ssh agent switch, and the Dock launch of Zed that does not see the mise environment. Each has a line of how long it takes.

The second part is what was changed since the quarterly review: the shared helper, the function tests, the SSH config merge and the mise Python setting. I checked that each is part of the bootstrap path and not only on my machine.

The third part is a list for a last full run on a clean user, about one month before the machine arrives. It includes the defaults script, the Brewfile, the restore drill and the function tests.

I also wrote what to leave alone: no new tools, no change of the prompt, and no move of the config into a manager of dotfiles, since the scripts work.

I did not run anything today. The archive folder of unused functions is still there for one more week, and it is on the list to delete.

The plan shows no open problem. The weekly list is empty, the last backup is fresh and the startup time is 86 ms.
