summary: Ran the clean-user check again after the plan of an hour ago: two of the three manual steps are now scripted, and the third needs a permission prompt that cannot be skipped.
body:
The plan written earlier listed three manual steps for the next Mac setup, so I took the first one and tried to remove it. It was the step where the 1Password agent socket path is linked into the SSH config. I added it to the bootstrap script as a small function that checks whether the link exists and creates it if not.

The second step was setting the default shell for the new user. That was already in the notes as manual, but chsh works fine from the script once /opt/homebrew/bin/zsh is listed in /etc/shells. I added a line that appends it with sudo only when it is missing, and the script prints what it did.

I then created a fresh clean user on the machine and ran the bootstrap from the start. Homebrew installed, the Brewfile ran through in about eleven minutes, and mise installed Node and Python with the precompiled build option, so Python took under a minute this time. The defaults script ran without the key that prompts for permission, as last week's change intended.

The third manual step is signing in to 1Password and turning on the SSH agent in its settings. I looked for a way to do it from the command line and found none; the setting lives in the app and is not exposed. So that step stays manual, and I wrote it at the top of the notes file in one line with the exact menu path.

One small problem showed up on the clean user: the bootstrap check reported the commit signing test as failed. This was expected, because the agent was not running yet, and the loud failure from the signing check last month did its job. I made the check print a hint that points to the manual step instead of just the error.

I deleted the clean user afterwards and left the plan file with two items crossed off. What remains is the one manual step and a last full run on a real new Mac.

summary: Looked at why a new shell took 90 ms longer on one terminal tab and found a stale completion cache rebuilt on every start because its timestamp check used the wrong file.
body:
I noticed that opening a new tab in Ghostty felt slower than the quarterly numbers suggested. Timing with zsh -i -c exit gave about 210 ms, against 120 ms measured at the review. Something had regressed since then.

I used zprof to see where the time went. Almost all of the extra time was in compinit, which was doing a full rebuild instead of reading the dump file. The cause was in my .zshrc: the check that decides whether to rebuild compared the age of .zcompdump with a file in the completion folder that the mise completion change of two weeks ago touches on every install.

Because that generated file was newer than the dump, the check always said the dump was stale. I changed the check to look at the dump against the list of fpath folders only once a day, using a glob qualifier on the dump file's modification time, which is the usual pattern. The generated completion file is no longer part of the comparison.

After the change the shell started in 118 ms over ten runs, with a spread of about 6 ms. I also checked that the mise completion still shows up in a new shell, since I did not want to break last week's fix. It did.

I added the startup time to the list of things the monthly check prints, so a jump like this appears there and not by feel. Nothing else changed today.

summary: Moved the Neovim plugin list from a loose set of files to one lockfile-backed spec and updated everything once, with two plugins rolled back because of changed options.
body:
The Neovim config had grown a plugin spec in four different files, which made it hard to see what was installed and to update it in one go. I started today by listing every plugin that is actually loaded with the plugin manager's own status command and comparing that with the spec files. Three plugins were in the files but never loaded, because the conditions that enabled them referred to a variable I removed months ago.

I removed those three and merged the rest into one folder with a file for each area: editing, git, LSP and UI. Each file returns a plain table, and the plugin manager's lockfile now sits in the dotfiles folder, so a new Mac gets the same versions as this one. I checked that the lockfile is not matched by the backup exclude file, since the cache pattern problem from last month is still in my mind.

Then I ran a full update with the lockfile in place. Fourteen plugins changed. Starting Neovim right after, two gave errors. The statusline plugin had renamed its section option, and the fuzzy finder integration failed on a removed function in its picker config.

For the statusline I read the changelog and renamed the option; that took five minutes. For the picker integration the changelog mentioned a rewrite with a different setup call, and I did not want to rewrite my per-project override for ignored folders in the middle of this. I pinned that plugin to the previous commit in the lockfile and wrote a note in the file about why.

I measured the Neovim start with --startuptime. It was 61 ms before the change and 58 ms after, so the merge did not cost anything. Opening a large TypeScript file with the language server attached still took about the same time as before.

I went through the keymaps for the git and finder plugins by hand, since those are the ones I use all the time: staging a hunk, blame in the gutter, file search and grep. All worked. The one thing I did not test is the spell checking, which I rarely use.

Next I want to look at the pinned picker plugin and decide whether to adopt its new setup. The note in the lockfile file says to check it again in about two weeks.

summary: Followed up on the pinned Neovim picker plugin and ported my ignored-folder override to its new setup call, so the pin is gone after one evening.
body:
After the plugin cleanup this afternoon I had the pinned picker plugin on my mind, so I looked at it before it could be forgotten. The new setup call takes a table of sources, and each source has its own options for hidden and ignored files. My old override read a per-project file and passed extra arguments to the file finder command.

I rewrote the override as a function that returns the source options when the project file exists. The project file format did not change, so the two projects that use it needed nothing. I tested in one of them: files inside the ignored build folder showed up in the picker again, and in a project without the file they stayed hidden.

The grep source had a second difference. It used to follow the same ignore rules as the file source, and now it has its own flag. I set it from the same function so both behave the same way.

I removed the pin from the lockfile, updated the plugin to the current version and restarted Neovim a few times without errors. I also deleted the note about checking it in two weeks.

The journal of the config is now simple: one lockfile, no pins, three plugins fewer than this morning.

summary: Set up a Brewfile check that compares what is installed with what is listed, and it found nine casks and formulas installed by hand that were never added.
body:
For the next Mac setup to be right, the Brewfile has to describe the machine as it really is. I never had a check for the opposite direction, meaning things installed that are not in the file. So I wrote one today.

The core is brew bundle cleanup without the force flag, which only lists what would be removed. I wrapped it in a small function in the bin folder that prints the result in two groups, formulas and casks, and exits with a nonzero code if either is not empty. Leaves only matter for formulas, so I used brew leaves for the comparison and ignored dependencies.

The first run listed nine items. Four were tools I installed for one task and forgot: a JSON viewer, a video converter, a diff tool and a network scanner. Two were casks I do use, a PDF reader and a menu bar clock, which were simply never written down. Two were formulas that came as dependencies of the converter and now stood as leaves. The ninth was an old font cask for JetBrains Mono Nerd Font, which I do want, because the terminal still uses JetBrains Mono.

I removed the four forgotten tools with brew uninstall and checked that nothing else depended on them using brew uses. I added the two useful casks and the font to the Brewfile in the sections where similar things already sit. After that, brew bundle cleanup came back empty and brew bundle check said the file was satisfied.

The opposite check, that everything in the Brewfile is installed, was already part of the monthly bootstrap check, so now both directions are covered. I connected the new function to the monthly check and made it print only a short line when clean.

One detail was awkward: brew bundle cleanup also lists VS Code extensions and Mac App Store entries if the Brewfile has lines for them. I do not use either in the file, so this did not matter, but I put a comment in the function so that I will not wonder about it later.

I also tested what happens when something is missing: I installed a small tool by hand, ran the check, saw it reported, and removed it again. The exit code and the message were as I wanted.

Disk use dropped by about 1.4 GB from the removed tools, mostly the video converter and its libraries. That fits what the disk answer of a few weeks ago said about Homebrew being the largest part after mise.

Next I will think about whether the weekly outdated list should also mention leaves that have not been used for a long time. That needs some measure of use, which Homebrew does not give, so I will probably skip it.

summary: Fixed the new Brewfile check printing a false positive for the font cask, which was listed under a renamed token, and made the check tolerate renamed casks.
body:
When I ran the Brewfile check again this evening to see the monthly output, it reported one cask as missing even though the font was installed. The Brewfile used the old token, font-jetbrains-mono-nerd-font, and Homebrew now knows it under a shorter name with the old one as an alias.

brew bundle check treated the alias as satisfied, but my wrapper compared names as plain strings from brew list --cask against the file, so it saw two different names. I looked at what brew info --json=v2 returns for the cask and found the old tokens in an array called old_tokens.

I changed the wrapper to ask Homebrew for the old tokens of each cask in the file and to accept either name. That added about two seconds to the run, which I found fine for a monthly check. As a second step I replaced the old token in the Brewfile with the current one, so the file is clean in any case.

I tested with the old token put back temporarily. The check passed, and with a wrong token it failed, as it should. I also reran it on the whole Brewfile and it printed the single clean line.

I left the alias handling in because other casks will be renamed over time, and I do not want the same false alarm to teach me to ignore the check.

summary: Started tracking down a shell start of about 640 ms; zprof showed nvm-free mise activation and compinit as the two biggest costs
body:
The shell had felt sluggish for a week, so I measured it with `time zsh -i -c exit` and got 640 ms on average over ten runs. Then I added `zmodload zsh/zprof` at the top of .zshrc and ran a new shell.

zprof put compinit first at about 210 ms. Second was the `eval "$(mise activate zsh)"` line at about 120 ms. The prompt functions took around 40 ms. The rest was spread over small things like the fzf key bindings and the git alias completion.

I looked at how compinit was called. It ran with a full security check every time, and the .zcompdump file was being rebuilt because it was older than the fpath changes I made when I added the Homebrew completions. The Homebrew site-functions directory was also in fpath twice, once from .zprofile and once from .zshrc.

I did not change anything yet. I wrote the numbers into a notes file in the dotfiles folder so that I can compare after each change. The plan is to cache the compdump and only rebuild it once a day, remove the duplicate fpath entry, and then see whether the mise activation can be made lazy.

I also checked that the 640 ms is not caused by the terminal. Running the same command from a plain Terminal window gave 630 ms, so it is the zsh config itself. Next session will start with compinit.

summary: Cut compinit from 210 ms to about 25 ms by caching the completion dump and removing the duplicate fpath entry
body:
I worked on the compinit cost found yesterday. First I removed the second `fpath+=` line for the Homebrew site-functions from .zshrc and kept the one in .zprofile.

Then I replaced the plain `compinit` call with a check on the dump file. If .zcompdump was modified in the last 24 hours, zsh runs `compinit -C`, which skips the security scan. Otherwise it runs the full `compinit` and rewrites the dump. In zsh this is done with a glob qualifier: `(#qN.mh+24)`.

A first version of the check failed silently because I forgot `setopt extended_glob` before the line. The dump was rebuilt on every start and nothing improved. After adding the option, the second start in a new shell dropped compinit to about 25 ms in zprof.

Total start time went from 640 ms to about 450 ms. That is better but still noticeable. The remaining big item is the mise activation at roughly 120 ms.

I also compiled the dump with `zcompile` in the same block so zsh reads a .zwc file. The gain was small, about 3 ms, but it costs nothing. I committed nothing, since the folder is not a repository, but I copied the old .zshrc to .zshrc.bak-before-compinit in case something breaks.

summary: Made mise activation lazy so the shell no longer pays 120 ms at start, using shims for non-interactive use and a first-prompt hook
body:
The mise activation line was the biggest remaining cost. I tried two approaches.

First I tried `mise activate zsh --shims`, which only adds the shims directory to PATH. Start time dropped by about 110 ms, but then `mise` hooks that switch versions on `cd` no longer worked, so entering a project with a .tool-versions file did not change the Node version in the prompt until I ran a command through a shim. That was acceptable for scripts but not for interactive work.

The second approach was to defer the full activation. I put the shims on PATH at start, then registered a one-shot `precmd` hook that runs `eval "$(mise activate zsh)"` after the first prompt is drawn and removes itself with `add-zsh-hook -d`. The prompt appears at once and the real activation happens about 100 ms later, before I can type anything meaningful.

There was one problem. The prompt showed the Node version segment empty on the very first line in a new shell, because the segment reads `mise current` and the hook had not run yet. I made the segment cache nothing and print nothing until the hook flag `_MISE_READY` is set.

Start time is now about 330 ms in `time zsh -i -c exit` and the first prompt visibly appears faster in Ghostty. I want to get under 200 ms, so the next look is at the fzf and the git completion files.

summary: Found that fzf key bindings and a sourced git-completion file cost 70 ms together; lazy loading brought start time to about 190 ms
body:
I used zprof again after the mise change. The top entries were now the fzf shell integration and a git completion script I had sourced by hand from an old Homebrew path.

The fzf line was `source <(fzf --zsh)`, which spawns a process every start. I changed it to generate the output once into a file, ~/.cache/fzf.zsh, and source that file. The file is regenerated when the fzf binary is newer than the cache. That saved about 35 ms.

The git completion was sourced from /usr/local/share, a path that does not exist on this Apple Silicon machine; the line was guarded with a test but the test used a slow `$(brew --prefix)` call. brew --prefix alone took 30 ms. I replaced it with the fixed /opt/homebrew path and kept the guard as a plain `[[ -r ]]` check.

Results over ten runs: average 190 ms, best 172 ms, worst 240 ms. The worst case happens when the compdump is rebuilt, which is expected once a day.

I wrote the final numbers next to the first ones in the notes file: 640 ms before, 190 ms now. I think this is enough for the topic and I will leave the rest. One open item is the cache files going stale after a Homebrew upgrade of fzf, which the timestamp check should cover.

summary: Set up commit signing with an SSH key from the 1Password agent instead of GPG, and verified a signed commit locally
body:
I wanted signed commits without keeping a GPG keyring around. Since the SSH keys already live in the 1Password agent, I used SSH signing.

In ~/.gitconfig I set `gpg.format = ssh`, `user.signingkey` to the public key string, `commit.gpgsign = true` and `tag.gpgsign = true`. The program line `gpg.ssh.program` points to `/Applications/1Password.app/Contents/MacOS/op-ssh-sign`, which is what makes the agent do the signing and prompt for Touch ID.

The first test commit failed with `error: Load key ... incorrect passphrase supplied` which was confusing. The cause was that I had put the path of a private key file in `user.signingkey` from an old attempt. With the key given as `key::ssh-ed25519 AAAA...` it worked.

For local verification git needs an allowed signers file. I created ~/.config/git/allowed_signers with my email and the public key, and set `gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile` to it. After that `git log --show-signature` printed `Good "git" signature` for the test commit in a scratch repository.

One side effect is that every commit now asks for Touch ID if 1Password is locked. That is fine for normal work, but scripted commits in loops would be annoying. I added a git alias `nosign` that runs `git -c commit.gpgsign=false commit` for those cases.

Still to do: upload the public key to the hosting service as a signing key, not only as an authentication key.

summary: Added tmux bindings for splitting in the current path and resizing panes, and moved the prefix handling so nested sessions over SSH still work
body:
The tmux config had the default split keys, which open new panes in the home directory. I rebound them so that `prefix |` and `prefix -` split with `-c "#{pane_current_path}"`, and the same for new windows with `prefix c`.

For resizing I added `prefix H/J/K/L` as repeatable bindings with `bind -r`, five cells per press. I first used the capital letters without `-r` and had to press prefix each time, which was tiresome, so I added the flag.

The second part was about nested sessions. When I SSH into another machine that also runs tmux, the inner session eats the prefix of the outer one. I added a binding on `F12` that toggles the outer tmux into an "off" key table: it sets `prefix None`, changes the status line colour to grey and sends all keys to the inner session. Pressing F12 again restores everything. This is the pattern from many public tmux configs but I wrote it with my own colours.

I tested it by running tmux locally inside tmux. The toggle worked, but the status line colour stayed grey after reload with `source-file`. The cause was that the reload set the status style before the key table check. I moved the style definitions into a separate `if-shell` block that checks `#{?prefix_disabled,...}`; it is simpler to use the conditional format in `status-style` directly, and that is what I did.

The binding table now has 14 custom lines. I added a comment above each so I can remember them later. Next time I want to look at copy mode keys and the clipboard integration.

summary: Pointed tmux copy mode at the macOS clipboard with pbcopy and vi keys, so yanking a selection lands in the system clipboard
body:
Short follow-up on the tmux work from earlier today. Copy mode used the default emacs keys and the yanked text stayed inside tmux only.

I set `mode-keys vi`, bound `v` to begin selection and `y` to `copy-pipe-and-cancel "pbcopy"`. I also bound `Enter` the same way so that mouse drag release copies too, via `MouseDragEnd1Pane`.

I checked it by selecting a line in a pane, pressing `y` and pasting into a text field in another app. It worked. Inside a nested SSH session the clipboard of the remote machine is not reachable, so there I would need the OSC 52 escape. I turned on `set -g set-clipboard on` and Ghostty accepted it, but I did not test it on a remote host yet.

The config is reloaded with `prefix r`, and I confirmed that one still works after the changes. Nothing else is open on tmux for now.

summary: Tested OSC 52 clipboard copy from tmux over SSH to a remote host; it works after allowing it in Ghostty and tmux's terminal-features
body:
I tested the open item from the last tmux session: copying from a tmux session on a remote Linux box into the clipboard of the Mac.

First attempt: in the remote tmux I selected text and pressed `y`. Nothing arrived in the Mac clipboard. The remote config only had `set-clipboard on` from my copied file, and the remote tmux version was 3.2, older than the local one.

I checked the local side next. Ghostty has `clipboard-write = allow` as its default, but I had set it to `ask` in the config some weeks ago while testing, so a prompt had appeared quietly behind another window. I changed it back to `allow`.

Then I tested the escape sequence directly without tmux: `printf '\e]52;c;%s\a' "$(printf hello | base64)"` on the remote. The text hello appeared in the clipboard. So the terminal was fine and the problem was in tmux.

Locally, tmux needs to know the terminal supports the clipboard feature. I added `set -as terminal-features ',xterm-ghostty:clipboard'` on the Mac side, and on the remote host `set -g set-clipboard on` plus the `Ms` override was not needed once the version was updated through the package manager to 3.4.

After that the yank from the remote tmux reached the Mac clipboard, also when there were two nested tmux layers, as long as the inner one had set-clipboard on and the outer one allowed passthrough.

I wrote a short comment block in tmux.conf listing these three settings, because I will forget them. Remaining: check the same on a second remote machine that I rarely use.

summary: Wrote a first Brewfile cleanup: listed 41 formulae and casks not in the file and decided which to keep or remove
body:
I ran `brew bundle cleanup --file=~/dotfiles/Brewfile` without `--force` to see what is installed but not listed. It printed 41 items.

Most were dependencies that are fine to leave, but some were real tools I had installed by hand and forgot: `jq`, `ripgrep`, `watch` and two casks for apps I still use. I added those to the Brewfile.

The rest looked like leftovers: three old language servers, `nvm` itself, which is not needed after the move to mise, and a cask for a screen recorder I used once. I wrote them into a list but did not remove them yet.

I also noticed that `brew bundle check` reported a missing item, a tap that was renamed. I fixed the tap name in the Brewfile.

Next step is running the cleanup with `--force` after looking at the list once more, to avoid losing something that a script uses.

summary: Ran the Brewfile cleanup for real, removed 17 leftovers, and found that a backup script depended on one of them
body:
Following last week's list, I ran `brew bundle cleanup --force` after removing the items I wanted to keep from the list by adding them to the Brewfile. It uninstalled 17 packages and casks, including nvm, the old language servers and the screen recorder.

The next morning's checks would have caught the problem, but I noticed it earlier: I ran the backup script by hand as a test and it failed with `rsync: command not found` in a branch that calls `/opt/homebrew/bin/rsync`. I had installed the newer rsync from Homebrew some time ago for the `--info=progress2` output, and I had not put it in the Brewfile. The cleanup removed it. macOS ships an old 2.6.9 rsync which does not support that flag.

I reinstalled it with `brew install rsync` and added `brew "rsync"` to the Brewfile with a comment saying that the backup script needs it. After that the script ran to the end and the dry run printed the usual 3.2 GB of changes.

To avoid this again, I added a check at the top of the backup script that exits with a clear message if the Homebrew rsync is missing or older than version 3.

I also searched my scripts and shell files for other absolute paths into /opt/homebrew/bin. There were four, all for tools that are in the Brewfile now. The cleanup is finished.

One more detail: `brew autoremove` removed nothing extra afterwards, so the dependency graph is consistent.

summary: Replaced the hand-written macOS defaults script's repeated lines with a small function and added the Dock and Finder settings I had been setting by hand
body:
The defaults script had about 60 lines of `defaults write` with the same pattern, and a few settings I change on every new setup were missing. I wrote a small function `setdef domain key type value` that does the write and prints what changed by reading the old value first.

The output is useful: on a rerun it shows only the lines that actually changed, instead of a wall of silent commands. I tested it by running it twice. The first run printed 9 changes after I changed two values by hand in System Settings, and the second run printed none.

I added the Dock settings: autohide on, a smaller icon size of 42, no recent apps. For Finder I added showing the path bar, the status bar, and a default of list view. I also set the screenshot folder to ~/Pictures/Screenshots and created it in the script if missing.

One setting did not take effect: the key repeat rate. `defaults write -g KeyRepeat -int 2` only applies after logging out. I added a message at the end of the script that says a logout is required.

At the end the script runs `killall Dock Finder SystemUIServer` so the changes are visible at once. There was a short flash of the screen when I tested it, which is normal.

summary: Fixed Neovim reporting a stale Node version in LSP because it started before mise had set PATH; the editor now reads versions through shims
body:
Neovim's TypeScript language server kept failing with `Unsupported engine` messages in a project that needs Node 20, although the terminal showed Node 20.

I checked `:!node -v` inside Neovim and it printed 18. So the editor process had a different PATH than the shell. The reason was my lazy activation of mise from a few weeks ago: when I start nvim from a fresh shell very quickly, or from a launcher, the full activation has not run and the PATH has the shims only. The shims should still resolve the right version, but the project directory was one level above the .tool-versions file, and the shim picked the global default of 18.

I looked at three options. One was to start the activation eagerly again, which costs 100 ms and I did not want it. A second was to launch nvim through `mise exec`, which is slower at start. The third was to make the shims honour the project: the .tool-versions file was in the repo root, but I had opened nvim from a subfolder, and mise looks upward, so that should work. Looking again, the file was named `.tool-version` without the s in that project. That was the real bug.

I renamed the file, and the LSP found Node 20. The lazy activation was not the cause, though it made it harder to see.

To catch this faster, I added `mise doctor` to my notes as a first check, and a small `:checkhealth`-like line in the Neovim statusline that shows the Node version the LSP uses. Not needed long term, and I will remove it later.

summary: Added a Zed keymap for the Neovim muscle-memory bindings I still miss: file finder, buffer switching and window splits
body:
I have been using Zed for TypeScript work and kept pressing Neovim keys in it. I spent a session writing a keymap.json so that the common actions match.

Zed's vim mode already covers motions. What was missing were my leader mappings. I bound space-f to the file finder, space-b to the tab switcher, space-g to the git panel and space-e to toggle the project panel. The leader is space in normal mode, with a context of `vim_mode == normal`.

Splits were more annoying. In Neovim I use `ctrl-w v` and `ctrl-w s`. Zed vim mode supports the ctrl-w family but `ctrl-w v` opened the new pane to the left by default. I added explicit bindings for `workspace::SplitRight` and `workspace::SplitDown` under the same keys.

For moving between panes I bound ctrl-h, ctrl-j, ctrl-k and ctrl-l, as I do in tmux and Neovim, to the `workspace::ActivatePane...` actions. This conflicted with the terminal panel, where ctrl-l clears the screen. I limited the binding to the `Editor` context, so the terminal panel keeps its normal behaviour.

The result is 22 lines of JSON. I tested every binding once. Not done: the Neovim `gcc` comment motion works in Zed already, and the surround plugin keys do too, so no work was needed there.

summary: Wrote down the dotfiles layout and the order for setting up a new machine in a README, after finding two scripts that assumed the other had run
body:
While reading the scripts for another reason I noticed that the macOS defaults script uses a folder that the Brewfile step is supposed to create, and the backup script expects a config file that no script writes.

I wrote a README.md in the dotfiles folder. It lists the order: install Homebrew, run `brew bundle`, run the symlink script, run the defaults script, log out, then sign in to 1Password and enable the SSH agent.

I fixed the two assumptions as well. The defaults script now creates the screenshot folder itself, and the backup script writes a default config on first start when none exists and then exits with a message so I can look at it.

I did not test the whole path from nothing, since that needs a clean machine. That is planned for when I set up the new Mac.

summary: Looked into why git status was slow in the prompt on a large repo; async git info in the prompt cut the lag from about 900 ms to none
body:
In the biggest repository I work in, every prompt took close to a second to appear. I confirmed it with `time git status --porcelain=v2 --branch` which took 880 ms, so the prompt was waiting on git.

The prompt called git status synchronously in precmd. I changed it to run asynchronously. The prompt is drawn at once with no git segment, and a background job writes the result to a temp file and signals the shell with `kill -USR1`. A TRAPUSR1 handler reads the file and calls `zle reset-prompt`.

The first version had a race. If I pressed enter quickly, the old job's result arrived at the next prompt and showed the status of the previous directory. I fixed it by tagging each job with the current `$PWD` and a counter, and ignoring results that do not match.

I also reduced the cost of the git call itself. `git status` was spending most of its time looking for untracked files, so for repositories with more than a set number of files I use `-uno` and mark the segment with a small dot meaning untracked files are not checked. Core `fsmonitor` is another option, but I did not want a background daemon yet.

The prompt now appears in about 15 ms in the large repo, and the branch name shows up some 300 ms later. In small repositories the segment fills in so fast that it looks the same as before.

Next check: that it behaves well inside tmux when switching panes quickly.

summary: Set up the new Mac from the scripts and recorded the eleven things that did not work without manual steps
body:
The new Mac arrived and I used it to run the whole setup path from the README for the first time on a clean machine. The agent followed the steps while I watched and fixed problems in the scripts.

Homebrew installed fine. `brew bundle` took about 14 minutes and failed on two casks because one app needed a password prompt that cannot be answered inside the script. I moved those two to a separate Brewfile.manual and noted it in the README.

The symlink script failed on the first line because ~/.config did not exist yet. I added `mkdir -p`. It also refused to overwrite a default .zshrc created by macOS. I changed it to move existing files to a `.pre-dotfiles` folder first, so nothing is lost and the script can run again.

mise was installed but the Node and Python versions were not, since the global versions come from a file that the symlink script links. After linking, `mise install` ran and took about 3 minutes.

The defaults script needed full disk access for the terminal to change one Safari key, and it printed an error that was hard to read. I removed the Safari lines, since I do not use that browser much.

SSH worked after enabling the 1Password agent and adding the `IdentityAgent` line. A test with `ssh -T git@github.com` greeted me by name. Commit signing worked after the first Touch ID prompt.

Ghostty read its config at once. The font was JetBrains Mono and it was not installed yet, so it fell back to a different font; I added the font cask to the Brewfile since it was missing there.

In total there were eleven fixes, now in the scripts or the README. The machine is usable after about 50 minutes, of which most is waiting. A list of things to do by hand remains: sign in to 1Password, sync the editor settings, and restore the backup folder.

summary: Restored the backup folder to the new Mac with rsync and checked file counts and permissions on the SSH directory
body:
After the machine setup of yesterday I restored my documents and project folders from the external drive with the Homebrew rsync, using `-aH --info=progress2`.

The transfer was 61 GB and took about 38 minutes. I compared the file counts with `find | wc -l` on both sides and got 214,903 files on each. A second rsync run with `-n` showed no differences.

One thing needed fixing: the ~/.ssh folder was restored with the permissions of the drive, 755, and ssh warned about it. I ran `chmod 700 ~/.ssh` and `chmod 600` on the config file. The private keys are not there, as they live in 1Password.

I also found that the backup script excluded `node_modules` by name but not `.venv`, which added 4 GB. I added the exclude for the next run.

summary: Switched Neovim from a hand-rolled plugin loader to lazy.nvim and cut startup time from 140 ms to 55 ms
body:
The Neovim config still used a loader I wrote a long time ago that sourced every plugin file at start. I measured with `nvim --startuptime /tmp/s.log +q` and got 140 ms.

I moved the plugin list to lazy.nvim. The bootstrap goes at the top of init.lua: it clones lazy.nvim into the data folder if missing and adds it to the runtimepath. Each plugin is now a table with `event`, `cmd` or `keys` so that it loads only when needed.

The move went plugin by plugin. Telescope loads on its key mappings, the treesitter config on `BufReadPost`, and the completion plugin on `InsertEnter`. The LSP setup loads on `BufReadPre`. For the colour scheme I used `lazy = false` with a high priority, otherwise the first screen flashes the default colours.

Three things broke. First, the git signs plugin was loaded after the buffer was open and showed nothing until I reopened the file; changing the event to `BufReadPre` fixed that. Second, a mapping defined in my old config for the file tree used a function that no longer existed; I moved it into the plugin's `keys` list. Third, treesitter parsers were reinstalled on every start because the `build` field was missing `:TSUpdate`.

I also generated the lock file `lazy-lock.json` and put it in the dotfiles folder, so the machines get the same plugin versions.

After the change startup is 55 ms on average over ten runs. `:Lazy profile` shows only 9 of 31 plugins loaded at start.

Still to check: the Zed and Neovim keymaps should stay in sync, which I will do when I next change either of them.

summary: Fixed the lazy.nvim lock file being ignored on the second Mac by restoring the right symlink target for the data folder
body:
On the new Mac, Neovim installed newer plugin versions than the lock file said. `:Lazy` showed several plugins marked as updated that I never updated.

The reason was that the symlink script linked the config folder, but lazy writes `lazy-lock.json` inside the config folder. On this machine a copy of the file had been created as a normal file next to the link, shadowing the one in the dotfiles folder. I deleted the stray copy and relinked it.

Then I ran `:Lazy restore`, which put all plugins back at the locked commits. It took about a minute. I added a check to the symlink script that warns when the lock file is a regular file and not a link.

summary: Added a Ghostty keybinding set for splits and tabs and removed the overlap with the tmux prefix keys
body:
Ghostty had some default bindings for splits that I sometimes triggered by mistake while using tmux, since both use the command key and similar letters.

I listed the active bindings with `ghostty +list-keybinds` and compared them with my tmux bindings. Three overlapped: split right, split down and close surface.

I decided that tmux owns the splits. In the Ghostty config I set `keybind = cmd+d=unbind` and the same for cmd+shift+d. Tabs stay in Ghostty, with cmd+t and cmd+number as usual, since I use one tab per project and tmux sessions inside.

I reloaded with cmd+shift+comma and tested each key once. No overlap remains. The change is four lines.

summary: Checked that the whole shell start is still under 200 ms after all recent changes and added a small timing script to catch regressions
body:
After several changes to the shell config, I wanted to know whether the start time had crept up since the work on the slow start. I ran `time zsh -i -c exit` ten times on both Macs.

The old Mac averaged 205 ms and the new one 150 ms. The old one was 15 ms above the last measurement of 190 ms. A zprof run showed that the async git prompt setup added about 12 ms for defining the functions and loading `zsh/datetime`. That seemed an acceptable price for the prompt that never waits.

To see regressions earlier, I wrote a small script `bin/shell-time` that runs the interactive start twenty times, drops the highest and lowest and prints the mean. It exits with a non-zero code if the mean is above 250 ms, so I can use it by hand or in a login check.

I tested the failure path by adding a `sleep 0.1` to .zshrc temporarily. The script printed a mean of 312 ms and exit code 1. Then I removed the sleep.

I added the script to the README with the numbers of today as the baseline. The shell topic is closed for now.

summary: Moved the Neovim LSP setup to the native vim.lsp.config API and dropped a plugin layer, which removed two startup warnings and 9 ms from the editor start
body:
The LSP setup had been going through nvim-lspconfig with a wrapper function I wrote years ago. Neovim now has a native way to define and enable servers, so I tried it for lua_ls, ts_ls and pyright first. The wrapper was only adding default capabilities and an on_attach, and both can be set once through a global config.

I created lsp/ in the Neovim config folder with one small file per server. Each file returns a table with cmd, filetypes and root_markers. The shared settings went into a single vim.lsp.config('*', {...}) call in lua/lsp.lua. After that, vim.lsp.enable({'lua_ls','ts_ls','pyright'}) turns the servers on.

Two warnings at start had come from the old wrapper calling a deprecated function. Both are gone now. I measured startup with --startuptime ten times before and after. The median fell from 55 ms to 46 ms.

The keymaps for go to definition, rename and code action lived in the old on_attach. I moved them to an LspAttach autocommand, so they are set per buffer only when a server attaches. I checked it by opening a Lua file, a TypeScript file and a Python file and running :checkhealth vim.lsp, which showed the right root for each.

One problem came up. The TypeScript server picked the home folder as its root in a loose file with no package.json. Adding .git and tsconfig.json to root_markers for ts_ls fixed this. It still looks at the home folder for a scratch file, which I accept.

I did not touch the formatting setup, which still uses conform.nvim. I left a comment in lsp.lua about the root markers so I do not repeat the search later. Next I want to check that the lock file for lazy.nvim does not still list the old wrapper plugin, and remove it from the plugin list.

summary: Removed nvim-lspconfig from the plugin list after the native LSP move and cleaned its entry out of lazy-lock.json; the editor started clean on both Macs
body:
After this afternoon's LSP change, nvim-lspconfig was still in the plugin spec because the old wrapper required it. I deleted the spec file and ran :Lazy clean, which removed the folder from the data directory.

The lock file still listed the plugin until I ran :Lazy sync. Then I committed the lock file in the dotfiles folder. Because this folder is not a git repository, the committing is really just the lock file copy that the symlink points to. I checked that the symlink target is still the one I fixed last time.

On the second Mac I synced and opened a Lua file. The server attached and the diagnostics showed. There was one hiccup: nvim-cmp used a capability helper from lspconfig. It threw an error on the first insert. I replaced it with the capabilities from the cmp-nvim-lsp plugin directly and the error went away.

I also searched the config for the string lspconfig to see if anything else referenced it. Only a comment was left, which I reworded. The startup time is stable at 46 ms on both machines.

summary: Set up a Zed task and a tasks.json for running project tests, so the same test command works from Zed and from the Neovim terminal split
body:
Until now I ran tests in Zed by switching to a terminal and typing the command. Zed has tasks, so I wanted one place to define them and use them from the keyboard.

I started with the global tasks file in the Zed config folder. It has three tasks: test file, test project and lint. Each calls a small script from my bin folder instead of holding the command itself. That way the Neovim side can call the same script.

The script is named run-tests. It looks at the working directory and picks a runner: pnpm test if there is a package.json with a test script, pytest if there is a pyproject.toml, and cargo test if there is a Cargo.toml. For the file variant it passes the file path along. I tested it in three small scratch projects, one for each runner.

Zed passes the current file through the variable $ZED_FILE. In the first try I forgot to quote it, and a path with a space broke the run. I added quotes and tested with a folder called My Project. It worked.

I bound the tasks in the Zed keymap to the same leader-style keys that I use in Neovim for tests. That uses the keymap work from some weeks ago. The task output opens in the bottom panel, which I like better than a new tab.

On the Neovim side I added a mapping that runs the script in a tmux split below with the current file. It uses tmux split-window with -c so the path stays the same, as I set it up earlier.

There is one thing left. The pytest case does not find the mise Python when Zed starts from the Dock, because the environment does not have the shims in the PATH. I will look at this next.

summary: Zed launched from the Dock did not see mise shims, so tasks used system Python; fixed by prepending the shims directory in the script itself
body:
This follows the Zed tasks work from earlier in the week. Running the pytest task from a Zed window opened by the Dock used /usr/bin/python3 instead of the version mise pins in the project.

The reason is that apps started by launchd do not read my zsh files, so the PATH has no shims. Zed opened from the terminal with the zed command inherits the shell environment and works fine. That explained why it passed in my first test.

I considered three options. One was setting the PATH globally with launchctl setenv, but that is lost at restart and I do not want another script for it. The second was telling Zed to load the shell environment, which it already does per project directory, but in my case the lazy mise activation never runs in a non-interactive shell. The third was to fix run-tests itself.

I chose the third. At the top of the script I added export PATH="$HOME/.local/share/mise/shims:$PATH". The shims are the thing I already use for non-interactive work, as I decided when I made the activation lazy.

To check it I added a line printing python --version and which python at the start of the pytest branch. From the Dock-launched Zed it showed 3.12 from the shims, matching .tool-versions. I removed the debug lines afterward.

The Node case already worked because pnpm is installed by Homebrew in a fixed path. I noted the shim line in the README under the section about editors.

summary: Looked at why the backup script's log grew to 600 MB and found rsync was run with -v on a folder of caches; excluded them and the log is now a few KB per run
body:
The backup script from some months ago writes one log file and I had never looked at its size. It was 600 MB. Inside, almost every line was a file under a Library/Caches path and a node_modules folder in an old project.

rsync was running with -av. I kept -a but replaced -v with --stats and --itemize-changes limited to changed files. I also created an exclude file next to the script with the cache folders, node_modules, .venv and the Trash.

A dry run with -n showed that 38 GB of data would no longer be copied. The next real run took 4 minutes instead of 19. I checked that the SSH directory and the documents folder were still included by listing the destination.

I also added a simple log rotation: the script keeps the last five logs and deletes the older ones. The old 600 MB file was removed.

summary: Added a restore check to the backup script that compares file counts of Documents and the SSH directory against the source after each run and prints a warning on mismatch
body:
Since the exclusions changed this afternoon, I wanted a small check that something important is not silently left out. After the rsync step the script now counts files in the Documents folder and the SSH directory on both sides with find and wc -l.

If the numbers differ, the script prints a line starting with WARN and exits with code 2. A normal run still exits with 0. I ran it once normally and it passed with 2,114 files in Documents.

To test the failure path I touched a new file in the source after the sync step in a copy of the script. It printed the warning as expected. I also checked permissions of the SSH directory on the destination with stat and they were 700.

One caveat is that Documents contains files that change while the script runs, such as a sync lock file. I excluded that file name to avoid false warnings. The check takes about 3 seconds.

summary: Replaced the hand-written prompt git segment's branch and dirty-state code with one git status --porcelain=v2 call, and fixed ahead/behind arrows that were wrong after a rebase
body:
The prompt showed the wrong ahead/behind count after a rebase onto a moved upstream. I looked at the segment and saw that it ran four git commands: one for the branch, one for dirty files, one for untracked files and one for rev-list counts. The counts used the wrong range after the rebase because they compared against a cached upstream name.

I rewrote the segment to run git status --porcelain=v2 --branch once. The output has the branch name in a line named branch.head and ahead/behind in branch.ab. File lines start with 1, 2 or ? for changed, renamed and untracked entries. One parsing loop in zsh reads the lines and sets the variables.

The rebase problem disappeared, since git computes branch.ab against the current upstream itself. I reproduced the old bug in a scratch repo first. I made a branch, pushed it to a bare remote, advanced the remote by two commits, rebased locally and checked that the prompt now shows two arrows pointing down, then one up after a local commit.

The prompt is async since a few months ago, so the new code runs in the worker. I only had to change what the worker prints and how the main shell parses the result. The result is passed as one line separated by tabs, which is less fragile than the earlier format.

I compared timing on the large repo that was slow before. The old segment took about 310 ms in the worker, the new one 190 ms. The prompt itself still appears at once since it does not wait.

There were some special cases to test. A detached HEAD shows the short hash, because branch.head then reads (detached) and I use branch.oid. A fresh repository with no commit has branch.oid set to (initial), and I show the name only. Both cases work.

The stash count was also in the old segment. porcelain=v2 can give it with --show-stash, so I added the flag and read the line branch.stash... actually this line is called stash and appears only if there are stashes. I tested with git stash and it showed a small marker.

I deleted the old helper functions. The shell start time script still reports under 200 ms. Next I will add a test file for the parser with canned output, since I only checked it by hand.

summary: Added a small test script for the prompt's git status parser using canned porcelain v2 output, covering detached HEAD, initial commit, renames and stash
body:
This follows the porcelain v2 rewrite from this morning. The parser was only checked by hand, and I did not want to repeat the rebase bug without noticing.

I moved the parsing into its own function that takes the text on standard input and sets variables. A file in the tests folder holds six canned outputs, one for each case: clean branch, ahead and behind, detached HEAD, initial commit with no commits, a rename line, and a stash line.

The test script is plain zsh. It sources the function, feeds each sample, and compares the variables with the expected values. It prints PASS or FAIL per case and exits with the number of failures.

On the first run the rename case failed. Type 2 lines have a tab between the new and old path, and my loop split on spaces only, so the count of changed files was right but the path variable was wrong. The prompt does not use the path, so it did not hurt, but I fixed the split anyway.

All six pass now. I added the script to the list in the README of things to run after changes in the prompt, next to the timing script.

summary: Wrote the git alias for a safer force push and a log view that shows signed state, after confusing a plain force push on a shared branch
body:
I nearly force pushed over a colleague-style change on a shared branch of my own side project, because git push -f does not check the remote. I added an alias named pushf that runs git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes.

I tested it in a scratch repo with two clones. In the second clone I pushed a commit. Then in the first clone, after a rebase without fetching, pushf was rejected with a stale info message. After a fetch it still refused since the commit was not included in my local history, which is what I want.

I also changed the log alias to show a short signature mark with %G? in the format. Since the signing change some weeks ago, my commits should show G. A commit from before shows N. It fits on the line and uses a colour.

I left the old -f habit alone but removed my alias that called git push -f. Done in the gitconfig file.

summary: Fixed Ghostty not restoring the working directory in new tabs when the shell was started through tmux, by sending the OSC 7 escape from the prompt hook
body:
New Ghostty tabs opened in the home folder when the previous tab was inside tmux. Without tmux the directory carried over fine, so shell integration was working.

Ghostty learns the directory from the OSC 7 escape sequence. Inside tmux the sequence is swallowed unless it is wrapped for passthrough. I first tried set -g allow-passthrough on in tmux.conf, which is the same option I used for the clipboard test a while ago. It was already on for the clipboard but my hook did not send OSC 7 at all, because I had disabled Ghostty's shell integration for zsh to keep the prompt simple.

I added my own chpwd hook that prints the escape with the host name and the path, URL-encoded with a small function. Inside tmux it wraps the sequence in the tmux passthrough form with doubled escape characters. Outside tmux it prints it plain.

I tested with a path containing a space and a non-ASCII letter. Both opened correctly in a new tab. The cost in the prompt is not measurable, since the function only runs on cd.

One remaining thing is that panes created with the tmux split key already use the current path, so only tabs were affected. I wrote the reason in a comment above the hook, because it is not obvious why the wrapping is there.

summary: Moved the tmux config's plugin handling to a small manual clone list and fixed the status line colors that turned wrong under Ghostty's true color mode
body:
The tmux status line had looked washed out since the move to Ghostty, and the cause turned out to be the terminal-overrides line, which still named the old iTerm2 setup. I checked what tmux thought the terminal was with tmux info and saw that the RGB capability was missing for xterm-ghostty. Colors were falling back to the 256 palette, which explained the dull blue in the status bar and the odd gray of the pane borders.

I replaced the old override with a terminal-features entry for RGB and kept a fallback for xterm-256color so SSH sessions into older hosts still look fine. After restarting the tmux server the status line colors matched the theme. I compared a test gradient script before and after, and the banding was gone.

While in the file I looked at the plugin manager. It cloned plugins at first start and ran a network call on every new server, which added a visible pause. I dropped the manager and wrote a short list of three plugins as plain git clones into a folder under the dotfiles directory, each pinned to a commit. A tiny script updates them on request. Sourcing them directly from tmux.conf with run-shell works and the server start is quicker by a noticeable margin.

One snag: the resurrect-style plugin expected the manager's path variable and failed silently. I set the path by hand in the config and confirmed that saving and restoring a session works. The new layout is described in the README under the tmux section. What is left is a check in the broken-link script for the plugin folder, which I will add next time I touch that script.

summary: Looked into a tmux status bar that showed the wrong battery state after wake and replaced the shell call with a cached value refreshed every 30 seconds
body:
The tmux status line showed 100 percent for a while after waking the laptop. The status script called pmset -g batt on every refresh, which is every 5 seconds, and sometimes it returned stale output right after wake.

I changed the script so that it writes the result to a temp file and reads from it when the file is younger than 30 seconds. After wake the first call is a fresh one, since the cache is old by then. I checked it by closing the lid for a minute and the value was right when I opened it.

The change also removed a lot of small process starts. I counted before and after with a loop over a minute, and it went from 12 calls to 2.

summary: Added a mise task setup that installs the pinned Node and Python for a new project folder, and fixed a global config that was overridden by an old .tool-versions in the home folder
body:
In a new project folder, node --version printed an old version even though I had set the global one with mise use -g. I ran mise doctor and mise ls and found a .tool-versions file in the home directory, left from the time I used asdf. It pinned Node to a version two majors behind and took priority over the global config.

I moved it to a backup name and the global value took effect. To avoid this happening again I added a line to the check script that warns if there is a .tool-versions in the home folder.

Then I did the planned part. I wanted a single command to prepare a new project. The mise config in the dotfiles folder now has a task named setup. It creates a mise.toml with Node 22 and Python 3.12 if none exists, runs mise install, and prints the resulting versions. Tasks are defined in a tasks section of the global config, so they are available everywhere.

I tested it in an empty folder. The file appeared, the install took 40 seconds for the first time because Python had to compile a build, and the second time it took one second. The versions it printed were the ones I expected.

The lazy activation made one thing awkward. In an interactive shell, the first prompt hook loads mise, so the cd into the project and the mise run setup call must happen after that. A command typed immediately after a cd worked, but a script running cd and mise in one line did not find the new versions because mise had not yet hooked. That case uses the shims, so it still resolved to the right tool after the install.

I wrote down in the README that new projects should start with mise run setup. I also checked that the tmux new-window key opens in the project and that the right Node shows up there.

One leftover is that the setup task does not yet handle projects with a .nvmrc. I decided not to build that, as I no longer have any projects with only that file.

summary: Pinned the Homebrew bundle to skip casks that update themselves, so brew upgrade no longer replaces Ghostty and Zed in the middle of work
body:
Brew upgrade had replaced the Zed app while it was open, and the editor crashed on the next save. I looked at the Brewfile and found that all casks were upgraded by default, including the ones that update themselves through their own channel. That produced two update paths for the same app and sometimes a version mismatch between the cask record and the installed app.

I went through the nine casks in the file. Ghostty, Zed and 1Password update themselves, so I marked those with greedy turned off and added a comment explaining why. The rest, such as the font casks and a few small utilities, stay under brew control. I then ran brew outdated --cask to see what would be touched, and the self-updating apps no longer appeared.

I also wrote a small wrapper alias, bup, that runs brew update, shows the outdated list and asks before upgrading anything. It refuses to run while Ghostty or Zed is the frontmost app, which sounds fussy but is the exact situation that caused the crash. The check uses osascript to read the frontmost application name and takes about 80 ms.

The brew bundle check still passes on both Macs. I did not change the formulae section. A later step is a weekly reminder about outdated packages, but I decided against automating upgrades for now, since the last cleanup showed that a backup script depends on one formula and a surprise upgrade could break it.

summary: Moved the Zed file exclusion list to a per-project .zed/settings.json for the big repo only, after finding the global rule hid a vendored folder I need elsewhere
body:
This morning's global file_scan_exclusions hid a folder called dist in a small project where I keep hand-written output that I do need to open. That was the downside I noted, and it showed up faster than expected.

I removed the list from the global settings and put it into .zed/settings.json in the big repo. Zed merges project settings over the global ones, so the other projects are back to defaults.

I tested both. The big repo still stayed at about 900 MB after a restart and a build. The small project listed dist in the finder again.

The .zed folder is not committed there, since I added it to the local git exclude file with the path in .git/info/exclude. That keeps my editor setup out of the shared repo history.

summary: Checked why the macOS defaults script reset the key repeat rate after a reboot, and found the setting needs a logout, not just a restart of the Dock
body:
After running the defaults script on a second user account, the fast key repeat was not active. The script wrote KeyRepeat 2 and InitialKeyRepeat 15 correctly, and defaults read showed the values.

The settings only take effect after logout and login, since the input system reads them at session start. My script only restarted the Dock and Finder with killall, which is enough for the other settings.

I added a message at the end of the script that lists the settings which need a logout, instead of trying to do it for the user. After logging out, the repeat rate was right.

I also checked that the script runs twice without error. It does, since defaults write is idempotent.

summary: Replaced the clumsy zsh history setup with shared, deduplicated history and a fzf-based search on the up key, and trimmed a 180,000 line history file
body:
The history file had grown to 180,000 lines with many repeats. Searching with the up key stepped through the same command over and over.

I set HISTSIZE and SAVEHIST to 100000 and turned on HIST_IGNORE_ALL_DUPS, HIST_REDUCE_BLANKS and HIST_IGNORE_SPACE. SHARE_HISTORY was already on, but I removed INC_APPEND_HISTORY because it is implied.

Before touching the file I made a copy. Then I deduplicated it with a short awk command that keeps the last occurrence of each command and respects the extended history format. It went from 180,000 lines to 41,000. I checked that the multiline commands still looked fine, as they use a backslash at the line end.

For search I had Ctrl-R from fzf already. I wanted the up key to search by prefix, so I added history-substring-search style widgets with the built-in up-line-or-beginning-search and down-line-or-beginning-search. Typing git c and pressing up now steps through only the matches.

In tmux the up key sent a different code than outside. I bound both forms, the one from terminfo and the plain escape sequence, and it worked in both places.

I also added a rule that stops commands with a token or password pattern from being saved. It uses the zshaddhistory hook and checks for the words TOKEN= and password=. I tested it with a fake line and it was not saved.

The shell start time stayed the same at about 190 ms, because reading the smaller file is cheap.

One open point is that the secret filter only catches obvious patterns. I will not try to make it clever.

summary: Set up Neovim to use the system clipboard only on explicit yank, and fixed paste in tmux inserting a stray character at the start of each line
body:
Pasting multi-line text into Neovim inside tmux added a stray character at the start of each line and made the indent grow with each line. That was auto-indent working on the pasted text as if it were typed.

Bracketed paste should prevent that. I checked if tmux passes it on with the escape sequence test, and it did, but my config disabled it: an old line in the Neovim config set paste mode with a key toggle and an autocommand that reset it. That fought with the built-in handling.

I removed the toggle and the autocommand. Neovim handles bracketed paste by itself now. After that the paste inserted the text as is, with 40 lines and no change of indentation.

The second part was the clipboard option. I had clipboard=unnamedplus set, which made every delete go to the system clipboard and overwrite what I had copied. I removed it and added two mappings: leader y and leader p for the plus register. A normal d no longer replaces my clipboard.

Over SSH the plus register needs the OSC 52 provider, which I tested before. I added a condition that picks the OSC 52 provider when SSH_TTY is set and the default one otherwise. I tried a yank on a remote host and it landed in the Mac clipboard.

One case still fails. Yanking more than about 70 KB over OSC 52 is cut by the terminal. I do not do that often, so I noted it in a comment.

summary: Wrote a script that checks the dotfiles folder for broken symlinks and missing links after a new install, and used it to find three stale links on the old Mac
body:
The setup order is in the README, but after setting up the new Mac I had no way to see whether all links were still right. Over time some targets move and links break without a message.

I wrote a script named check-links. It reads a list of source and target pairs from a file called links.txt in the dotfiles folder. For each pair it tests if the target exists, if it is a symlink, and if it points to the expected source. The result is one line per pair with OK, MISSING, WRONG or BROKEN.

The list had to be created first. I took the link commands from the setup script and turned them into 31 lines of pairs. The setup script now reads the same file to make the links, so the two cannot differ. That was a small change of about ten lines in a loop.

On the new Mac all 31 were OK. On the old Mac the script found three problems. Two were links for the iTerm2 profile and its helper, which no longer exist since the move to Ghostty. The third pointed to a Neovim folder in the old path from before the lazy.nvim change.

I removed the two terminal links from the list and deleted the files. For the third I fixed the target. The next run printed 29 lines, all OK.

The script exits with the number of problems, so it can be used in the setup script at the end to confirm. I added that call. During a test I deleted one link by hand and the end of the setup showed MISSING for it and an exit code of 1.

I also thought about checking file permissions, in particular for the SSH config, which must not be writable by others. I added a separate small check for the mode of the SSH config and the folder, and tested by changing it to 664. The script reported it.

The README now has a line telling to run check-links after any change in the layout. Next I will see if the backup script should run the same check before a backup.

summary: Added a Ghostty config for a dim unfocused split and tuned the theme colors so git diff red and green are readable on the dark background
body:
The red of deleted lines in git diff was hard to read on the dark theme, and I could not tell which Ghostty split had focus at a glance.

For the focus I set unfocused-split-opacity to 0.85 and a fill color slightly darker than the background. The effect is subtle. When I used tmux panes inside one Ghostty split, nothing changed, since the dimming only applies to native splits, which I use less.

For the colors I looked at the palette entries. Palette 1 and 9 are the reds. The theme had a dark red that had a contrast ratio of about 3 to the background. I changed color 1 to a lighter red and checked with a contrast tool, which gave 5.2.

I also set the diff colors in the gitconfig to use bold for new lines and plain for removed ones in addition to the colors, so they are readable without them.

I looked at the result in delta too, since I use it as the pager. It has its own color settings, which were fine, so I left them.

To check everything I ran a diff of the zsh config in a split, with the other split dimmed. Both were easy to read. I saved the color changes in the Ghostty config file with a short comment.

summary: Investigated a broken git credential prompt for HTTPS remotes after the SSH signing change and set the 1Password agent as the only path for SSH remotes
body:
A clone of a repository over HTTPS asked for a username in the terminal, although my other repos used SSH keys. I had set up signing with the SSH agent and thought the two were linked, which they are not.

I looked at git config --show-origin --get-all and found a credential helper from an old install pointing to a path that no longer existed after the Brewfile cleanup. It printed a harmless error but then fell back to the prompt.

I removed that helper from the global config. For HTTPS remotes I rely on the osxkeychain helper, which comes with git from Homebrew. I tested a clone of a private repo and the keychain stored the token after one prompt.

For GitHub remotes I added a url insteadOf rule that rewrites https://github.com/ to git@github.com:, so a pasted HTTPS URL becomes an SSH one. A test clone with the HTTPS URL used the agent and asked for the Touch ID confirmation.

The signing key still works. I made a commit and checked it with git log --show-signature.

I wrote the insteadOf rule down in the README, as it may surprise me later when I see an SSH remote that I did not add.

summary: Built a first version of a bootstrap check that runs on a fresh user account and reports which setup steps still need a manual action, covering seven of the eleven known gaps
body:
When I set up the new Mac I recorded eleven things that did not work without manual steps. I wanted to make the number smaller, so today I made a test account on the Mac and ran the setup scripts from a clean state.

I started with the list. Four items were about permissions that macOS asks for in a dialog, such as full disk access for the terminal and the accessibility permission for the keyboard tool. Those cannot be granted by a script, so I left them as a printed checklist at the end of the setup.

The other seven I tried to fix:
- Xcode command line tools were assumed to exist. The setup now checks xcode-select -p and starts the install, then waits.
- Homebrew was installed after a step that needed it. I changed the order.
- The 1Password agent socket link was created before the app had run. The script now only warns and tells which step to do.
- mise was not on PATH on the first run, so the Node install failed. The script now calls it by full path.
- The Ghostty config folder did not exist yet. I added mkdir -p.
- The tmux plugin manager needed to be cloned first. It is part of the setup now.
- The defaults script needed the logout message I added recently, so it is shown at the end.

I ran the whole thing twice in the test account. The first run took 23 minutes, mostly the Brewfile. The second finished in under a minute and did nothing, which is what I wanted.

One failure appeared on the first run: the Brewfile contained a cask that needs a password. The script stopped at the prompt in a non-interactive way. I moved that cask into a separate Brewfile for steps that need a human.

The check-links script from last week ran at the end and gave 29 OK lines in the new account, so the layout is right there as well.

I updated the README with the new order and the list of what is still manual. The count of manual items is four now, all permission dialogs, plus one note about signing in to 1Password. I will repeat the test in a month to see if anything changed with macOS updates.

summary: Checked the shell start time again after the history and mise changes and found it at 205 ms, then traced 18 ms to the new history filter hook
body:
The timing script flagged a start of 205 ms, above my limit of 200. The recent changes were the history setup and the mise tasks, so I looked at them first.

zprof pointed to the zshaddhistory hook, but that runs per command, not at start. The real cost was a function definition that was loaded with autoload and a zmodload for the pattern matching, about 18 ms together.

I replaced the pattern test with a plain case statement, which needs no module. The start time came back to 187 ms over ten runs.

summary: Cleaned old Neovim swap, undo and shada files that had piled up to 2.3 GB and set the undo directory to prune files older than 90 days at start
body:
The Neovim state folder had 2.3 GB of undo files, because persistent undo was on with no cleanup. Most files belonged to paths that no longer exist.

I deleted the undo files older than 90 days with find and mtime, which removed about 2.1 GB. Swap files from crashes were also there, 14 of them, which I removed after checking that none had unsaved work with nvim -r.

To keep it small I added a small function at start that runs the same find command in the background with vim.system, at most once a day. It uses a stamp file to know when it ran last. Startup time did not change, still 46 ms.

summary: Finished the shell start-up work: moved the history filter hook to precmd-free lazy loading and brought the full start back to 176 ms
body:
The history filter hook found this morning cost 18 ms on every shell start. I looked at where it ran and found it sourced a helper that built a regex list from the history file each time. I moved the list build into a function that runs on the first up-key press instead of at start.

After that change I ran the timing script from the earlier regression work ten times. The median fell from 205 ms to 187 ms. That was still above the 200 ms goal by no margin I liked, so I kept looking.

The next cost was the mise activation line, which took about 11 ms. I switched it to the shims-only mode for non-interactive shells and kept full activation for interactive ones. The median moved to 176 ms.

I also checked that the fzf history search still works after the lazy load. The first press has a small delay of about 30 ms because the list builds then, and later presses are instant. That is acceptable for me.

One thing broke on the way. The deduplication step expected the list to exist and printed a warning in a fresh tmux pane. I guarded it with a check for the function and the warning went away.

I committed the changes to the dotfiles folder by copying the files into the backup set, since the folder is not a git repository. The timing script output is saved next to the previous runs so I can compare later.

What is left is checking the same numbers on the older Mac, which I will do when it is on the desk. If the lazy load behaves differently there, the guard may need a second look.

summary: Measured the shell start on the old Mac and found 241 ms, mostly from a slow compinit that ignored its cache dump
body:
Yesterday's numbers of 176 ms were from the new Mac. On the old Mac the timing script reported 241 ms, so I looked for the difference.

A zprof run showed compinit taking 58 ms there. The completion dump file was being regenerated on every start because its path pointed at a folder that did not exist on that machine. The script that sets the zsh data folder had a hard-coded path from the new Mac.

I changed the path to use the XDG-style variable with a fallback, and created the folder if missing. The first start rebuilt the dump and later starts used it. Compinit dropped to 9 ms.

The total then came to 189 ms on the old Mac, which is under the 200 ms goal. The remaining gap to the new Mac is just slower disk and CPU.

While there I found that the same hard-coded path was used by the history file setting. History had still worked because the folder happened to exist for that one. I fixed both to use the same variable so they cannot drift apart.

I ran the broken-symlink checker afterwards and it reported nothing new. I also opened a new tmux session and a Ghostty tab to see that nothing printed an error at start.

The timing script now also prints the compinit time as a separate line, so a regression in the dump is easy to see. I added a note in the script's comment about why the line is there.

Nothing is left open on shell start for now. If it goes over 200 ms again I will start from the zprof output.

summary: Added a git alias that lists local branches already merged into main so they can be deleted in one step
body:
I wanted a quick way to clean old local branches after merges. I added an alias called cleanup to the git config that lists branches merged into main and excludes main and the current branch.

The first version also listed a branch named develop, which I keep on purpose. I added an exclusion pattern for it. The alias only prints the list; deleting needs a second alias that pipes the same list to git branch -d.

I tested both in a scratch repository with five branches, three of them merged. The list showed exactly the three. The delete alias used the safe -d flag, so unmerged work would be refused rather than lost.

I wrote both aliases into the aliases section of the config with a one-line comment each.

summary: Set up commit signing checks in the git config so unsigned commits show a warning in the prompt, and tested with a deliberately unsigned commit
body:
After the signing change of earlier weeks I wanted a visible hint when a commit in the current repository is not signed. The idea was a small marker in the prompt's git segment.

First I looked at what git offers cheaply. The format placeholder %G? in git log gives one letter for the signature state of a commit. Running it for HEAD takes about 4 ms, which is acceptable if done only when the prompt redraws after a commit.

I added the call to the prompt hook but cached the result per HEAD hash in a shell variable. The prompt only calls git log again when the hash changes. That kept the prompt redraw time flat in my measurements, at roughly 6 ms total for the git segment.

The marker is a small red x when the state is N, meaning no signature, and nothing when it is G. For other letters such as E, where the key is missing, it shows a yellow question mark.

I tested with a scratch repository. A signed commit showed no marker. A commit made with commit.gpgsign set to false showed the red x. Switching the allowed signers file away made the state E and the yellow mark appeared.

One problem came up: in a repository with no commits yet the call printed an error to the terminal. I added a check for a valid HEAD first, and the error went away. This matches the initial commit case in the porcelain parser tests.

I added a test case for the marker logic to the prompt test script using canned letters. All cases pass.

What is left is deciding whether merge commits made by the hosting site should show the marker. For now they show the E state, which is noisy, so I will look at that next.

summary: Merge commits created by the hosting site no longer show the yellow signing marker, after teaching the prompt to skip commits with more than one parent
body:
The yellow marker from the signing check showed up on every pull of a branch whose tip was a merge commit made on the hosting site. Those are signed with the site's own key, which I do not have in the allowed signers file.

I considered adding the site's public key. That would make them show as good, but it would mean trusting a key I had not verified, so I chose against it for now.

Instead the prompt now checks the parent count with git rev-list --parents -n 1 HEAD. When the commit has two parents, the marker is skipped. This costs one more git call, again cached per HEAD hash.

I tested with a scratch repository that had a merge commit created with --no-ff. No marker appeared. A normal unsigned commit on top of it showed the red x as before.

I also added a test case with a canned two-parent output to the prompt test script. It passes along with the others.

The cost of the prompt redraw stayed at 6 to 7 ms. I checked it with the timing script run twenty times.

One open question is whether skipping the check hides a real problem on a merge I made myself locally. Those would be signed by my key, so I would want to see the marker if not. A small follow-up is to skip only when the author is not me, which I will try later.

summary: Limited the merge-commit marker skip to commits not authored by me, so my own unsigned merges still show the warning
body:
Following up on yesterday's question, I changed the prompt so that the skip for merge commits applies only when the author email differs from my configured one.
