The check reads user.email once at shell start and compares it with the author email from git log -1 --format=%ae. Both calls are cached by HEAD hash with the signature state, so the cost stays the same.

I tested three cases in a scratch repository. A local merge of mine with signing turned off showed the red x. A merge with another author email set through GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL showed nothing. A normal signed commit showed nothing as before.

I added the matching cases to the prompt test script. The script now has eleven cases for the signing marker and all pass.

I also noticed that the cache variable was not reset when changing directory to another repository with the same HEAD hash, which is unlikely but possible after a clone. I included the repository path in the cache key.

The prompt still redraws in about 7 ms. This topic is finished for me, and I will watch whether the marker gives false alarms in daily use.

summary: Added a tmux binding to open the current pane's directory in Zed, and fixed it failing for paths with spaces
body:
I wanted to jump from a terminal pane to Zed in the same folder with one key. I added a binding on prefix plus z that runs zed with the pane's current path as the argument.

The first version used #{pane_current_path} without quotes. It worked for most folders but failed for one with a space in its name, where Zed opened two empty windows. I wrapped the format in quotes inside run-shell and it opened the right folder.

I also checked that the binding does not clash with the zoom key that I had on prefix plus z earlier in the tmux config. It did. I moved zoom to prefix plus Z with the shift key and removed the old line.

The Ghostty keybinding set does not use prefix plus anything, so there is no overlap there.

I tested it from three panes in different folders, including a symlinked one. In the symlinked case Zed opened the resolved path, which is fine for me.

The zed command line tool had to be on the path. It was, through the Homebrew bin directory, so nothing more was needed.

I wrote the binding into the key bindings table at the end of the file with a short comment.

summary: Looked at why the tmux binding to open Zed was slow on the first call after login and found it was the zed CLI starting the app
body:
I noticed that the new prefix plus z binding took about four seconds the first time after login, and half a second afterwards. I wanted to know if tmux or the shell was to blame.

I timed the pieces. Running the zed command directly in a terminal showed the same four seconds on a cold start, so tmux was not involved. The cost is Zed itself launching, not my config.

I tried the --new flag to see if it made a difference. It did not change the cold time but opened a second window in the warm case, which I do not want.

As a small improvement I made the binding print a short message with display-message when Zed is not running, so the pause does not look like a broken key. The check uses pgrep -x zed.

I tested it by quitting Zed and pressing the key. The message appeared and Zed opened after a few seconds with the right folder. With Zed already running, no message showed and the folder opened in the existing window.

I considered launching Zed at login, but I do not want another login item for this, so I left it alone.

The quoting for paths with spaces still holds in the new version. I tested with the same folder as before.

That finishes the binding. The only open point is whether pgrep matches the right process name on the old Mac, where the app was installed differently.

summary: Wrote a first draft of a script to compare installed Homebrew packages against the Brewfile and list drift in both directions
body:
The Brewfile and the real machine had drifted apart over the months, and I wanted a report instead of guessing. I wrote a script called brew-drift in the scripts folder.

It does two comparisons. First it runs brew bundle cleanup without --force, which lists installed items missing from the Brewfile. Second it runs brew bundle check --verbose, which lists Brewfile items that are not installed.

The first run on the new Mac showed 14 installed formulae not in the Brewfile. Most were dependencies that brew leaves flagged as top-level because an older install had been done by hand. Three were tools I use: jq, hyperfine and watch.

It also showed one cask in the Brewfile that was not installed, an old PDF viewer I had replaced. I removed the line.

The cleanup command only reports casks and formulae, and it does not report Mac App Store entries well. I decided to ignore the App Store lines in the report to keep the output readable.

I added a flag to the script so that it can print the result as a diff-like list with plus and minus signs. Plus means installed but not in the file, minus means in the file but not installed. That is easier to scan than the raw text.

I tested the script on a copy of the Brewfile with two lines deleted and one fake package added. It reported all three correctly.

The run takes about 6 seconds, mostly brew itself. I did not try to speed it up.

One thing that went wrong was that brew bundle cleanup exits with status 1 when it finds drift. My script used set -e and stopped before the second comparison. I changed the first call to continue on error and collect the status at the end.

I have not yet decided what to do with the three tools I use. The plan is to add them to the Brewfile in the next entry, then run the script on the old Mac to see what differs there.

summary: Added jq, hyperfine and watch to the Brewfile and ran the drift script on the old Mac, which showed nine more extra packages
body:
Following the first draft of the drift script, I added the three tools I use to the Brewfile: jq, hyperfine and watch. I placed them in the section for command line utilities, in alphabetical order like the others.

The drift script on the new Mac then reported 11 extra formulae, all of them dependency leftovers. I checked a few with brew uses --installed and confirmed that other packages need them, so they are fine and I added an ignore list file for those.

The ignore list is a plain text file read by the script, one name per line. Matching names are dropped from the plus lines. It keeps the output short without hiding real drift.

On the old Mac the script found nine more extra packages. Four were old tools I no longer use, such as a Python 2 era helper and two language servers that I replaced with the native Neovim setup. I uninstalled those with brew uninstall.

The other five were small things I do use there but never added to the Brewfile. I added two of them to the Brewfile, tree and ripgrep-all, and decided the remaining three are not needed.

After the cleanup I ran brew bundle check on both machines and both reported that the dependencies are satisfied.

I noticed that the script failed on the old Mac with a different version of brew, because the verbose flag prints a slightly different format. The parsing of lines starting with Using was off. I changed it to match only lines starting with a plus-style marker I generate myself, which does not depend on the format.

The script now works on both machines.

I also noted the cask pin from the earlier Homebrew change: the casks that update themselves are skipped, and the script respects that because it reads the same Brewfile.

The next step is to run the script from the bootstrap check on a fresh account, so that drift is reported as part of setup.

summary: Hooked the Brewfile drift script into the bootstrap check, which now covers eight of the eleven known setup gaps
body:
The bootstrap check from earlier covered seven of the eleven known gaps. Package drift was not one of them, so I added the brew-drift script as a step.

On a fresh user account, the Brewfile is not installed yet, so the interesting output is the minus lines. The step runs brew bundle check and prints the missing items as an action: run brew bundle. That counts as a gap that needs a manual action.

I ran it on a fresh test account. The step reported 63 missing items and one line telling me what to run. It took 3 seconds because nothing needed comparing in the other direction.

I also wanted the step to skip cleanly when Homebrew itself is not installed. In that case it now prints a line saying Homebrew is missing and gives the install command, rather than failing with command not found.

The bootstrap check now has eight steps that report gaps. The remaining three gaps are the 1Password agent login, the macOS privacy permissions for the terminal, and the Zed sign-in.

The privacy permissions are the hard ones, since they can only be granted through the settings window and cannot be checked from a script without a prompt.

I updated the summary line at the end of the check to print how many gaps are covered and how many need a person. It says 8 of 11 now.

Next I will look at whether the 1Password agent state can be checked by listing keys with ssh-add -l. That should work without prompting if the agent socket is set.

summary: Added a bootstrap check step for the 1Password SSH agent that uses ssh-add -l, and handled the locked-app case that returned a misleading error
body:
The next gap in the bootstrap check was the 1Password agent. The idea was to run ssh-add -l with the agent socket set and see if keys are listed.

On the working Mac it printed the two keys I have. On a fresh test account it printed Error connecting to agent: No such file or directory, because the socket path in the config pointed to a folder that only exists once the app has been opened.

I also tried it with the app installed but locked. In that state ssh-add -l printed The agent has no identities, which looks like a missing key but is really a locked vault. The two cases need different advice.

I split the step. If the socket file does not exist, it says to open 1Password and turn on the SSH agent in the developer settings. If the socket exists but no identities are listed, it says to unlock the app and check that the keys are in the vault used by the agent.

The config file for the agent has a list of allowed vaults, and I want the check to read it. I added a simple grep for the vault name and printed a warning if the file is missing.

I tested three states: no app, locked app and unlocked app. Each printed the matching message. The unlocked case printed OK and the key count.

One snag was the time the check waits when the socket exists but the app is stuck. ssh-add can hang for a long time. I added a timeout of three seconds by running it in the background and killing it, since macOS has no timeout command by default.

The bootstrap check now covers nine of the eleven gaps.

That leaves the privacy permissions and the Zed sign-in. Zed sign-in is stored in the keychain, so I will see if it can be detected from there.

I also noted the 3 second wait in the script comments, so that future me knows why the code looks odd.

summary: Tried to detect the Zed sign-in from the keychain and the settings file, found neither is reliable, and left it as a manual note in the bootstrap check
body:
With nine gaps covered, I looked at Zed sign-in. The first idea was to look for an entry in the keychain with security find-generic-password.

I searched for a service name containing zed. On the Mac where I am signed in there were two entries, but one belonged to a collaboration feature I do not use. The names are not documented, so a script could break after an update.

The second idea was the settings file. Zed stores no sign-in state in settings.json, and I found nothing relevant in the application support folder that looked stable.

I tried to see if the zed command line tool gives a status. It does not have one in the version I have.

Given all that, I stopped trying to detect it. The check now prints a manual line for Zed: open Zed and sign in if you want settings sync. It counts the item as a manual action and does not try to verify.

I also thought about whether I need sign-in at all. My settings are in the dotfiles folder and linked, so sync adds nothing except the AI features, which I do not use there. I marked the item as optional in the output.

That brought the bootstrap check to nine automatic gaps and two manual notes, one required and one optional. The required one is the privacy permissions for the terminal.

For the permissions I considered tccutil, but it can only reset, not read. Reading the TCC database needs full disk access for the terminal, which is the very permission I would be checking. So that stays manual too.

I rewrote the summary at the end of the script to show three groups: ok, needs action and manual. On a fresh account it printed 5 ok, 4 needs action, 2 manual.

I ran the whole check on the real Mac as well, and it printed 9 ok and 2 manual, which is what I expect.

The bootstrap work is now done for this round. If a twelfth gap shows up on the next install I will add it then.

summary: Fixed the bootstrap check printing the Zed note twice because the manual step list was appended in two places
body:
After yesterday's rewrite the bootstrap check printed the Zed sign-in line twice in the manual group. The count said 3 manual instead of 2.

I looked at the script and found that the Zed step appended to the manual array in its own function and again in the loop that collects results from all steps. The loop was added when I made the groups.

I removed the append from the function and left the loop as the only place that builds the groups. That is cleaner, since every step now only returns a status and a message.

I ran the check on the real Mac and on a fresh test account. The counts are 9 ok and 2 manual, and 5 ok, 4 needs action and 2 manual.

I also added a small test that runs the check with all the steps replaced by stubs, so the grouping logic can be checked without touching the machine. The test has three stubs returning ok, action and manual, and it checks the counts.

The test passes. I put it next to the prompt tests in the same folder and added it to the script that runs them all.

summary: Planned the move of the editor font and terminal font settings into one shared file, after finding three places that each set a font size
body:
I noticed the font size had drifted: Ghostty said 14, the Zed settings said 15, and the Neovim GUI config I rarely use said 13. Before changing anything about fonts I wanted a plan, since a font change is coming and I do not want to edit three places.

First I listed every place that names a font. Ghostty has font-family and font-size. Zed has buffer_font_family, buffer_font_size and ui_font_size. The tmux config names none, but its status line uses special glyphs. The prompt uses a few symbols from the Powerline range.

Second I checked which symbols the prompt needs. The git segment uses a branch glyph and the ahead and behind arrows. The branch glyph is from the Powerline set. If the new font lacks it, the prompt shows an empty box.

Third I thought about how to share values. Ghostty and Zed use different formats, so a real shared file is not possible. A small generator script can write both from one list of two values, family and size.

I sketched the generator in a few lines. It reads a file called font.env with FONT_FAMILY and FONT_SIZE. It then rewrites the font lines in the Ghostty config and the Zed settings using sed for Ghostty and jq for Zed.

The Zed settings file has comments, which jq cannot parse. I checked and found it has no comments right now, but Zed allows them, so the generator would break if I add one. I decided to use a marker comment approach for Ghostty only and a tiny Python script for Zed that edits keys with a regex.

I also thought about ligatures. Ghostty controls them with font-feature, and Zed with buffer_font_features. The generator should write both from one flag. I put LIGATURES=on or off in font.env.

I did a dry run of the generator against copies of the real files and printed the diffs. It changed the Zed size from 15 to 14 and nothing else. For Ghostty it changed nothing, since it was already 14.

The Neovim GUI file I removed from the plan, because I have not opened it in a year. I noted its font line as stale and deleted the file after checking nothing links to it.

The plan has four steps: write font.env, write the generator, run it, and add it to the bootstrap check. I did the first two today and left the rest for the next session.

One risk is that the generator overwrites a manual tweak. I made it keep a backup copy of each file with a suffix before writing.

summary: Wrote a small generator that reads font.env and writes the Ghostty and Zed font settings, so the font family and size now live in one place instead of three
body:
Yesterday's plan found three places that each set a font size: the Ghostty config, Zed's settings.json and an old line in the Neovim GUI file. Today I started on the shared file. I created font.env in the dotfiles folder with FONT_FAMILY, FONT_SIZE and FONT_LINE_HEIGHT, all holding the current JetBrains Mono values. Then I wrote gen-font.sh, which reads it and writes a small include file for Ghostty and a font block for Zed.

Ghostty read the include file without trouble through its config-file option. Zed has no include mechanism, so the script rewrites only the buffer_font and ui_font keys in settings.json using jq and leaves everything else untouched. I checked this by diffing the file before and after a run, and the only change was a trailing newline, which I fixed. The Neovim GUI line was dead code from the iTerm2 days, so I deleted it instead of generating it.

I ran the script twice to confirm it is idempotent and both runs left identical files. The font size change from 14 to 15 in font.env showed up in Ghostty after a reload and in Zed on the next window open. Still open: a separate family for Zed and a symbols fallback, which I will add next, before trying any new font.

summary: Added the font generator to the bootstrap check and the symlink script, and fixed it clobbering Zed settings when settings.json had comments in it
body:
Today I hooked gen-font.sh into the rest of the setup so a new Mac gets the same fonts without manual work. The first problem showed up straight away: Zed's settings.json allows comments, and jq refused to parse it with the error 'Invalid numeric literal'. My first run left the file empty, which I restored from the backup copy the script makes before every write.

I changed the script to strip full-line comments before passing the text to jq, and to abort without writing if jq fails. That is safer than the first version, which wrote the output unchecked. Trailing comments on a line with a value are still not handled, so I added a check that stops with a clear message if it sees one. My own settings file has none, so this only matters for edits I make later.

Next I added the script to the symlink check so a missing include file for Ghostty is reported after a fresh install. I also added a line to the bootstrap check that fails if font.env is absent or if the generated Ghostty include is older than font.env. I tested the stale case by touching font.env, and the check printed a warning and the command to regenerate. I tested the missing case by renaming the include file, and it was reported as a broken link.

Finally I ran everything on a fresh user account. The fonts came out the same in Ghostty and Zed, and the bootstrap check ended with no new warnings from the font steps. The next step is to test a candidate font through font.env alone.

summary: Checked that the tmux status files from the stutter fix are written atomically, after seeing one empty branch name in the status line
body:
Since the status line now reads a per-pane file, I saw the branch name go blank once for a moment. I suspected that the status read happened while the prompt hook was writing the file.

The hook used a plain redirect, which truncates the file first and then writes. A read in between gets an empty file. The window is tiny, but with several panes it can be hit.

I changed the hook to write to a temporary file in the same folder and then move it over the real one with mv. A rename on the same filesystem is atomic, so the reader sees either the old or the new content.

To test it I wrote a loop that updated the file 10,000 times in the background and read it 10,000 times in the foreground. With the old write, 14 reads came back empty. With the new write, none did.

I also made sure the temporary file name includes the pane id, so two panes cannot overwrite each other's temporary file. The pane id is already in the real file name.

The pane-exited cleanup now removes the temporary files too, with a glob that matches both.

I checked the status line during normal use for an hour and saw no blank branch. The related prompt timing is unchanged at about 7 ms.

That closes the stutter topic. The numbers are in the previous entry, and nothing else is open.

summary: Prepared the font switch by testing three candidate monospaced fonts for Powerline glyphs, ligature support and width in tmux, and picked one to try
body:
I want to try a different font for the terminal, and since the generator now makes it a small edit, I spent the morning comparing candidates rather than just switching. The main worry is that tmux and the prompt depend on glyphs and on cell width.

The candidates were JetBrains Mono as the baseline, Berkeley Mono, and Iosevka. I installed what I could from Homebrew casks and from a file I had already licensed for Berkeley Mono.

Test one was the prompt glyphs. I printed the branch symbol, the ahead and behind arrows and the signing marker in each font. JetBrains Mono Nerd and Iosevka Nerd showed all of them. Berkeley Mono showed empty boxes for the branch symbol, because the plain version has no Powerline range.

Test two was ligatures. I printed a line with arrows, comparison operators and triple equals. JetBrains Mono joined them. Iosevka joined them too but with a different shape for some. Berkeley Mono has a set of ligatures that are switched on by a font feature and off by default in some builds.

Test three was width. I printed a ruler of 80 characters and compared its length in pixels between fonts at size 14. The widths differed by up to 6 percent, which changes how many columns fit in a split. For my usual two-split layout this meant 3 columns less with Berkeley Mono.

Test four was tmux. I opened a session with the status line and a split, and looked at box drawing characters for the pane borders. All three fonts drew the lines without gaps in Ghostty, but Iosevka showed a one pixel gap at some sizes.

I took notes on how each looked in a git diff with long lines, since that is where I spend most of the time. Berkeley Mono was the clearest to me, with a more open look for characters like 0 and l.

The missing glyphs are the problem for Berkeley Mono. Ghostty supports a fallback font list, so I can name Berkeley Mono first and a Nerd Font symbols-only font second. The symbols font is a small cask I already have.

I tried that fallback by adding a second font-family line. The branch symbol then showed in the fallback font, though slightly larger than the text. Ghostty has an option for adjusting the cell size, and a size tweak for the fallback was not available, so I accepted the slight mismatch.

I also tried the Zed side. Zed has no per-glyph fallback list in the version I use, so for buffer text it falls back as a whole. That is fine, because the editor does not use Powerline symbols.

My decision is to try Berkeley Mono in Ghostty with the symbols fallback, and to keep JetBrains Mono in Zed until I have lived with it. I decided not to change the generator yet, as it writes one family for both.

What I need to do next is extend font.env with a second family for Zed and a fallback entry for Ghostty. Then I will test ligatures inside tmux specifically, since that is where I expect trouble.

summary: Extended font.env and the generator with separate families for Ghostty and Zed plus a symbols fallback, and tested it with JetBrains Mono still active
body:
To prepare for the new font, I changed font.env to have TERM_FONT, TERM_FALLBACK, EDITOR_FONT and the shared size. LIGATURES stays as one flag.

The generator now writes TERM_FONT and TERM_FALLBACK as two font-family lines in the Ghostty config, and EDITOR_FONT into the Zed buffer font key. If TERM_FALLBACK is empty it writes only one line.

I kept the existence check for families, and made it run for all three names. Berkeley Mono is installed from the licensed file, so it passes.

To test without changing what I use, I ran the generator with the current values: JetBrains Mono Nerd for both, and an empty fallback. The diff against the backups was empty for Ghostty and Zed, which is what I wanted.

Then I ran it with a copy of font.env that names Berkeley Mono and the symbols font, writing into scratch copies of the configs. The Ghostty copy had both lines in the right order. The Zed copy stayed on JetBrains Mono.

Ghostty has a quirk where the order of font-family lines defines the priority, and a repeated key in a config resets the list when the first line is empty. I used the exact form from the documentation and it behaved.

I also updated the bootstrap check step so that it compares all three names and the size against the real files. It still reports ok with the current values.

I wrote a short test for the generator that runs it on scratch files and checks the output with grep. Three cases: no fallback, with fallback, and a missing family. All pass.

Nothing visible changed yet. The real switch is the next step, and the ligature behavior inside tmux is what I will look at then.

summary: Wrote down what the planned Berkeley Mono switch should check, then tried it in a scratch Ghostty config and saw broken ligatures inside tmux only
body:
Before the real switch I wrote a short checklist in the comments of the generator: prompt glyphs, ligatures outside tmux, ligatures inside tmux, column count in a two-split layout, and Zed unaffected. Then I tried the new font with a scratch Ghostty config launched with the config-file flag, so my normal config stayed untouched.

The prompt glyphs showed correctly through the symbols fallback. The branch symbol was a little larger than the text, as I expected, but not distracting.

Outside tmux, ligatures worked once I enabled the feature. Berkeley Mono names its ligature set with a feature tag, and Ghostty takes it through font-feature. I added the entry and arrows and comparison operators joined as they should.

Inside tmux the same line printed the operators as separate characters. A line like -> showed the two characters apart, while the same text outside tmux joined them. That is the problem I had expected to find.

My first thought was that tmux does not pass the feature on. It cannot, since fonts are a terminal matter, so I looked at how tmux redraws text. When tmux repaints a line it can send characters one cell at a time with cursor movement in between, and some terminals then shape each character alone.

I tested that idea by running a program that prints a long line with ligatures, once in a full-width pane and once after a resize. After a resize the ligatures sometimes joined, which fits with the repaint theory.

I looked at the tmux options and the terminal type. My default-terminal was tmux-256color with an override for true color. I did not find an option in the tmux manual that changes how runs of text are sent.

I also checked whether Ghostty has its own setting for shaping across cells. It has a setting that controls whether the shaper breaks runs at cursor position, which did not apply here as far as I could tell.

The time was late for me, so I stopped and kept the finding: ligatures with the new font work outside tmux and fail inside it. JetBrains Mono showed the same split in a quick check, so it is not specific to this font. I had just never looked, since the old font's ligatures are less obvious to me.

My next step is to check the terminal type and the tmux terminal overrides, and to try the line printing test with different settings. I will keep the real configs on JetBrains Mono until it is solved.

I saved the scratch config and the test line file in the dotfiles folder under a notes subfolder so I can come back to them.

summary: Cleaned up the notes folder from the font tests and removed the scratch Ghostty config that duplicated the real one
body:
The scratch Ghostty config from the font tests was a full copy of the real config with three changed lines. Keeping a full copy is a risk, since it will go out of date and confuse me later.

I replaced it with a small file that only holds the three differing lines and a comment saying to launch Ghostty with both files. Ghostty accepts the config-file option more than once, so the later file overrides the earlier one.

I tested it by launching with the real config first and the small file second. The font was Berkeley Mono and everything else was as normal.

The test line file for ligatures stayed as it was. I added a second line with the operators I use most in code, such as != and =>.

I also deleted two old backup files with the .bak suffix from the first generator run, since the diffs had been checked.

The notes folder now has three files and a one-line readme about what each one is for.

summary: Found that tmux ligature breakage came from the status of the terminal feature flags and tried three settings, with partial success in a scratch session
body:
I picked up the ligature problem inside tmux from a few days ago. The goal was to find a setting that makes Berkeley Mono ligatures join inside tmux the way they do outside it, using the scratch config so my real setup stays on JetBrains Mono.

First I measured how often it happens. With the test line file printed in a fresh tmux pane, none of the ligatures joined. After running clear and printing again, they still did not. So it was not only a resize issue as I had thought.

Second I tried the terminal-features option, which tells tmux what the outer terminal supports. I added entries for true color and for extended keys. This changed nothing for ligatures, which I now expect, since they are not part of that list.

Third I looked at the escape sequences tmux sends. I recorded the output with script and looked at it with cat -v. For a line with an arrow, tmux sent the two characters in one run, so the cell-at-a-time theory was wrong for plain printing.

The difference I found was an attribute sequence between the characters. tmux emitted a reset of attributes and then set them again inside the line, which splits the run for the shaper. That happens because my status of the line colors are set by the terminal override with a background that tmux repaints.

I traced it to the default-terminal override that sets colors with the RGB flag. When I switched default-terminal to xterm-256color in the scratch session, the extra attribute sequences were fewer, and about half of the ligatures joined.

Half was not good enough. The remaining breaks were in lines that contain the cursor or a selection, and in lines right after a prompt redraw. I found that the prompt hook sends a cursor shape sequence and an OSC 7 for the working directory on every redraw.

The OSC 7 came from the fix of some weeks ago for restoring directories in new tabs. I turned it off for a test and more ligatures joined, so it adds to the problem, but it is needed.

I then tried moving the OSC 7 to run only when the directory changes, using the chpwd hook instead of the prompt hook. That kept the tab restore working in my test and removed one source of splits.

With the xterm-256color change and the chpwd change together, nearly all ligatures joined in the scratch session. One case remained: the line being edited at the prompt.

I did not want to change default-terminal in the real config without checking side effects. The tmux-256color value gives correct italics and some key codes, and a different value could break them in Neovim inside tmux. I listed what to check: italics, undercurl in Neovim, and key sequences for the function keys.

For now the state is a working scratch configuration and a list of three things to verify before using it for real. I wrote the findings in the notes folder, including the escape sequence recordings.

The next step is to run the three checks with the scratch config and then decide about the real switch of font and terminal type.

summary: Verified italics, undercurl and function keys with the xterm-256color setting in tmux and found only undercurl needed an extra terminal override
body:
I ran the three checks from the notes with the scratch tmux session. Italics worked, shown correctly in a shell test and in Neovim comments.

Function keys and arrow keys with modifiers worked in Neovim and in the shell with the new terminal type. I tested F1 to F12 with cat -v and compared them with the old output; they were identical.

Undercurl did not work. Neovim diagnostics showed a straight underline instead of a wavy one. With the old tmux-256color value it had worked, thanks to a terminal override I had added months ago that only applies to that name.

I added the same override to the terminal-overrides for xterm-256color, using the Smulx capability and the colored underline entries. After reloading tmux, undercurl came back in Neovim.

That gives a complete list. The setting plus the override and the chpwd change are ready to move into the real configs.

I will make the real change together with the font switch in one session, so that I can test them as a pair, and keep the old values in comments in case I need to go back.

summary: Fixed the tmux ligature breakage in a scratch session by setting the terminal feature flags explicitly, but the status line still showed one wrong glyph width.
body:
Picked up the ligature problem from the notes of the last few days. In the scratch Ghostty config, ligatures worked outside tmux and broke inside it, so the cause had to be what tmux told programs about the terminal.

Checked the three settings from before one at a time with a fresh tmux server each time. The first, a changed default-terminal, did nothing for ligatures. The second, terminal-features with the extended-keys flag, fixed function keys but not the text shaping. The third, a terminal-overrides line for the Ghostty terminal name, had no effect either, so I ruled out the overrides as the cause.

Then compared the rendering of the string '=> != ==' in a plain shell, in tmux with the status line off, and in tmux with the status line on. The ligatures held in the pane when the status line was off. With it on they broke again after each status refresh.

That pointed at the status redraw rather than the terminal type. The status script wrote a Powerline separator right next to the branch name, and the redraw forced tmux to repaint the whole line, which resets the shaping run in Ghostty.

Tried a variation that puts a plain space after the separator and the ligatures survived in three of four tests. The fourth failed after a window rename. I left the scratch config as it was and wrote the four results into the notes file.

Still open: the failing case after the window rename, and whether the real config needs the same space. Next step is to repeat the test with the Berkeley Mono family active instead of JetBrains Mono.

summary: Reproduced the ligature break after a tmux window rename and found that the rename hook triggers an extra status refresh that fires before the pane redraw.
body:
Went back to the one failing case from this morning. A window rename ran the automatic-rename hook, which called the status refresh script a second time.

With a log line in the script I saw two refreshes within about 40 ms after each rename. The pane was repainted between them, and the second refresh broke the shaping again.

Set automatic-rename off for the test session and the ligatures held through ten renames. That confirmed the double refresh as the trigger.

I did not change the real tmux config yet. Turning off automatic rename would lose the directory names in the window list that I like, so I will try to make the hook skip the refresh instead.

Wrote the log excerpt and the ten-rename test into the notes. Tomorrow I will look at the hook order in tmux.conf.

summary: Made the tmux rename hook stop calling the status refresh directly, so each rename now causes one refresh and ligatures survive in the scratch session.
body:
Read the hook section of tmux.conf. The window-renamed hook ran the status script, and tmux itself also refreshed the status after the rename, so there were two refreshes by design.

Removed the direct call from the hook and let the normal status-interval refresh and tmux's own refresh do the work. The branch name in the status line still updated, because the script reads the file written by the earlier stutter fix and does not need a trigger.

Tested with twenty renames, a split, a zoom and a session switch. Ligatures held in all of them in the scratch session. The refresh log showed one run per rename, down from two.

One side effect: after switching directories the branch name lags by up to the status interval, which is five seconds. I accept that for now.

The change is only in the scratch copy of tmux.conf. I will carry it into the real file once the font itself is switched, so that one thing changes at a time.

summary: Ran the planned Berkeley Mono checklist in the scratch setup and found Powerline glyphs and widths fine, with only the status separator gap left to adjust.
body:
Worked through the checklist written a few days ago, using the scratch Ghostty config with Berkeley Mono and the shared font.env generator.

Powerline glyphs in the prompt rendered correctly through the symbols fallback. Box drawing lines in tmux borders joined without gaps at the font size of 14. Nerd symbols in the Neovim statusline were the right width.

Ligatures worked in the shell, in Neovim and, with the rename hook fix, in tmux. Italics and undercurl also worked with the override from last time.

Two small things were left. The separator after the tmux branch name looked slightly too tight, so I will add a thin space in the status format. The line height was a little tall, and adjust-cell-height at minus 4 percent fixed it.

Both values went into the notes, not into the real config. The switch itself is the next step.

summary: Checked that the font generator can switch Ghostty and Zed together and found Zed buffer font size needs a separate value from the UI font size.
body:
Before the real switch I ran the generator against a copy of the real settings, with Berkeley Mono for both editors.

Ghostty picked up the family and size from font.env as intended. Zed changed its buffer font but left the UI font alone, which is what I want.

The size was a problem. Zed at 14 looked larger than Ghostty at 14 on the same screen, because Zed uses points differently in its rendering. A buffer size of 13 matched visually.

Added a ZED_SIZE_OFFSET variable to font.env, defaulting to minus 1, and taught the generator to apply it. Ran the symlink script and the bootstrap check afterwards, and both passed.

The real switch is ready. I need a quiet moment to do it, so it waits for a day with no pressing work.

summary: Prepared the real switch by bringing the scratch tmux fixes into the real config and making a backup of the working JetBrains Mono setup first.
body:
Started by copying the current font.env, the Ghostty config, the Zed settings and tmux.conf into a dated folder under the backups directory, so the switch can be undone in one command. Wrote a tiny restore script next to the copies and tested it once on the scratch setup.

Then moved the two tmux changes into the real tmux.conf: the removed direct call in the window-renamed hook and the thin space after the branch separator in the status format. Reloaded with source-file and checked that the status line looked right with JetBrains Mono still active.

With JetBrains Mono the thin space was slightly visible, a gap about half a character wide. That is acceptable, but I looked at it carefully because it should not make the current setup worse. It did not.

Ran the bootstrap check and the symlink script. Both passed, with the same manual notes as before.

Ran the ligature test string in a plain shell and inside tmux with the real config. Both showed the JetBrains Mono ligatures correctly, so the tmux changes cause no regression.

Did not touch the font itself. That is for a later session, since I want the tmux changes to run for a while first and see whether anything odd shows up in normal work.

summary: Used the new tmux config through a full evening of work and found no stutter or empty branch names, so the font switch can go ahead.
body:
Spent the evening in normal work with the changed tmux config and JetBrains Mono, watching for regressions.

The status line refreshed once per interval and once per rename. I counted the log lines for two hours and found no double refreshes. The branch name was never empty, which confirms that the atomic writes from before still hold.

One annoyance remained. After a git checkout in a pane, the branch name took up to five seconds to change. I tried lowering the status interval to two seconds and measured the cost: the status script used about 0.8 percent CPU at five seconds and about 2 percent at two. That is more than I like for a status line.

Instead I added a git hook for post-checkout that touches the status file directly. That made the branch name update at once after a checkout. It does not cover a switch made from another tool, but that is rare for me.

The hook goes into the global hooks folder of the git config, so it works in every repository. Tested in three repositories, including one with signing enabled, and nothing changed in the signing warnings.

Note for later: if the global hooks folder replaces a repo's own hooks, some repos may lose their hooks. I checked that none of my repos use a hooks folder of their own, so this is fine.

summary: Found that the new global post-checkout hook shadowed one repository's own pre-commit hook, so the hook now chains to the local one.
body:
A pre-commit check did not run in one repository this afternoon. At first I thought the check itself was broken.

Running the commit with GIT_TRACE showed no hook invocation at all. The cause was core.hooksPath: setting it globally for the branch-name hook meant git stopped looking in .git/hooks, and that repo did have a pre-commit script there. My earlier check had missed it because I only looked for a hooks folder of the repo's own, not for files in .git/hooks.

Fixed it in two steps. First I wrote a small wrapper in the global hooks folder that, for each hook name, runs the hook in .git/hooks if one exists and then continues. Second I linked the wrapper to the names pre-commit, post-checkout and commit-msg.

The wrapper passes through the arguments and the exit code, which matters for commit-msg. I tested it with a pre-commit script that fails on purpose, and the commit was blocked as expected. Then with a passing script, and then with no local hook.

The post-checkout call still touches the status file, now after the local hook finishes. A failing local post-checkout is not allowed to stop the touch.

Also searched all repos under the projects folder for files in .git/hooks that are not samples. There were two, both now covered by the wrapper.

I added a line to the bootstrap check noting that hooks in .git/hooks are only honored through the wrapper.

summary: Moved the real setup to Berkeley Mono through font.env, checked every tool, and kept JetBrains Mono as a documented fallback until the next day of work.
body:
Did the switch at last, after the backup and the tmux fixes had been in use for several days.

First ran the restore script in dry-run mode to confirm that it points at the right backup folder. Then edited font.env to set the Ghostty family to Berkeley Mono, the Zed family to Berkeley Mono, the size to 14 with the Zed offset, and kept the symbols fallback as before.

Ran the generator and then reloaded Ghostty. The prompt looked right, and the Powerline glyphs came from the fallback font with the correct width.

Inside tmux the ligature test string showed the right glyphs, and window renames, splits and zoom did not break them. That was the case I worried about most.

Neovim looked good, but the statusline icons needed a check. They are Nerd symbols and came from the fallback, with the correct width. The diagnostic signs in the sign column were also fine.

In Zed the buffer font changed and the UI font did not. The size looked the same as in Ghostty, so the offset was right.

One issue came up. Bold text in git diff output looked too heavy in the terminal. The font has several weights and Ghostty picked the heaviest for bold. I set font-style-bold to the semi-bold name and it was better.

Then ran the bootstrap check and the symlink script on the changed files, and both passed. The generator also kept the comments in Zed's settings.json.

The backup stays in place, and the restore script is listed in the notes. I will use the new font for a few days of normal work before deciding whether the last small points need more.

summary: Looked at Berkeley Mono in a long review session and adjusted cell height and the bold weight, which cut the eye strain that the first day showed.
body:
After a day of normal work with the new font I wrote down what felt off. Two things came up: lines felt a little cramped in the terminal, and bold text was still a bit loud.

The cell height was already reduced by 4 percent in the scratch tests. I carried that over, but in real use it was too tight with long diffs. Setting it to minus 2 percent felt better.

For the bold weight I compared semi-bold and medium side by side in a git log. Medium was too close to regular, so semi-bold stayed.

In Zed I changed the line height from 1.6 to 1.55 in the settings, because the font looked airy there. I put this into the generator as ZED_LINE_HEIGHT.

Also checked the prompt at the font size of 13 on the laptop screen without the external display. It still read fine, so I did not add a separate size.

Ran the generator and the bootstrap check. Both passed, and the Ghostty reload showed the new height at once.

I will watch for another day before touching the values again.

summary: Wrote a short tmux ligature test script that can be run in any pane, so the font and tmux behavior can be checked again after upgrades.
body:
The ligature problem took many manual steps to find, so I wrote a script to repeat the checks.

The script prints a line of sample ligature strings, a line of Powerline glyphs, a box drawing block, italic and undercurl samples, and the current TERM and tmux version. It is in the scripts folder as fontcheck.

Inside tmux it also does a rename of the current window and a split, prints the sample lines in the new pane, and closes it. The result still needs a human look, as there is no way to read the rendering from a script.

I added a one-line report at the end that shows the terminal features tmux believes it has, taken from tmux info. That would have saved the time I spent on the wrong settings.

Tried it with Berkeley Mono and then with JetBrains Mono via the restore script's test mode. Both looked right.

Tried it in the old iTerm2 as well, since it is still installed. It showed the undercurl without the override, which matches what I found before.

Added the script to the symlink script and mentioned it in the README of the dotfiles folder. Did not add it to the bootstrap check because the output needs a person to judge it.

One gap remains: the script cannot tell whether ligatures are on or off in Zed, as that is a separate app.

summary: Checked ligatures in Zed with Berkeley Mono and found they were off in the terminal panel but on in the editor, which matches Zed's settings.
body:
Opened the fontcheck output in the Zed terminal panel and compared it with the editor buffer.

In the buffer the ligatures worked. In the terminal panel they did not, even though the font was the same. Zed has a separate terminal font setting block, and the generator only wrote the buffer and UI values.

Added the terminal font family, size and font features to the Zed section of the generator. The features value is a map that turns calt on, and I wrote it as a JSON object with the comments kept.

After a reload of Zed the panel showed ligatures. The size was one too large again, so the terminal block also uses the Zed offset.

Checked that the generator kept the existing comments in settings.json by diffing before and after. Only the three new keys changed.

Ran the bootstrap check afterwards and it passed. I added a short comment in font.env about the terminal block so I remember why it exists.

summary: Switched the Neovim statusline and tabline icons to read the same fallback as the terminal and removed a font name that had been hard-coded for the GUI.
body:
While looking at fonts I noticed an old line in the Neovim config for a GUI client: guifont set to JetBrains Mono with a size. I do not use a GUI client any more, but the line was still there and would show the old font if I ever opened one.

Removed it and checked that nothing else in the Neovim config names a font. A grep over the whole dotfiles folder for JetBrains found four more places: the old iTerm2 profile export, a note in the README, the restore script test mode and an old tmux comment.

The iTerm2 profile is archived, so I left it. I changed the README to say that the font lives in font.env. The restore script's test mode needs the old name by design, and the tmux comment is now out of date and was removed.

In Neovim I checked the statusline and the tabline in the terminal. Both showed the icons correctly with the fallback. The only icon that looked off was a git branch glyph, which was a different width from the others. It came from the main font rather than the fallback.

Put that glyph's code point into the symbols-map of the Ghostty config, so it comes from the fallback with the others. After a reload it was the right width.

The generator did not manage the symbols-map, so I added the new range there as well and ran it again. The output file was identical except for the new range.

summary: Wrote a backup script check that restores the font files from the backup folder into a temp directory, to prove that the one-command undo of the font switch really works.
body:
The restore script for the font switch had only been tested against the scratch setup. I wanted to know that it works with the real files before I trust it.

The script copies four files from the backup folder: font.env, the Ghostty config, the Zed settings and tmux.conf. I wrote a test mode with a target directory argument, so it can restore into a temp folder instead of the real locations.

First run: the restore into the temp directory worked for three files. The Zed settings were missing from the temp folder. The cause was that the script expected the file under the name settings.json but the backup had it in a subfolder named zed, so the copy line silently skipped it.

Fixed the path and made the script report a missing source file with a non-zero exit code. Before, a missing file only printed nothing.

Second run: all four files restored. I diffed each against the backup and against the current real files. Three of the real files differed from the backup, as expected: font.env, the Ghostty config and the Zed settings. The tmux.conf differed by the thin space and the hook.

Then restored into the temp folder, ran the generator against the restored font.env, and compared. The output matched the old JetBrains Mono setup, which shows that the undo path leads back to a working state.

Also tested that the restore script refuses to run when the target is the real home folder and no flag is given. It asked for the flag and exited.

Added a line to the bootstrap check that the backup folder from the switch exists, with a count of the files in it. For now the check only warns.

One point left: the backup folder is inside the dotfiles folder, so the rsync backup script already covers it. I confirmed this by listing the rsync dry run for that path.

The next thing is to delete the backup after the new font has been in use for a few weeks.

summary: Looked at why the first Ghostty window after login showed the fallback font for a second and found it was the font being loaded lazily at app start.
body:
After a restart I noticed that the first Ghostty window showed the prompt in a wrong-looking font for about a second, then jumped to Berkeley Mono.

The jump happened only on the first window after login. Windows opened later were right at once. That suggested font loading rather than the config.

Checked the font was installed for the user and not only in a project folder. It was in the user fonts folder, so that was fine.

Tried a few ideas. Removing the symbols fallback did not change the jump, so the fallback was not the cause. Setting font-thicken did nothing either. Starting Ghostty at login with a hidden window made the first visible window correct, because the loading had already happened.

I do not want a hidden login item for a small cosmetic effect. I left it and wrote the finding down in the notes with the test results.

If it starts to bother me I will revisit the login item idea.

summary: Reworked the git alias file into small groups and fixed two aliases that broke when the branch cleanup alias was added, with a test script that runs each one.
body:
The git aliases had grown to about forty lines in one block and I found that two of them did not work after the merged-branches alias was added a few weeks ago.

The first broken alias was 'last', which shows the last commit with stat. It used an exclamation mark and a shell function that referenced an argument with a name that collided with a variable used in the new alias. The second was 'co', which got the wrong argument count when called with no arguments.

I split the alias section of the gitconfig into four groups with comment lines: status and log, branches, commits and signing, and helpers. The order inside each group is alphabetical now.

For the two broken ones I renamed the variable in the new alias and made 'co' call checkout directly without the function. Both work again.

To avoid this in future I wrote a test script that runs each alias in a temp repository with a few commits, a branch and a merge. It checks only the exit code and that the output is not empty, since the output format is a matter of taste.

First run: 38 aliases passed, 2 failed. The two were an alias for opening the remote in a browser, which needs a remote, and one for a stash helper that needs a dirty tree. I gave the temp repository a fake remote URL and a modified file, and the stash helper then passed. The browser alias still failed, because it calls open, so I made the test skip aliases that start a GUI.

Second run: 38 passed, 1 skipped, 0 failed.

I also checked that the signing aliases work in the temp repository without touching the 1Password agent. They use a config flag to disable signing in the test, set only in the script's environment.

The test script lives in the scripts folder, runs in about two seconds, and is not part of the bootstrap check. I may add it later.

One alias, 'wip', commits everything with a fixed message. I thought about removing it, since I rarely use it, but it is harmless and I left it.

summary: Added the alias test to the bootstrap check and investigated a slow git status in the prompt, which turned out to be an untracked-files scan in a large folder.
body:
Added the alias test script from yesterday to the bootstrap check, as a fast step that runs after the gitconfig link is in place. It adds about two seconds, which is fine. The check now covers nine of the eleven known setup gaps, counting the alias step as part of the git setup.

While testing it I saw the prompt hang for about a second in one folder. Not in the dotfiles folder, but in a large folder of downloaded data that is a git repo with many untracked files.

Measured it with time on git status. It took 940 ms, with most of it in the untracked scan. The prompt calls git status in the background but waits for it before drawing the dirty marker.

First idea: use git status with -uno in the prompt. That was fast, 70 ms, but then the prompt never shows untracked files, and I do like that marker in normal repos.

Second idea: use core.untrackedCache and the fsmonitor setting. I enabled both for that repo. The status went to 310 ms on the first call and 60 ms after that. That is good, but it needs the setting per repo.

Third idea: let the prompt use -uno for repos where the status takes longer than 300 ms, and remember that choice for the session. I wrote this as a small function with an associative array keyed by the repo path.

I tried the third approach for an hour. It worked but felt more complicated than it was worth, and a repo that gets slower later is hard to notice.

In the end I put untrackedCache and fsmonitor into the global gitconfig, so every repo gets them. The cost is a daemon per repo in use. I checked process counts after an hour of work, and there were four fsmonitor daemons, using about 12 MB each.

The data folder now shows the status at 60 ms. Other repos did not change in speed, since they were already fast.

One thing to watch: after a reboot the daemons start again on the first status call, which means the first prompt in each repo is slower. I measured it at about 300 ms for the data folder. I accept that.

Next time I should check that the fsmonitor daemons are removed when a repo is deleted. Git does this by itself, but I have not verified it.

summary: Checked that fsmonitor daemons are cleaned up after a repository is deleted and found a leftover process from a moved folder, then added a prune step to the shell.
body:
Following the note from last week, I deleted a throwaway repository with fsmonitor running and looked at the process list. The daemon stopped within a few seconds, so deleting works.

A moved folder was different. I moved a repo to another path while the daemon was running, and the old daemon stayed alive, watching a path that no longer existed.

I found one such process from earlier in the week. It had used about 10 MB and no CPU. I killed it by hand with git fsmonitor--daemon stop in the new path, which failed because it was the wrong path, so I used kill on the process.

To avoid piles of these I wrote a small function, gitprune, that lists processes of the daemon and stops those whose working directory no longer exists. It uses lsof to find the directory.

Tested on the leftover and on a living one. Only the leftover was stopped.

I hooked it into the login shell start, but only when the last run was more than a day ago, using a stamp file. That keeps the shell start time unchanged, and I checked with hyperfine that it still shows 176 ms.

summary: Looked into a Homebrew upgrade that replaced a tmux build and checked that the ligature and status fixes still held after it.
body:
A brew upgrade this evening included a new tmux version. After the upgrade I wanted to know whether the fixes of the last weeks still held.

Ran the fontcheck script inside tmux. The ligature strings were fine, the Powerline glyphs were fine, and the undercurl showed with the override.

The rename test also worked: one status refresh per rename in the log. The post-checkout hook updated the branch name straight away.

Then compared the tmux info output with the one saved from before the upgrade. One feature flag was now listed that had not been there before, but it was unrelated to text rendering, and nothing changed visibly.

Checked the tmux key bindings for opening Zed and the pane directory, and both still worked. The first call after login was slow as before, because of the zed CLI.

I wrote the new tmux version into the notes next to the earlier one, so if something breaks later, I know which upgrade to suspect.

Nothing needed fixing. I will repeat this check after the next tmux upgrade, now that the script makes it quick.

summary: Planned a cleanup of the notes folder and the old iTerm2 profile into an archive, then moved the font test notes into one summary file and deleted duplicates.
body:
The notes folder had grown during the font work and had many files with similar names. I wanted one place that tells the story, and an archive for the rest.

Listed the folder first: 31 files, of which 14 were about fonts, 6 about tmux ligatures, 5 about the shell start, and 6 others.

Plan: write one font-switch summary, move the raw test notes into an archive folder, and delete exact duplicates. I did not want to lose the numbers behind the decisions.

Checked duplicates with a hash of each file. Four pairs were identical, mostly copies made while testing the scratch Ghostty config. I removed one of each pair, leaving 27 files.

Wrote the summary file: which fonts were tested and why Berkeley Mono won, which tmux settings were tried and which one was the cause, the rename hook finding, the Zed terminal block, and the bold weight choice. It came to about 60 lines.

Moved the 14 font notes and the 6 tmux notes into notes/archive/font-switch. Left the shell start notes where they were, since they are about a different topic.

Then the iTerm2 profile. It lives in the dotfiles folder as an exported plist and is not used any more, but it also contains a few key mappings I might still want to look at. I opened it and extracted the mappings that differ from the defaults: three in total.

Two were already covered by the Ghostty keybinds. The third, a binding for word-wise deletion, was not, so I added it to the Ghostty config and tested it.

After that I moved the plist into the archive folder as well and removed the symlink step for it from the symlink script. The bootstrap check no longer mentions iTerm2.

Checked the backup script's rsync exclude list. The archive folder is included, which is what I want, because it is small.

The whole cleanup freed little space, but the folder is much easier to read. I added a short index file listing what is in the notes folder and archive.

summary: Tested the word-wise deletion keybind from the old iTerm2 profile in Ghostty, tmux and Neovim and found it conflicted with a tmux binding.
body:
The keybind I added yesterday worked in a plain shell. Inside tmux the same keys did something else.

The cause was a tmux binding of mine on the same key combination, which switched to the last window. In the root table, tmux caught the key before it reached the shell.

I checked list-keys for the combination and confirmed the binding. Since I use the window switch more than the word delete, I moved the delete to another combination, one with the alt modifier, and left tmux alone.

Updated the Ghostty config with the new combination, reloaded, and tested in the shell and in tmux. Both worked.

In Neovim insert mode the keys did nothing, since Neovim has its own mapping for deleting a word with control-w. I did not map anything there.

Tested in the Zed terminal panel, where Zed passes the keys through. It worked there too.

Added the combination to the keymap notes in the README, next to the other terminal keys, with a line about the tmux conflict.

summary: Measured the effect of the git fsmonitor setting on battery over a long session and decided to keep it, since the daemons used almost no CPU.
body:
I had been unsure about leaving fsmonitor on for every repo, so I measured it on a long working day on battery.

With Activity Monitor and a small script I sampled the CPU use of the daemons every minute. Across five hours with six repos in use, the total averaged 0.1 percent, with short spikes to 3 percent when a large checkout ran.

To compare, I turned fsmonitor off for one afternoon and watched the prompt. Status time in the big data repo went back to 310 ms with the untracked cache alone, and 940 ms before that.

Battery use was not measurable with the tools I have, because other apps changed more from hour to hour.

Given the almost-zero CPU and the clear gain in the prompt, I kept both settings. The gitprune function handles the stale daemons.

I noted the numbers in the notes file about the prompt so that I do not repeat the test.

summary: Set up a first draft of a Zed keymap file that matches the Neovim leader mappings, and listed the eight mappings that cannot be matched.
body:
Started a pass over the Zed keymap, because I still reach for Neovim muscle memory in Zed and get surprised.

First I listed the leader mappings in the Neovim config: 34 in total. They cover file search, buffer switching, grep, git, diagnostics, and a few window commands.

Then went through the Zed actions list and matched them by name. 26 had a direct equivalent: file finder, project search, go to definition, rename, code actions, next and previous diagnostic, and so on.

For those 26 I wrote the Zed keymap in keymap.json with the vim mode context, so that the leader keys apply only in normal mode in the editor. I took care that the mappings do not trigger inside the terminal panel or in the file tree.

The remaining eight have no good match. Examples are the mapping that opens a scratch buffer with the output of a shell command, one that toggles a quickfix list, and some that call my own Lua functions. I wrote them into a comment block in keymap.json with the reason for each.

Tested the 26 in a real session. Four did not work at first. Three had a typo in the action name, and one needed the context changed from Editor to vim_mode == normal.

After the fixes, all 26 worked. The file tree needed a separate small block, which I added.

The keymap file is linked by the symlink script, but the generator does not touch it, since it only handles fonts. I checked that the bootstrap check reports the link as present.

Next step: use Zed with these mappings for a week and see which of the missing eight I miss.

summary: Replaced the Neovim scratch-buffer shell output mapping in Zed with a task that runs a command and shows the result in the terminal panel.
body:
Of the eight mappings with no match in Zed, the one I missed first was the scratch buffer with the output of a shell command. I use it for quick data checks.

Zed has tasks, which can run a command and show the output in a terminal panel. That is not the same as a scratch buffer, but close enough for reading output.

I wrote a task in tasks.json named shell-run that asks for a command through a prompt variable and runs it in the project directory. The output stays in the terminal panel after the command ends, so it can be scrolled and searched.

Then added a keymap entry to the leader mapping, with the same key as in Neovim, calling the task spawn action.

Tested with three commands: a ls, a grep over the project and a command that fails. The failing one showed the exit code in the panel, which I liked, since the Neovim version did not.

One difference remains. In Neovim I can edit the output and save it, and in Zed the panel is read-only. For my use that is mostly fine.

I did not link tasks.json yet. It sits in the dotfiles folder and I added a line to the symlink script and checked that the link works on a fresh user account through the bootstrap check.

The bootstrap check passed. Seven of the eight mappings are still open, and I will see which of them I need.

summary: Added a Zed keymap entry for toggling the diagnostics list after finding the quickfix equivalent is the problems panel, leaving six mappings unmatched.
body:
Continued with the list of eight mappings, now down to seven. The Neovim mapping that toggles the quickfix list is mostly used for diagnostics and grep results.

In Zed, project search results open in a multi-buffer view, which already replaces the grep use. For diagnostics there is the project diagnostics view, which I can open with an action.

Added a leader mapping for the diagnostics view with the same key as the Neovim quickfix toggle. It opens the view, and pressing it again does not close it, so I use the normal close key.

Tested with a project that has a few type errors. The view lists them by file, and the next-diagnostic keys work with it.

The quickfix toggle in Neovim also holds results of other commands, like the build output. In Zed, I use the terminal panel for that, so I left it.

Updated the comment block in keymap.json: the diagnostics mapping moved from the unmatched list to the matched one, and the quickfix part about build output is noted as covered by the terminal panel.

Now six mappings are still unmatched, mostly the ones calling my own Lua functions. I think I will not port those, because I rarely use them.

Ran the symlink script and the bootstrap check. Both passed, and the keymap file is still the same link as before.

summary: Finished the Zed keymap pass by testing all mapped leader keys in a real editing session and noting which ones felt wrong in muscle memory
body:
I spent the evening editing real files in Zed with the keymap file from the last two days. The goal was to see whether the mappings that exist on paper work when typed fast. Of the mappings I had matched, most worked at once.

Two of them did not. The file-finder mapping opened the project search instead, because a default Zed binding took priority in the editor context. I fixed it by adding the context line `Editor && vim_mode == normal` to the keymap block. The buffer-switch mapping was fine, but it showed the list in the opposite order from Neovim, which is a Zed setting and not something the keymap can change.

I also tried the six mappings that cannot be matched. Four of them I did not miss at all. Two, the macro-replay key and the jump-list back key, I reached for several times in the evening. I wrote those two into a short list in the notes file as the ones to look at again.

The keymap file now has a comment above each block naming the Neovim mapping it copies. This should make later changes easier to check. I did not touch the Neovim config today.

Next step is to see whether the jump-list key has an equivalent in Zed's navigation history. If it does, only one unmatched mapping remains that I actually use. After that I want to put the Zed settings and keymap under the same backup script check as the font files.

summary: Found that Zed's navigation history covers the jump-list back key, so only the macro replay mapping is still missing from the keymap
body:
I looked at the two mappings that I missed in the last session. The jump-list back key turned out to have an equivalent in Zed: the actions `pane::GoBack` and `pane::GoForward`. I bound them to the same keys as in Neovim, in the normal mode context.

The behavior is not identical. Neovim's jump list only records big moves like searches and file jumps. Zed's history also records some cursor moves inside a file, so going back sometimes lands on a place I only scrolled to. After a bit of use this seemed acceptable. There is no setting that I found to narrow it.

The macro replay key has no equivalent. Zed's vim mode does support recording with `q`, but replay with the repeated-at key was flaky in my test with a counted replay. I did not want to bind something that only works half the time, so it stays on the unmatched list.

The unmatched list now has five entries. I updated the notes file and the comments in the keymap to say that. I also ran the keymap file through Zed's own validation by opening it, and there were no warnings.

Nothing was changed in the backup script. Next I want to check the Zed settings file for hard-coded font names, since the font generator should be the only place that sets them.

summary: Checked the Zed settings for hard-coded font names and found two leftovers that the font generator did not control, which I moved into generated output
body:
After the keymap work I looked at the Zed settings file for font values. The font generator from the Berkeley Mono work writes the buffer font and the UI font, but I suspected there were more. I searched the file for `font` and found two extra places.

The first was the terminal panel font family, which still said JetBrains Mono. It had been set by hand a long time ago, before the generator existed. It was hidden because the generator's value for the terminal was the same name at that time. The second was `agent_font_size`-like UI text size for the assistant panel, which was fixed at a number that did not follow the UI font size value in font.env.

I changed the generator template so that both values come from font.env. The terminal panel now uses the Ghostty family value, and the panel text size uses the UI size. I ran the generator and compared the output with the old settings using diff. Only those two lines changed.

Then I opened Zed and looked at the terminal panel and the assistant panel. Both showed Berkeley Mono at the expected sizes. The panel text looked slightly larger than before, which is the correct result of linking to the UI value.

I added a check to the generator test that fails if the generated Zed file contains a font name that is not in font.env. This should catch the same mistake if someone adds a font line by hand again. The test passed on the current files.

The next thing is to include the Zed files in the backup script check, which I left from last time.

summary: Added the Zed settings and keymap to the rsync backup and extended the restore check to prove they come back intact in a temp directory
body:
The backup script already copied the font files and the main dotfiles. It did not copy the Zed config folder, so a lost laptop would have meant rebuilding the keymap from memory. I added `~/.config/zed/settings.json` and `~/.config/zed/keymap.json` to the include list. I left out the Zed cache and the language server folders, since those are large and can be rebuilt.

I ran the backup once by hand with `--dry-run` first. The listing showed the two files and nothing else from that folder, as intended. Then I ran it for real. It took a few seconds because only changed files are copied.

The restore check from the font work restores into a temp directory and compares checksums. I extended it with the two Zed files. On the first run it failed for settings.json. The reason was that the generator rewrites the file with a new timestamp comment each run, so the backup copy differed from the file on disk when the generator ran between backup and check. I changed the generator to drop the timestamp line. After that the checksums matched.

I ran the check three times, once after running the generator again, to make sure the output was now stable. All three runs passed. I also deleted the temp directories after each run, which the script does with a trap.

There is one open point. The keymap file has comments that I edit often, so the backup always has a recent copy, but there is no history. I thought about putting the file in a small git repository inside the backup folder. I decided against it for now, since the daily snapshots in the backup script already keep seven versions.

Next I want to look at the slow-ish first start of Zed when many projects are open.

summary: Investigated why Zed took several seconds to show the window with many projects open and found the restored workspace list was the cause, not extensions
body:
Zed had felt slow to start over the last week, so I measured it. I closed all windows, started it from the terminal with the log visible, and timed the first window with a stopwatch. It took about four seconds to show anything and about nine seconds until the editor accepted input. That was longer than I remembered.

My first guess was extensions. I have six installed. I disabled them all in settings and tried again. The times dropped by less than half a second, so extensions were not the main cost.

Then I looked at the Zed log, which is in `~/Library/Logs/Zed/Zed.log`. It showed that on start it restored eleven workspaces, among them four folders that no longer exist because I had moved or deleted the projects. For each of those it logged a failed path lookup and a retry. Together the retries took a few seconds.

I found the setting `restore_on_startup`. It was on `last_session`, which restores every window from the last run. I changed it to `last_workspace`, which restores only the last one. I also cleared the recent project list for the dead folders using the open-recent menu.

After the change, the first window showed after about one second and accepted input after about three seconds. I ran the measure three times and the numbers were close each time.

The downside is that when I had several projects open and restarted, only one came back. I decided this is fine, since I mostly work in one project in Zed and use Neovim for the others. If I miss it, I can set the value back.

I wrote the setting into the generator template, not into the generated file, so that it stays after the next run. I checked with the generator test, and it still passed.

I also noticed that the dead folders came from the old scratch config tests, which I should have cleaned. I removed two more leftover folders in the notes directory while I was there. No further work is planned here.

summary: Planned a cleanup of the Brewfile after seeing that about a third of the listed packages were never used in the last months, and made a first sorted list
body:
The Brewfile had grown since the first version, and the last Homebrew upgrade took a long time because of packages I did not recognize. I decided to plan the cleanup before touching anything. First I ran `brew leaves` and compared the output with the Brewfile. There were 14 leaves installed that are not in the file, and 9 entries in the file that are not installed.

For the installed ones, I checked what each package does with `brew desc`. Most were tools pulled in by experiments, like a video converter and two image tools. For the file entries that are not installed, most were casks I removed by hand and never took out of the list.

I made three groups in a notes file: keep, remove, and unsure. The keep group has the core tools such as git, tmux, neovim, mise, ripgrep and fd. The remove group has 11 packages. The unsure group has 6, mostly small command line tools that I may have used in scripts. For those I searched the dotfiles folder for their names with ripgrep. Three showed up in the backup script or the shell functions, so they moved to keep.

I did not remove anything yet. A package that a script uses silently would only fail at the moment I need it, so I want to test the scripts afterward. The plan is to remove the unused ones in small batches, run the bootstrap check after each batch, and then update the Brewfile.

I also noticed that the Brewfile has no comments. I want to add a short comment for each group so the next cleanup is easier.

summary: Removed the first batch of five unused Homebrew packages and ran the bootstrap check, which passed with no missing commands
body:
Following the plan from the afternoon, I took the first five packages from the remove list: the video converter, two image tools, a JSON viewer I replaced with jq, and an old network tool. I ran `brew uninstall` for each, one by one, and watched for messages about dependents.
