Two of them had dependents that were also on the remove list, so Homebrew warned and I took them in the right order. Nothing in the keep group was affected.

Then I ran the bootstrap check script, which tests that every command used by the shell functions and aliases can be found. It passed. I also opened a new tmux session and a new Ghostty window to check that the shell started without errors, and it did.

I deleted the five matching lines from the Brewfile. The Brewfile check with `brew bundle check` now says that all dependencies are satisfied. Six more packages are left on the remove list for the next batches.

summary: Removed the remaining packages from the cleanup list in two batches, found one alias that needed a removed tool, and fixed it and added Brewfile comments
body:
I continued with the remove list and took the next batch of three packages: two small archive tools and a font preview tool. I uninstalled them and ran the bootstrap check. It passed again, so I took the last three in a second batch.

After that batch the alias test failed. One of the git aliases, the one that prints a graph log with a pager option, called a tool that I had just removed, a small diff colorizer. The alias was old and I had forgotten it. The bootstrap check had not caught it because it only tests that the alias exists, and the alias test is a separate script that I had not run.

I looked at the alias. The colorizer was only used to color the diff lines in the graph output. Modern git can do that with `--color`, so I removed the pipe to the tool and used the built-in coloring. I ran the alias test again and it passed. I compared the output of the old and new alias on a small repository, and they looked the same except for one slightly different shade of green.

This made me change the bootstrap check. It now runs the alias test as its last step, so one command covers both. I ran it end to end, and it printed an all-green summary.

Then I looked at the Brewfile. It has three groups now: core tools, editor and language tools, and apps. I added a one-line comment above each group, and a comment next to the four entries where the reason is not obvious. For example, one tool is used only by the backup script, and I wrote that next to it.

I ran `brew bundle check` and `brew bundle cleanup` without the force option to see what Homebrew would remove. The cleanup listing was empty, which means the Brewfile and the installed leaves are in sync.

The remaining thing is the casks. A few apps are in the file that I rarely open. I will decide on those separately, since removing an app is more of a personal choice than a cleanup.

summary: Decided which rarely used casks to keep by checking last-opened dates, and removed two apps from the Brewfile and the machine
body:
Today I went through the casks in the Brewfile. There are 12. To decide I looked at when each app was last opened, using `mdls -name kMDItemLastUsedDate` on the app bundles.

Nine had been opened in the last weeks. Three had not been opened for many months: a screen ruler app, a markdown preview app that Zed and Neovim make unnecessary, and a disk analyzer. I opened the disk analyzer once to check that I did not need it, and it was not important, since `du` and `ncdu` cover the same job.

I removed the ruler and the markdown preview with `brew uninstall --cask` and `--zap` for the leftovers. The zap listing showed some preference files in `~/Library`, which I let it delete. I kept the disk analyzer for now because I sometimes use it to look at a full disk quickly, and one view helps more than the command line there.

I updated the Brewfile and ran `brew bundle check`, which was fine. Then I ran the bootstrap check and it passed.

The free disk space went up by around 400 MB, which is small but it does not matter much. The main value is a Brewfile that matches what I use.

Nothing is left from the cleanup plan. I will look at the Brewfile again after the next Mac setup test.

summary: Wrote a small script that lists Brewfile entries not matched in installed leaves so drift is easy to see before an upgrade
body:
Since the cleanup showed how far the Brewfile had drifted, I wrote a small script called `brew-drift` in the scripts folder. It compares `brew bundle list` for formulae and casks with `brew leaves` and `brew list --cask`, and prints two lists: installed but not in the file, and in the file but not installed.

The first version used `comm` on sorted output. It printed names with tap prefixes for some entries, so the same package appeared in both lists. I stripped everything before the last slash with `sed` to fix that. After that the two lists matched correctly in a test.

I tested it by installing a small package that I did not add to the file. The script showed it under the first list. After I uninstalled it, the output was empty. It exits with code 1 when there is any drift, so the bootstrap check can call it.

I added a call at the end of the bootstrap check, but as a warning and not a failure, since a temporary install should not break the check. The warning prints the names.

I wrote a short usage comment at the top of the script. That is all for today.

summary: Looked into a shell start that had gotten slower after the Brewfile cleanup and traced it to a mise hook running on every prompt, then moved it to directory change only
body:
After the cleanup I opened a few new windows and the shell start felt a little slow. I measured with `time zsh -i -c exit` ten times. The average was about 310 ms. Earlier in the project I had the start under 150 ms, so something had changed.

I used `zprof` by adding `zmodload zsh/zprof` at the top of the zshrc and calling `zprof` at the end. The top entry was the mise activation, with several calls to a hook function. That was surprising since mise itself starts quickly.

Looking at the zshrc, I found that I had two lines that set up mise. One was `eval "$(mise activate zsh)"`. The other, a few lines below, added the hook for the prompt through a custom function that I wrote to show the Node version in the prompt. That function called `mise current node` on every prompt and also at start. Each call took around 40 ms.

The duplicated setup was from an old experiment with a different way to show versions. I had left the function in when I moved to the standard activate. I removed the second setup.

For the prompt I still wanted the Node version, but only inside projects. I changed the function to run on `chpwd` instead of every prompt, and to cache the result in a variable. It reads the cached value when the prompt draws.

I measured again ten times. The average was about 140 ms, which is back to the earlier level. The prompt still showed the right Node version after I changed directories between two projects with different versions.

One edge case: when the `.tool-versions` or `mise.toml` file changes without a directory change, the cached value is stale. I decided to refresh the cache with a precmd check of the file's modification time. That costs a single `stat` call, which is cheap.

I tested it by editing the file in one pane and looking at the prompt in another. The prompt updated on the next command. I also checked that the Python version display works in the same way.

I ran the bootstrap check and the alias test. Both passed.

The time was measured with the machine on power. I did not test on battery, but I do not expect a difference. Next I will look at whether the compinit call can use the cache more aggressively, since it is now the largest item in the profile.

summary: Made compinit use its dump cache and only rebuild once a day, which cut another 40 ms from the shell start
body:
The profile from last week showed compinit as the largest item left. I looked at how the zshrc calls it. It ran `compinit` without any option, which checks every completion file for changes at every start.

I changed it to the common pattern: check the age of `~/.zcompdump`, and if it is younger than 24 hours, run `compinit -C`, which skips the check. Otherwise run the full `compinit`. In zsh this can be written with a glob qualifier: `if [[ -n ${ZDOTDIR:-$HOME}/.zcompdump(#qN.mh+24) ]]`.

I measured before and after with ten runs each. The average went from about 140 ms to about 100 ms. The first start after the dump gets old is slower, around 220 ms, but that happens once a day.

I had a concern that new completions from a Homebrew install would not show up. I tested it by installing a small tool with completions and opening a new shell. The completion did not work until I deleted the dump file. I added a small function `rebuild-comp` that removes the dump and runs `compinit`, and added a line to the Brewfile comments that says to run it after installs. I also call it from the bootstrap script.

I then checked that tab completion for git branches, mise commands and ssh hosts all work. They did.

There is another thing I saw in the profile: the `nvm` leftovers. A function stub from the old nvm setup was still in a file that I source. It does nothing but costs about 5 ms to define. I removed the file and the line that sources it. I searched the folder for `nvm` and found two comments, which I left.

The start time is about 100 ms now. I think that is good enough and I will stop here.

summary: Set up git commit signing with an SSH key from the 1Password agent on the work-side config, and tested that a signed commit verifies locally
body:
I wanted all commits signed. Since the SSH keys already live in the 1Password agent, I used SSH signing and not GPG. The setting needed in git config is `gpg.format ssh`, `user.signingkey` with the public key, and `commit.gpgsign true`.

I took the public key from 1Password and put it in `~/.config/git/signing.pub`. Then I set `user.signingkey` to the path of that file. I also set `gpg.ssh.program` to the 1Password signing helper in the app bundle, since the plain `ssh-keygen` cannot talk to the agent for signing in all cases.

The first test commit failed with `error: Load key ... invalid format`. The reason was that I had copied the key with a trailing comment line break, so the file had two lines. I fixed the file to a single line and the commit worked. 1Password asked for approval with Touch ID once.

To verify locally, git needs an allowed signers file. I created `~/.config/git/allowed_signers` with my email and the key, and set `gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile`. Then `git log --show-signature -1` printed `Good "git" signature`.

I noticed one problem: Touch ID was asked for every commit, which is annoying with rebases that rewrite many commits. In the 1Password settings I changed the approval for the agent to stay valid for the session while the app is unlocked. I tested a rebase of five commits and it asked once.

The alias file has a few aliases that create commits, like the fixup one. I ran the alias test and it passed, so signing does not break them.

I also thought about the global post-checkout hook and other hooks. None of them make commits, so they are not affected.

The config is in the dotfiles git folder now and the backup includes it. What is left is to tell the hosting service about the signing key so that commits show as verified there. That is a step in the web interface, so I will do it myself.

summary: Added the signing key setup to the bootstrap script so a new Mac gets the same git signing config without manual steps
body:
Since signing took several steps, I put them into the bootstrap script. It now writes the public key file from a variable that holds the key, creates the allowed signers file, and sets the git config values with `git config --global`.

The public key is not secret, so it is fine to keep it in the dotfiles folder. I stored it as `git/signing.pub` and let the script link it into `~/.config/git/`.

I tested the script on a temporary HOME directory by running it with `HOME=$(mktemp -d)`. The resulting config had all five values. A test commit in a temp repository could not be signed there, since the agent is bound to the real HOME, but the config check passed.

I noted in the script that the 1Password agent must be turned on first.

summary: Reviewed the tmux key bindings after a month of use, removed four that were never pressed, and fixed the copy mode binding that clashed with the word deletion keybind
body:
I went through the tmux config to see which key bindings I actually use. To check, I ran a small count over a week: I added `-n` logging through a wrapper? No, tmux has no built-in key log, so I used a simpler approach and read the config together with my shell history of `tmux` commands and what I remembered pressing.

That gave a rough list. Four bindings were clearly unused: a layout cycle binding, a binding for synchronized panes, one for a clock, and one for a second prefix. I removed them from the config and from the cheat sheet in the notes.

The copy mode binding was the real problem. Earlier I found that the word-wise deletion keybind from the old iTerm2 profile clashed with a tmux binding. I had put off a decision. The clash was that Ghostty sends `Escape` followed by `Backspace` for Option-Backspace, and tmux with `escape-time` set low took the escape as the start of a different sequence in copy mode.

I looked at `escape-time` in the config. It was 10 ms. That is fast, but when the machine is busy the two bytes can arrive with more delay, and tmux treats them as separate keys. I raised it to 25 ms and tested. Option-Backspace deleted a word in the shell inside tmux every time, ten tries out of ten. At 10 ms it failed three times in ten.

The cost of a higher escape-time is a short delay when I press Escape in Neovim inside tmux. 25 ms is not noticeable to me. I checked by pressing Escape quickly in insert mode and normal mode switching felt immediate.

I also changed the Ghostty config to send the sequence directly. There is a keybind option `keybind = alt+backspace=text:\x17`, which sends Ctrl-W. That avoids the escape handling entirely and works in the shell. But in Neovim, Ctrl-W in insert mode deletes a word too, and in the command line as well, so it behaves the same. I kept the Ghostty keybind and the tmux timing change, so that both paths work.

Then I ran the ligature test script in a pane to make sure nothing in the font behavior changed. It passed.

I updated the cheat sheet with the final list of bindings, which now has 23 lines. I want to check the config for the copy-mode vi bindings next, since I still use the mouse for selection more than I should.

summary: Set up copy mode vi bindings in tmux with a yank to the system clipboard, replacing mouse selection for most cases
body:
I wanted to copy text from tmux without the mouse. The config had `mode-keys vi` but only the default bindings. I added `v` to begin selection and `y` to copy and leave copy mode. For the system clipboard I used `copy-pipe-and-cancel "pbcopy"`.

The first test worked in a pane but not in a second window that I started over SSH to another machine. There the clipboard is the remote one, so pbcopy does not exist. The better route is the OSC 52 escape, which Ghostty supports. I set `set -g set-clipboard on` and checked `allow-passthrough`. With that setting tmux sends the copied text to the terminal, which puts it on the local clipboard.

So I split the binding. In local panes `y` uses pbcopy. Everywhere, tmux's own set-clipboard also sends OSC 52. In the SSH test, pasting on the Mac gave the right text.

I also added `Y` to copy the whole line, and `/` and `?` for search, which exist already. I tried them on a long build log and they worked.

One issue: the mouse drag still works, which is fine. I left `mouse on`.

I added the new bindings to the cheat sheet. Next, I will use them for a few days before changing more.

summary: Fixed the Ghostty config so Option-Backspace and Option-arrows move by word in tmux and Neovim after a check of each key in each tool
body:
I tested Option-Left, Option-Right and Option-Backspace in the shell, tmux, and Neovim. The shell and Neovim in tmux were fine. In plain Neovim without tmux, Option-Left jumped by character. The cause was that Ghostty's `macos-option-as-alt` was only set to `left`. With the right Option key it sent special characters.

I set it to `true`. After a reload, both Option keys work as alt. I checked that typing special characters, which I use rarely, still works with a shortcut for the compose key. It did not matter for my use.

The config is generated from the dotfiles, so I changed the file there and not the live one.

summary: Prepared the set-up test for a clean user account on the same Mac by writing a script that runs the bootstrap in a fresh home and reports what is missing
body:
Since a new Mac setup was done some time ago, I wanted a way to test the scripts without a second machine. I decided to use a new macOS user account created just for tests, with the dotfiles folder copied over, instead of a virtual machine, because the VM would need a license-free image and a lot of disk space.

I created a standard user named `dottest` in System Settings. Then I wrote a script, `scripts/test-fresh-home`, that copies the dotfiles into that user's home with `sudo cp -R`, fixes the owner with `chown`, and then runs the bootstrap script as that user using `sudo -u dottest -H zsh -lc`.

The first run failed early. Homebrew is installed under `/opt/homebrew`, owned by my user, so the test user could not run `brew` to install packages. I decided that this is fine for the test: the script skips the Homebrew step and only tests the parts that link files and set defaults. I added a `--skip-brew` flag to the bootstrap script that prints a notice and moves on.

The second run got further. It linked the zsh files, the tmux config, the git config and the Ghostty config. It failed at the macOS defaults step with `Could not write domain`, because one default needs the Dock to be running for that user, and the test user was not logged in. I made the defaults script check for a GUI session through `launchctl print gui/$(id -u)` and skip the Dock part with a notice if there is none.

The third run went through to the end and printed a summary. It listed 41 linked files and 3 skipped steps. I compared the list of links with the expected list in the script and they matched.

Then I checked the shell for the test user. The zshrc loaded without error messages, but the prompt printed a warning that `mise` was not found, which is true since skip-brew was set. I made the mise lines in the zshrc conditional with `command -v mise`. This is a good change anyway: the shell should start cleanly on a machine where a tool is missing.

I also checked the git config for that user. The signing settings were there, but the 1Password agent socket did not exist, so a commit would fail. The bootstrap script already prints a reminder about that.

At the end the script deletes nothing, so the test user keeps the files. I added an optional `--clean` flag that removes the copied dotfiles in that home. The account stays.

The test took about two minutes. I will run it after each bigger change to the scripts from now on.

summary: Ran the fresh-home test after the Ghostty and tmux changes, found three problems in the bootstrap on a clean account, and fixed all three
body:
I ran `scripts/test-fresh-home --clean` first, to start from an empty home for the test user, and then the full run. It printed three warnings that I had not seen before, because the earlier test had left files from the first run in place.

The first warning was that the Ghostty config linked to a font.env file that did not exist yet. The font generator is supposed to run before the links are made, but the bootstrap ran the links first. I changed the order in the script so that the generator runs first, then the links. On the earlier test the generated files were still there, which hid the problem.

The second was a tmux error on start: `unknown option: allow-passthrough`. The test user's shell found an older tmux in `/usr/bin`? No, the test user had no Homebrew path, so tmux was not found at all, and the error came from a version check in my config that called `tmux -V` and got an empty string. I wrapped the check so that it only applies when the version string is not empty, and I put a notice in the bootstrap that tmux must be installed. With `--skip-brew` that is expected.

The third was in the Neovim config. On first start Neovim tried to install its plugins from the network and printed a long error since the test account has no cached plugin manager. The plugin manager bootstrap code cloned the manager with git, which worked, but the clone used the SSH URL, and the test user has no key. I changed the clone URL to HTTPS. That is the more robust choice for a first install anyway.

After the three fixes I cleaned the account and ran the whole test again. It finished with 41 linked files, the notices for the skipped steps, and no warnings. I opened Neovim as the test user in a terminal and the plugins installed in about twenty seconds. The statusline icons showed the fallback font correctly through the shared setting.

As a last check I opened a Ghostty window under the test user. The window needs a GUI session, so I used fast user switching. The font was Berkeley Mono and the tmux ligature test script passed there too. That was reassuring because it is a different home directory and a different font cache.

I wrote a short section in the notes on how to run the test and what each skipped step means. I also added the test to my reminder list for after bigger script changes. I will switch back to my own account and delete the cached files in the test home later today.

summary: Looked at why the macOS defaults script reported success but the key repeat rate had not changed, and found it needed a logout to apply
body:
After the fresh-home test I checked the defaults script more closely. It sets about thirty values with `defaults write`, and I wanted to know which ones actually take effect without a restart. I started with the key repeat rate, since it was the one I noticed on the test account: the script said it was set, but typing still felt like the old rate.

I read the value with `defaults read NSGlobalDomain KeyRepeat` and it was 2, as intended. So the write worked. The system keeps the active value in memory and reads the preference at login for this one, so a logout or restart applies it. The settings pane does it live because it also calls a private API.

I tried `killall cfprefsd` to refresh the cache. That helped for some values, like the Finder ones, but not for key repeat. So I decided to keep it simple: the script now prints a list at the end with the settings that need a logout, and for the Dock and Finder it restarts those processes.

I went through the thirty values and sorted them by hand into three groups: live, needs app restart, needs logout. Only four needed a logout: key repeat, initial key repeat, the tap-to-click setting, and the function key mode. I put the groups into comments inside the script.

The printed message at the end of the script lists the four names under a line that says to log out. I ran it on the test account and the message appeared as expected.

summary: Set up a Zed task for running the ligature test script and found the terminal panel reports a narrower width than Ghostty, so the script now prints a ruler first
body:
Today I wanted the tmux ligature test script from a while ago to be runnable from inside Zed too, since the terminal panel there has its own ligature setting. I added a Zed task called ligature-check that calls scripts/ligtest.sh in the panel. The first run looked wrong: the alignment row of the script was two cells narrower than in Ghostty, and the arrows lined up differently.

I suspected the font at first, but the Zed terminal font comes from the generated output, so it was the same Berkeley Mono family as everywhere else. The real cause was the line height and cell width setting of the panel, which Zed computes on its own and does not take from font.env. I added a ruler line of 80 digits at the top of the script so the width of the panel is visible at once, and the script now prints the column count it reads from tput next to it. In Zed the count matched the visible width, so the tool itself is honest and only the cell size differs by a small fraction.

I then tried setting the terminal line height in the Zed settings to the same value as the Ghostty cell height from the earlier adjustment. That removed the vertical gap but not the width difference, so I left it generated from font.env with a comment. Ligatures in the panel stay off by design, as noted before, so the script only needs to confirm that the glyphs are not broken into odd pieces. They are not.

What remains is to decide whether the width difference matters. It does not touch the editor buffer, only the panel, so I will not chase it further unless a Powerline status line is used there. I added a line about it to the font summary notes and committed nothing, since the folder is not a repository, but the backup run picked up the new task file.

summary: Cleaned the SSH config of old host entries and tested that each remaining host still connects through the 1Password agent
body:
The SSH config had 17 host blocks. Many were for servers I no longer use. I first listed them with `grep '^Host '` and went through each one. For each I checked the last use by looking in the shell history with `atuin`? No, I used plain `history` and a search for the host name.

Six hosts had no use in the history at all. Three more pointed to addresses that no longer answered: I tried `ssh -o ConnectTimeout=5 host true` and got timeouts. I moved all nine blocks into a file `ssh/archive.conf` that is not included, so I can bring one back if needed, and left eight active hosts.

Then I tested each active host with the same command. Seven connected. The eighth failed with `Permission denied (publickey)`. The block had `IdentityFile ~/.ssh/old_key`, a file that was deleted when I moved the keys into the 1Password agent. Since `IdentitiesOnly yes` was set in that block, ssh did not try the agent keys. I removed the two lines for the identity file and kept the `IdentityAgent` setting from the global block. After that the host connected.

I looked at the global block at the top of the file. It has `IdentityAgent` for the 1Password socket, `AddKeysToAgent` that is not needed anymore, and `UseKeychain yes`, which belongs to the old way of storing keys. I removed the last two lines. I tested a connection to make sure nothing depended on them, and it worked.

I added `ServerAliveInterval 30` for all hosts, since a long-idle connection through tmux had dropped twice in the last weeks and this is the usual fix. I could not prove that it fixes it right now, so I will watch whether drops happen again.

The config is now 41 lines instead of about 110. I ran the fresh-home test again, and it linked the file without trouble.

One last thing: the archive file contains host names and users, but no keys. It is still in the dotfiles folder and the backup. I think that is fine.

summary: Audited the zsh startup after the compinit and mise changes and found the remaining cost is two plugin sources and a slow git prompt call, so the prompt now reads git status lazily.
body:
I started with zprof enabled in a clean shell to see where the start time went after the earlier compinit and mise fixes. Total start was about 190 ms, still above the 120 ms I wanted. The profile showed three items: two plugin sources (syntax highlighting and autosuggestions) at about 35 ms together, the prompt's git status call at about 28 ms, and a leftover brew shellenv eval at about 20 ms.

The brew shellenv eval was the easy one. I replaced it with the fixed paths it exports, guarded by a check that the brew prefix exists, so a new Mac still works. That saved about 18 ms.

The prompt called git status synchronously on every draw, even outside repositories, because the check for a repository ran after the call. I swapped the order, so the prompt now asks git rev-parse first and skips everything outside a repository. Inside a repository the status is now read through a small async function that updates the prompt when the result arrives. The first draw shows the branch name only and the dirty marker follows after a moment.

For the plugins I tried deferring them to the first prompt with a precmd hook that sources them once and removes itself. This worked for autosuggestions but the syntax highlighting plugin broke the first typed line, so I left that one eager and deferred only the suggestions.

After all this the start measured 118 ms over twenty runs with hyperfine, median. I checked that the tmux panes and the Zed terminal panel also start without errors. What is left is to see if the async prompt flickers in a very slow repository; I will test it in the large monorepo checkout later this week.

summary: Tested the async git prompt in the largest repository and found a flicker when status took over a second, so the prompt now keeps the old marker until the new one is ready.
body:
I went to the largest checkout on the machine, where git status takes about 1.4 seconds even with fsmonitor, to see how the async prompt from last week behaves. The dirty marker disappeared on each prompt and came back a second later, which looked like flicker.

The cause was that the async function cleared the cached status variable before starting the job. I changed it to keep the previous value until the new result arrives, and to mark it with a dim color only if the job has run longer than 300 ms. That removed the flicker in my test.

I also found that a job started in a previous prompt was never cancelled when I pressed enter quickly several times. Several git processes stacked up. I added a check that kills the earlier job before starting a new one, and verified with ps that only one git status runs at a time.

The small repositories are unchanged. Start time is still at 118 ms.

summary: Added a git alias for a clean branch overview that lists local branches with last commit age and upstream gone markers, replacing a manual loop I kept retyping.
body:
I kept typing a for-loop over git branch to find stale local branches, so I wrote an alias called brs. It uses git for-each-ref with a format string that shows the branch name, relative commit date, upstream tracking state and the subject line, sorted by commit date.

The first version broke on branches with slashes in the name because I cut the string on slash. I switched to using the refname:short format and tab separators instead. Branches whose upstream is gone get a marker through the track format, which is how I find ones that can be deleted.

I also added a companion alias, brclean, that only prints the delete commands for gone branches and does not run them. I prefer to review the list first. Both aliases are in the gitconfig under the alias section, and I added two lines to the aliases comment block. I tested in three repositories, including one with detached HEAD, where the output was fine.

summary: Fixed the Neovim startup warning about a deprecated LSP call after a plugin update and measured that startup stayed at 41 ms.
body:
Neovim printed a deprecation warning at startup after the last plugin update. The message pointed at a call in my lsp config file that used an old function for getting clients.

I replaced it with the newer function that takes a filter table. The semantics differ slightly: the old call returned all clients for the buffer, the new one needs the buffer number in the filter, otherwise it returns all clients globally. I passed the current buffer explicitly in the format-on-save helper, where this mattered.

I checked with the health command that no other deprecations were listed. Then I opened Lua, Python and TypeScript files and saved each one to confirm formatting still ran. Startup time measured with the startuptime flag stayed at 41 ms. Nothing else needed changing.

summary: Started moving Python version handling fully to mise by listing every project that still used a pyenv shim and finding four that need a .tool-versions file.
body:
The move from nvm to mise happened earlier, but Python was only half done. A leftover pyenv init line in the zshrc still existed behind a check, and I wanted to remove it. Before doing so I needed to know what still depended on it.

I searched the code folder for .python-version files and found seven. Three had a matching entry in mise already. Four did not, and in those mise silently fell back to the global Python, which is 3.12. I ran each project's test command under both versions to see if anything differed. Three passed with both. One, an old scraping script, failed under 3.12 because it imports the removed distutils module.

For the three that passed I wrote a .tool-versions file with the version from the old file. For the scraping script I pinned 3.10 in mise and installed it. mise installed 3.10 in about 40 seconds, since it compiles from source with the python-build plugin, and I had to add the openssl path to the environment for the build to succeed.

I did not yet remove the pyenv lines. First I want to run the bootstrap in a fresh home, which would show whether a new Mac gets all the versions right. I wrote the list of the four projects and their versions into the notes file so the next step can check them. The bootstrap script has a section for mise installs that reads the global config only, so it needs a change too. I will do that in the next session, together with the cleanup of pyenv itself and its Brewfile entry.

summary: Extended the bootstrap script to install tool versions from mise config files in known project folders, and the fresh-home test passed for all four Python versions.
body:
Following the earlier session, I changed the mise section of the bootstrap. Before, it ran mise install against the global config only. A new Mac would therefore miss the 3.10 that the scraping script needs.

I added a loop over a list of project folders kept in a small text file next to the script. For each folder that exists it runs mise install inside it. Missing folders are skipped with a note, since a new Mac will not have the code cloned yet. This keeps the bootstrap from failing, but it also means the versions come only after the clone. I added a line to the final report that says which project versions were not installed because the folder was missing.

Then I ran the fresh-home test script. The first run failed in mise because the build of 3.10 could not find openssl in the clean environment. I had set the path by hand last time in my own shell. I moved it into the bootstrap, where it reads the brew prefix of openssl and exports the flags only during the install step.

The second run passed. The report listed the folders as missing, as expected in a clean account, and the global Python and Node versions were correct. I checked python --version in each of the seven project folders on my own account and all matched their files.

Open: removing pyenv from the zshrc and the Brewfile, which I will do this evening.

summary: Removed pyenv from the zshrc and Brewfile, fixed a broken virtualenv that pointed at a pyenv path, and confirmed the shell start and bootstrap still work.
body:
With the mise versions verified this morning, I removed pyenv. First I deleted the guarded init lines from the zshrc and the pyenv entries from the Brewfile, including pyenv-virtualenv, which I had forgotten about.

Then I opened a new shell and ran the test commands in all seven projects. Six worked. One older project failed with an error that the interpreter at a pyenv path did not exist. The cause was a virtualenv created years ago whose bin/python was a symlink into the pyenv versions folder. I deleted the virtualenv and recreated it with mise's Python and pip installing from the lock file. The tests then passed.

I searched the other virtualenvs on the machine for symlinks pointing into the pyenv folder with find and a readlink check. Two more existed in archived projects. I did not recreate them, since those projects are not in use, but wrote their names into the notes so I know why they would fail.

Next I uninstalled the brew packages and removed the pyenv folder in the home directory, after a copy of the versions list to the notes. The folder was 2.1 GB, so the disk space is welcome.

Shell start time went from 118 ms to 111 ms, because the guarded pyenv check had still cost a little. I ran the Brewfile drift script from the cleanup, which showed no entries missing or extra. Then I ran the fresh-home test again and it passed with no missing commands.

One small thing remained: the zsh completion for pyenv was still in the completion cache. I removed the dump file and let compinit rebuild it once.

The move to mise is now complete for Node and Python. If I need Ruby or Go later, I will add them the same way and not install another version manager.

summary: Looked into why Ghostty showed a bell badge on every tmux window switch and found the tmux bell-action setting was passing bells through, so I limited it to the current window.
body:
Ghostty showed a bell marker in the tab title after almost every window switch in tmux. At first I suspected a program ringing the bell. I tested by running printf with the bell character in one pane, and that did produce the marker as expected, but switching windows without that did also.

The cause was in tmux: the monitor-bell option was on and bell-action was set to any, so a bell in any window was passed to the outer terminal. A prompt hook from my own config printed a bell when a long command finished, which I had added months ago for notifications. That hook ran in background windows too.

I set bell-action to current in the tmux config, so only the visible window passes the bell through, and kept the window status highlight for others. I reloaded the config and ran a long sleep in a background window. The status line highlighted that window and Ghostty stayed quiet. The badge no longer appears on switches.

summary: Wrote a short check script that prints which of the main tools resolve to a mise shim versus a Homebrew path, to make the version source clear at a glance.
body:
After the pyenv removal I wanted a quick way to tell where each tool comes from. I wrote a script called whichtools that takes node, python, pip, ruby and git and prints the resolved path and a label: mise, brew or system.

The labels come from matching the path prefix against the mise shims folder, the brew prefix and the system folders. If a tool is missing it prints a dash. I ran it and found ruby resolving to the system Ruby, which is expected, since I never installed another one.

It also showed pip resolving to a brew path in one shell, which turned out to be a tmux pane opened before the mise change that still had the old PATH. A new pane fixed it. I put the script in the bin folder of the dotfiles and added it to the bootstrap check output.

summary: Tried a different tmux status line layout with the git branch on the right, found it overflowed on narrow panes, and reverted to the shorter layout with a trimmed branch name.
body:
I wanted to see the current git branch in the tmux status line, so I tried a version that calls a small script in status-right. The script prints the branch of the active pane's directory.

It worked, but on a narrow terminal window the right side pushed the window list out and cut off the window names. Long branch names, such as feature names with ticket numbers, were the main reason.

I changed the script to cut the branch name to 22 characters with an ellipsis in the middle, and reduced the status-right-length setting to 40. I also moved the time to the left of the date and removed the seconds. On a window with 80 columns it now fits.

The script is called every five seconds because of status-interval. I measured it with time and it takes 9 ms, which is fine. I kept the change. The first layout is saved in the tmux config as a comment in case I want it on a wide display.

summary: Investigated why autosuggestions in zsh offered commands from the history that included secrets pasted as arguments, and added a history filter that skips lines matching token patterns.
body:
While typing a curl command I saw the autosuggestion offer a full line from the history that contained an API token. It was pasted from a session long ago. That made me look at what ends up in the history file at all.

I searched the file with grep for common patterns: long strings after Authorization, and variables named TOKEN or SECRET set on the command line. I found 23 lines. I removed them by hand from the file after a backup copy.

Then I wrote a zshaddhistory hook. It checks the line against a small list of patterns and returns 1 for a match, which keeps it out of the history file but still lets it be in the session's memory for the up arrow. The patterns cover bearer tokens, the word password followed by an equals sign, and strings that start with the prefixes used by the main services I use.

I tested with echo commands that include fake values. Matching lines were not written to the file and non-matching lines were. One false positive came up: a command with the word tokenizer in a path. I tightened the pattern to require an equals sign or a space and a long string after the word.

The hook adds no measurable time to the prompt. I put the patterns in a separate file so I can extend them without editing the hook. One limit remains: it cannot catch secrets that do not look like anything known.

summary: Checked the Neovim treesitter parsers after an update broke highlighting in Markdown code blocks and reinstalled the two outdated parsers.
body:
Markdown files lost highlighting inside fenced code blocks after the weekend's plugin update. Plain Markdown text was fine, but the code blocks were uncolored.

I ran the treesitter health check. It reported that the markdown and markdown_inline parsers were older than the queries the plugin now ships, and the version mismatch caused the injection query to fail silently.

I ran the update command for those two parsers and restarted Neovim. The code blocks were highlighted again. I also changed the plugin config to set auto_install to true and added a post-update hook that runs the parser update, so the mismatch cannot return after the next plugin update.

I opened four Markdown files with Lua, shell, JSON and Python blocks to check each one.

summary: Set a consistent color theme across Ghostty, tmux and Neovim from one small palette file and verified that the three tools agree on the dark background value.
body:
The background in tmux panes was slightly different from Ghostty's. It was a small difference, but visible when a split touched the terminal edge. I traced it to three separate hex values for the same dark color, one in each config.

I made a palette file with the named colors and a small generator script, like the one that already handles the font, that writes the Ghostty theme, the tmux color options and a Lua file for Neovim. The generator runs from the bootstrap and from a make-style command.

The first run showed that tmux used the 256-color index for its status line rather than true color, which produced a different shade. I turned on the RGB capability in terminal-overrides for Ghostty, and the status line then matched.

I looked at all three side by side with a split layout and a Neovim window. No visible edge remained. The old hard-coded values were deleted from the three configs. One leftover was a color in the zsh prompt, which I also moved to the palette.

summary: Planned and began a test of the whole backup and restore path after the Zed and mise changes, found that the rsync exclude list was skipping the new mise config folder, and fixed it.
body:
It had been a while since the full backup was verified against all the recent changes, so I decided to run the complete cycle: backup, restore into a temp directory and compare. I wrote the plan down first: check the include list, run the backup, restore, diff, then list what is missing.

The include list was reviewed first. It covered the shell files, the Neovim and tmux configs, the Ghostty and Zed folders and the SSH config without keys. The mise config folder under the home config path was not there. The tool-version files in the projects are part of the repositories, but the global mise config is not, and it holds the global Node and Python versions.

The exclude list had a pattern for cache folders, written as a broad match on the word share. That pattern also matched the mise data folder, which is fine to skip, but also a folder named for the config. I replaced the broad pattern with specific folders and added the mise config file explicitly.

I ran the backup with the dry-run flag first. It listed 412 files and the mise config now appeared. Then I ran it for real, which took 38 seconds for the incremental part.

The restore check from the earlier work restores to a temp directory and diffs. The first run reported one difference: the file permissions of the SSH config were 644 in the restore instead of 600. rsync had the archive flag, but the backup target was on a volume that does not keep modes. I added a chmod step to the restore script for the SSH folder and a check in the test that fails on wrong modes.

The second run passed with no differences. I also looked at the size of the backup, 1.8 GB, which is mostly the Neovim plugin folder. I excluded the plugin install folder, since it can be restored from the lockfile, and the backup dropped to 340 MB.

The restore script now runs the plugin sync at the end in the temp test to show that this works. It took two minutes and passed.

Still open: the backup runs by hand. I would like a launchd job, but that is for another day.

summary: Set up a launchd job for the nightly backup, found it did not run when the Mac was asleep, and added a catch-up check at login with a record of the last success.
body:
I wrote a launchd agent plist that runs the backup script at 02:00. After loading it with launchctl bootstrap I tested it by kickstarting the job, and the log showed a clean run.

The problem is the Mac is usually asleep at 02:00. Launchd runs a missed calendar job on wake, but only one, and my test after a night of sleep showed it had not run at all. The log was empty. The cause was that the lid was closed and the power nap setting was off, so the Mac did not wake, and the missed job had been dropped after a long sleep.

Instead of relying on the time, I changed the approach. The script now writes the time of its last success to a small file. A second agent runs at login and every four hours while the Mac is awake, and it calls the script only if the last success is older than 24 hours. So the backup runs at the first opportunity after a missed night.

I tested by changing the stored time to two days ago and loading the agent. The backup started within a minute and updated the file. With a recent time, the check exits at once in under 50 ms.

I also added output to the log folder with rotation by size, so the log does not grow without bound, and a macOS notification only on failure. I forced a failure by unmounting the target volume. The notification appeared and the log held the rsync error.

The plists are kept in the dotfiles and the bootstrap now links them to the LaunchAgents folder. I tested this in the fresh-home account, where the job loaded without errors.

Next time I want to see how the job behaves with the target volume absent for several days. For now it keeps trying every four hours and notifies once a day at most.

summary: Checked what the backup notification does when the target volume is missing for days and limited it to one message a day, with a count of missed days in the text.
body:
After the launchd catch-up job from two days ago, I tested the case I had left open: the target volume absent for a long time. I unmounted it and set the clock-file back by three days, then let the agent run its four-hour checks by kickstarting it several times.

Every run sent a notification. That would be six a day, which is annoying and would teach me to ignore them. I added a second small file with the time of the last notification and a check that sends one only if the last was over 20 hours ago.

The text now says how many days since the last good backup, which I compute from the success file. For the three-day test it read that the backup was three days old and the volume was not found.

I also found that rsync was started even though the volume was missing, and failed after a long wait on a stale mount path. I added a check at the start of the script that tests the folder exists and is a mount point, and exits with code 3 immediately. The run time for this case fell from about 12 seconds to under a second.

I reconnected the volume and the next run completed and cleared both files. The log showed the sequence as expected.

summary: Looked at a request to share the tmux config with a work laptop and decided to split machine-specific settings into a local override file that is not tracked or backed up.
body:
I wondered if the same dotfiles could be used on a second, managed laptop. The questions were what differs and what must not be copied.

I listed the differences by reading each config. The shell has paths that only exist here, the git config has the personal email and the signing key from the 1Password agent, and tmux has a path to the clipboard tool that differs. Ghostty and Neovim are the same.

The cleanest way is an override file in each tool that is sourced if it exists. zsh already had a zshrc.local line. I added the same to tmux with source-file -q for tmux.local, and to the gitconfig with an include path for config.local.

I moved the email, the signing settings and the clipboard command into the local files here and checked that git log still shows signed commits as verified and that copy mode still yanks to the clipboard. Then I added the local files to the gitignore-like exclude list for the backup scripts of the shared part, but kept them in the personal backup, since they are needed to restore this machine.

The bootstrap now creates empty local files if they do not exist so the includes do not warn. I tested it in the fresh home and no errors appeared. The work laptop itself I have not touched; this only prepares the layout.

summary: Reduced the Neovim plugin list from 46 to 38 after checking which had not been loaded in a month, and the startup time dropped from 41 ms to 34 ms.
body:
I used the lazy plugin manager's profile view to see which plugins had actually loaded in the last weeks. It shows load counts only for the current session, so I used a small autocmd that wrote loaded plugin names to a log file on exit, and let it run for a month. I checked the log now.

Of 46 plugins, eight were never loaded in that time. Four were colorscheme variants I had tried when picking a theme, two were for a language I no longer write, one was a session helper replaced by the built-in features of tmux, and one was a file explorer I had replaced with the netrw tweaks.

I removed them from the plugin spec and ran the clean command. The lockfile lost eight entries. Then I opened files in each of my main languages and used the main leader mappings to see that nothing depended on the removed ones. A mapping for the session helper was still in the keymap, so I deleted it and the matching line in the Zed keymap comments.

Startup time with the startuptime flag went from 41 ms to 34 ms. The plugin folder shrank by 60 MB.

The log autocmd stays off now, and I removed it too. I wrote the removed plugin names into the notes so I know what to restore if I miss one. The backup excludes the plugin folder already, so nothing else changed there.

summary: Investigated a Ghostty crash when opening a very large paste into tmux, reproduced it with a 40 MB file and found the paste confirmation setting avoided it, with an alternative via tmux load-buffer.
body:
Ghostty froze for several seconds and then closed when I pasted a large log excerpt into a tmux pane running Neovim. It happened twice in one week, so I wanted to find out if it could be reproduced.

I created test files of 1, 5, 10 and 40 MB of text lines and pasted each with Cmd-V into a tmux pane with cat. Up to 10 MB the paste took a few seconds and worked. At 40 MB Ghostty used over 3 GB of memory and then closed. In a plain Ghostty window without tmux the 40 MB paste worked slowly, using about 1 GB.

So tmux's handling of bracketed paste made it worse. Each pasted chunk went through tmux's input parser and the pane buffer. The scrollback history limit in my config was high, 200000 lines, which kept all the pasted lines in memory.

Three changes were tried. First, I turned on the paste confirmation in Ghostty for pastes over a size threshold. This is a built-in option, and it asks before sending a large paste. Second, I lowered the history limit to 50000 and checked that it still covers my normal use; the long builds I read usually go to files anyway. Third, I wrote a tiny shell function, bigpaste, that takes the clipboard and loads it into a tmux buffer with load-buffer, so I can put it into a file instead of the terminal.

After the first two changes, the 40 MB paste asked for confirmation, and when I confirmed it the memory use reached 1.4 GB but Ghostty stayed open. With the function, the same data went through pbpaste into a file in under a second.

I do not think the crash is mine to fix in the terminal itself. I noted the version and the steps in a file in case I want to report it to the project. I will check after the next Ghostty update whether the behavior changed.

The config changes are in the dotfiles, and the history limit is a variable in the tmux config with a comment explaining the reason.

summary: Wrote a bug report draft for the Ghostty paste crash with exact steps, and tested the latest Ghostty build, which still used 1.4 GB but no longer crashed even without the confirmation.
body:
Following the paste investigation from earlier today, I prepared to report the crash. First I checked whether a newer build existed. There was one, so I updated through Homebrew and noted both version strings.

I repeated the 40 MB paste test with the confirmation turned off and the old history limit of 200000 lines set temporarily. With the new build, Ghostty did not crash. It used about 1.4 GB at the peak and returned to 300 MB after the paste had finished. The paste took about 25 seconds, during which the window did not respond.

Because the crash is gone, a report about it would be about slowness only. I still wrote the notes down with the steps, the sizes, the timings and the memory numbers for the three tests: plain Ghostty, Ghostty with tmux and low history, and Ghostty with tmux and high history. The values were 1.0 GB, 1.4 GB and 1.4 GB. So the history limit did not change the peak much in the new build, which surprised me.

I tried to understand that. I used the tmux command to show the memory use of the history with the info command, and the history was about 90 MB for 200000 lines. So most of the peak came from the paste buffer in the terminal and the escape processing, not from tmux history.

Given that, I decided to keep the history limit at 50000 since it still reduces memory a little, but to stop treating it as the cause. I updated the comment in the tmux config so it does not claim the limit prevents crashes.

The paste confirmation stays on. It is a useful guard against pasting the wrong large thing, and costs me one key press.

I did not send a report. The notes file is in the notes folder with the exact versions, so if the crash returns on some later build, I have the reproduction ready. I checked that the bigpaste function still works with the new build and that the font and ligature settings were unaffected by the update, by running the ligature test script in a tmux pane and in the Zed terminal panel.

Nothing is left open from this, except to watch for the crash after future updates.

summary: Moved the Ghostty paste crash notes and the 1.4 GB memory finding into a tracked file, and added a reminder to retest after the next Ghostty update.
body:
The Ghostty paste crash work was spread over three places: the bug report draft, a scratch note with the 40 MB reproduction steps, and a few lines in the weekly summary. Today I gathered all of it into one file, notes/ghostty-paste.md, so the next time I hit a large paste there is a single place to look.

The file has four parts. The first is the exact reproduction: generate a 40 MB text file with a short shell loop, copy it, paste into a Ghostty window running tmux. The second is the result on the older build, a crash within a few seconds when paste confirmation was off. The third is the result on the latest build, no crash but about 1.4 GB of memory held while the paste was processed. The fourth is the two workarounds, the paste confirmation setting and loading the file with tmux load-buffer followed by paste-buffer.

While writing it I reran the load-buffer path once to make sure the instructions were right. The same 40 MB file went in with no visible memory growth in the terminal process, and the pane stayed responsive. That confirmed the note is accurate and that load-buffer is the better choice for anything over a few megabytes.

I also added a short shell function, bigpaste, that takes a file name and does the load-buffer and paste-buffer calls into the current pane. It refuses to run outside tmux and prints a clear message instead of a tmux error. It is six lines and lives next to the other small helpers in the zsh folder.

The bug report itself was not sent yet. I decided to wait until the next Ghostty update and run the reproduction once more, since the crash is already gone and the remaining issue is only the memory use. If memory is still that high, I will send the report as a memory issue instead of a crash, and rewrite the first paragraph of the draft for that.

To make sure this is not forgotten, I added a line at the end of the note with the check to do after a Ghostty upgrade, and put the same line into the upgrade checklist I keep with the Brewfile comments. Nothing else changed in the config today, and the shell start time and the fresh-home test were not affected.

summary: Decided to turn the dotfiles folder into a private git repository after checking for secrets, and made the first commit with the local override files excluded.
body:
Following the drift script this afternoon, I looked at the question of version control for the folder. The main reason against was private values. I scanned the folder for secrets with grep patterns similar to the ones in my history filter, plus a check for long random strings and key file headers.

The scan found three things. A backup target volume name and path, which is not secret but personal. An email address in the old gitconfig copy. And a token in an old test script for a notification service, which I had forgotten. I revoked the token in the service's settings, since it had been stored in plain text for a long time, and replaced the script's use of it with a read from the macOS keychain through the security command.

I then wrote a gitignore with the local override files, the generated files, the log folder, the notes folder and the backup state files. I kept the notes out, since they contain personal remarks and may include more pasted values.

I ran git init, checked git status for the list of files to be added, and read it line by line. Forty-one files. I committed them as a first commit with a short message. Commit signing worked through the 1Password agent and the signature verified locally.

I did not set a remote. A private remote would be useful as another backup, but I want to wait until I have thought about the history: the first commit is clean, but I am not sure about the notes. For now the repository is local.

The driftcheck script can now be simplified in the future, since git diff could show the differences against the last commit. I left it as is. The bootstrap script is unchanged, as it copies the files from the folder and does not care if it is a repository.

I also added a line to the backup include list for the git folder so the history is backed up with the files. The restore check passed after that change.

summary: Checked that the new git repository for the dotfiles does not break the bootstrap in a fresh home and found the .git folder was being copied into the home directory, so I excluded it.
body:
After turning the folder into a repository, I ran the fresh-home test to see if anything changed. It passed, but the report's file listing showed a .git folder in the new home, which should not be there.

The bootstrap used rsync from the dotfiles folder to the home, and it had no exclude for .git. I added the exclude for .git and the gitignore file itself.

I also checked the fresh home for the generated files, which are ignored in the repository. They are produced by the generators during the bootstrap, so they existed. The test passed again with a clean listing.

summary: Added a pre-commit check to the dotfiles repository that runs the secrets patterns from the history filter over staged files and blocks the commit on a match.
body:
Since the folder is now a repository, I wanted a guard against committing a secret by accident. I wrote a pre-commit hook that reads the list of patterns from the same file the zsh history filter uses, so there is one list to maintain.

The hook runs git diff --cached with only added lines and checks each against the patterns using grep. On a match it prints the file name and line number, not the matching value, and exits with 1.

I tested with a staged file that held a fake bearer token, and the commit was blocked. A file with the word tokenizer in a comment passed. The hook takes about 30 ms on a typical commit.

Hooks are not part of the repository by default, so I set core.hooksPath to a hooks folder inside it and added that to the gitconfig and the bootstrap. A bypass with --no-verify remains possible, which is fine for a personal repository.

summary: Reviewed the week's dotfiles changes and wrote a short summary in the notes with what is finished, what is parked, and what to try next, including the remote for the repository.
body:
I used the end of the evening to read through the commits and notes from the last weeks and write a summary, so that the later sessions have a clear starting point.

Finished: the move of Python to mise and the removal of pyenv, the async git prompt and the faster shell start at 111 ms, the backup with the launchd catch-up job and the notification limit, the palette generator for the three tools, the history filter for secrets, and the repository with its pre-commit check.

Parked: the Ghostty paste slowness, which has no crash anymore and is kept as notes only, and the two archived virtualenvs that would fail until recreated.

To try next: a private remote for the repository, after I decide what to do with the history of the notes folder, which stays outside it. Also a look at whether the second laptop idea is still wanted, now that the local override files exist. And a check of the Zed macro replay mapping, the one item still missing in the keymap.

I also ran driftcheck and the fresh-home test one more time, and both were clean. The notes file now has a dated-free list in order, so it can be read in a minute.

summary: Pushed the dotfiles repository to a private remote and checked that the pre-commit secrets check also runs on a fresh clone, which needed the hook installed by the bootstrap.
body:
The week review had left the remote as the next step, so I created a private repository on the hosting service and added it as origin. Before pushing I ran the secrets patterns over the whole history, not only staged files, and found nothing.

Then I cloned the repository into a temporary folder to see what a new machine would get. The pre-commit check was missing there, because git hooks live in .git/hooks and are not part of a clone. I moved the hook script into a tracked folder called githooks and set core.hooksPath to it from the bootstrap script.

The fresh-home test passed with the new step and reported the hook path as set. The local override files stayed out of the push, which I confirmed by listing the tracked files and comparing them with the ignore list. The remote now holds 212 files.

Next I want a short README that says how to run the bootstrap and which files are never tracked. I did not write it yet.

summary: Wrote a script that builds the Neovim plugin lockfile snapshot into the dotfiles repository and tested restoring it in a fresh home, which exposed a missing plugin manager bootstrap step.
body:
The Neovim plugins had been updating freely, and after the treesitter breakage of a few weeks ago I wanted a way to pin them. I started by checking what the plugin manager already offered. It writes a lockfile with the commit of every plugin, but that file lived in the config folder and was not tracked. I moved it under the dotfiles repository and replaced the old location with a symlink created by the bootstrap.

The next step was a small script that copies the lockfile, shows a diff against the committed one, and refuses to continue when a plugin moved by more than a patch-sized change without my say-so. That turned out to be too clever, so I cut it down to printing the diff and asking for a yes. It runs in about 2 seconds, which is fine for something I run once after an update.

Then I tested the restore in the fresh-home script from earlier. The first run failed: Neovim started, found no plugin manager, and printed a wall of errors about missing modules. The plugin manager itself is cloned by a line in init.lua on first start, but the bootstrap ran Neovim headless with a short timeout, and the clone had not finished. I added an explicit clone step to the bootstrap before the first headless run, so it no longer depends on the timeout.

The second run restored all 38 plugins at the pinned commits. I compared the output of the plugin manager's list command in the fresh home with the one in my real home, and they matched except for one plugin that I had updated by hand yesterday. That was the lockfile doing its job, so I committed the newer snapshot.

One leftover: the headless sync still prints a harmless warning about a deprecated option in one colorscheme plugin. I left it alone because the upstream fix is not released yet. Next I want to add the snapshot step to the weekly review routine, so a changed lockfile shows up in the notes together with the other pending changes.

summary: Looked into why tmux sessions were not restored after a reboot and found the resurrect plugin saved to a folder the backup script excluded, so the save path moved.
body:
After a restart yesterday evening all tmux sessions were gone, though the plugin that saves them was installed. I checked the save folder and it held only a file from three weeks ago.

The plugin writes to a folder under the cache directory by default. The autosave interval was set to 15 minutes, but the continuum part was not starting because the status line setting that triggers it had been overwritten when I shortened the layout a few weeks ago. The autosave hook lives in status-right, and my shorter layout replaced it.

I fixed this in two steps. First I moved the hook into a small run-shell line that does not depend on the status line. Second I moved the save path to a folder inside the config directory, which is covered by the backup script but listed in the ignore file so the saved sessions do not enter the git repository.

To test it I opened three sessions with different layouts, waited for one autosave, killed the tmux server and started it again. All three came back with their windows and working directories. Panes running Neovim restarted the editor but not the files, which is expected.

I did not turn on restoring of running programs beyond the editor, because the long-running processes are better started by hand.

summary: Added a git alias and a small function to delete merged local branches safely, skipping the current branch and the main branches, after checking it against a throwaway repository.
body:
The branch overview alias from a few weeks ago showed many merged branches that I kept deleting by hand. I wanted a command that does it with a confirmation.

The alias is called sweep and it is a shell function, not a plain alias, because it needs a loop. It lists branches already merged into the default branch, removes the current branch and any named main, master, develop or release from the list, and prints the rest. Only after a y does it run git branch -d for each.

I tested it in a throwaway repository with six branches, two of them unmerged and one checked out. It listed three and left the others alone. Because it uses the lowercase -d, git itself refuses to delete anything unmerged, so a mistake in the list cannot lose work.

The default branch is read from the remote head reference, with a fallback to main when there is no remote. I tried it in a repository without a remote and the fallback worked.

The function lives in the git aliases file and the README lists it now.

summary: Moved the Zed keymap into the dotfiles repository with a symlink step in the bootstrap, then found two Neovim-style bindings that clashed with Zed's own and renamed them.
body:
Until now the Zed settings and keymap files lived only in the application support folder, so they were neither backed up through the repository nor present on a new machine. I moved both into a zed folder in the dotfiles and replaced the originals with symlinks.

The bootstrap got a new linking step for them. The step checks whether the target is already a symlink to the right place, so running it twice changes nothing. I ran the fresh-home test and both files linked correctly.

While reading the keymap through I found two clashes. My binding for leader plus f to open the file finder also matched a Zed default for find in buffer when the editor was in insert mode, and the binding for splitting the pane overlapped with a default that closes the pane. I had been working around the second one by habit without noticing.

I limited the first binding to the normal mode context and changed the split binding to use a different second key. I checked each with the key debug view in Zed, which shows which binding matched and from which file.

The settings file also had a font family entry copied from the terminal, still the old one in the editor font field. That is deliberate, since the editor and terminal fonts are chosen separately, so I left it.

Two more bindings are untested because they depend on an extension I have not installed on this machine. I wrote them down in the notes.

summary: Checked why the Brewfile install on the fresh-home test took twelve minutes and found two large casks downloaded every time, so the bootstrap now skips them when already present.
body: The fresh-home test had become slow, and I wanted to know where the time went. I timed each step of the bootstrap with a simple timestamp print. The Brewfile step took twelve of the fourteen minutes. Two large casks were downloaded again on every run because the test home had no cache, even though the apps themselves were already installed on the Mac. I set the Homebrew cache folder to a shared location outside the fresh home for the test only. The step then dropped to about three minutes on the second run. I also added a check so the bootstrap skips casks whose app already sits in the applications folder. That check is for the test, and a real new Mac still installs everything. I verified this by reading the script with the check switched off, and it behaves as before. The total test time is now under five minutes, which makes it easier to run after each change.

summary: Measured the new tmux and Ghostty startup together and found the shell start was 160 ms slower in tmux than outside it, caused by a login shell flag in the tmux default command.
body:
I noticed that new tmux panes took a visible moment to show a prompt, while a new Ghostty tab was fast. I measured both with a loop of ten starts using zsh -i -c exit under time, and then the same inside a tmux pane.

Outside tmux the average was 92 ms. Inside a new tmux window it was about 250 ms. The difference pointed to extra work at startup, and the tmux config had a default-command line that ran zsh as a login shell. A login shell reads the profile files again, including the one that runs the mise activation and the Homebrew environment setup a second time, though the environment is already inherited from the parent.

I removed the default-command line. tmux then starts the default shell without the login flag. I checked that PATH inside tmux still held the mise shims in the right order and that the Homebrew prefix appeared once.

There was one problem. On macOS a path helper reorders PATH in login shells, and without it the system paths came first in tmux windows. I fixed that by guarding the PATH setup in the zshenv so it does not depend on the login shell.

After the change the tmux start averaged 98 ms. I ran the which check script from earlier and every main tool resolved to the same source as outside tmux.

The change is small but removes a delay I felt many times a day. I added a comment above the config line explaining why it must not return.

summary: Set up git commit signing to also work in the repository clone on a fresh home and found the allowed signers file was missing there, so the bootstrap now writes it.
body:
Signing of commits with the key from the 1Password agent has worked for months, but verifying a signature with git log --show-signature printed a warning about a missing allowed signers file. In the fresh test account the problem was worse, since signing failed outright when the agent was not yet unlocked.

First I created the allowed signers file in the git config folder with my email and the public key, and set gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile to it. After that, git log --show-signature showed a good signature for my recent commits.

Then I looked at the clean account. The bootstrap did not write the file, and the public key was nowhere in the repository. A public key is not secret, so I put it in the dotfiles as a tracked file and made the bootstrap copy it into place and create the signers file from it.

The second problem was the unlocked agent. When the agent is locked, git commit fails with a vague message about the agent refusing the operation. I added a short wrapper in the git aliases that checks whether ssh-add -L lists the key and prints a clear line if it does not.

I tested three cases: agent unlocked, agent locked, and no agent socket at all. The wrapper reported each correctly.

I did not make signing mandatory for the repository yet. I want to see a week of normal commits first. The fresh-home test now includes a signed commit in a temporary repository and passed.

summary: Replaced the slow clipboard step in the tmux copy mode with pbcopy through a key table, and fixed copying from Neovim inside tmux so the text reaches the macOS clipboard.
body:
Copying text in tmux copy mode worked only inside tmux, and from Neovim inside tmux the yanked text did not reach the macOS clipboard at all. I had put up with this for a long time and used the mouse instead.

For tmux I set copy-command to pbcopy and bound y in the vi copy table to copy and cancel. Mouse selection also ends with the same command, so both give the same result. I checked with a short selection and a very long one, 20000 characters, and both pasted completely into a text editor.

For Neovim I first tried the clipboard setting unnamedplus, which needs a provider. Neovim found pbcopy and pbpaste by itself, but there was a delay of almost half a second on each yank because the provider was started through a slow check. I set the clipboard provider explicitly in the Lua config with the two commands and the delay vanished.

There was a third path: the terminal escape sequence for the clipboard, OSC 52. Ghostty supports it, and tmux can pass it on with set-clipboard on. I enabled it so that copying also works over SSH to another machine. I tested this from a remote host and the text arrived in the local clipboard.

One side effect: the escape sequence has a size limit in tmux, so the very long selection from before was cut off over SSH. Locally it is fine because pbcopy handles it. I noted this limit in the tmux config as a comment.

What is left is the paste direction in remote sessions. I did not change it, since the bracketed paste already works.

The three yank paths now each behave and the mouse is no longer needed for copying.

summary: Investigated why brew bundle check reported the Brewfile as unsatisfied after every upgrade and found three casks with auto-updating versions, which are now marked greedy-free in a separate list.
body:
The nightly check I run before backups printed that the Brewfile was not satisfied, almost every day, even though nothing had been removed. The message named three casks.

I ran brew bundle check with verbose output and saw that it considered those casks outdated. All three update themselves, so the installed version often differs from what Homebrew lists. brew bundle check treats that as a failure.

I looked at two options. One was to pass the greedy flag in the check, which would make it worse. The other was to separate the self-updating casks into a second file, Brewfile.auto, and have the check run on the main Brewfile only. I took the second option, since the bootstrap installs both files anyway.

While moving the lines I found two entries in the Brewfile that I no longer use, a screenshot tool and an old video player. I asked myself whether to remove them and decided to check last use first. The screenshot tool had not been opened in four months and the player in more than a year. I removed both from the file and ran brew bundle cleanup to list what would be uninstalled. It listed those two plus a formula pulled in as a dependency that is no longer needed.

I ran the cleanup for real after reading the list twice. Disk usage dropped by about 900 MB.

The fresh-home test now installs from both files and passed. The check script prints satisfied again.

One remaining question is the Mac App Store entries in the Brewfile. They need a signed-in account and fail quietly in the test account. I left them as they are and noted that the test skips them.

summary: Added a tmux key binding to jump to the previous session and one to open a scratch window, and removed two old bindings that nothing used any more.
body:
Switching between two sessions needed the session list each time. I bound prefix plus a capital L to switch-client -l, which jumps back to the last session like the last window command does for windows.

I also added a scratch window binding that opens a new window in the home folder with a name, so quick commands do not disturb project windows. Prefix plus s was taken by the session list, so I used prefix plus a capital S.

While in the file I listed all bindings with list-keys and compared them with my notes. Two old bindings, one for resizing by single steps and one for a layout I dropped, were never used. I removed them.
