I reloaded the config and tried all four cases. Both new keys worked and the removed ones now print nothing.

summary: Diagnosed a mise install that hung on a Node version because of a stale lock in the cache and wrote a repair step into the check script, which also found a Python build missing its headers.
body:
A new project asked for Node 22 and mise install hung for several minutes without output. I interrupted it and ran it again with the debug flag, and it stopped at a download that had started but never finished.

The cause was a partial archive in the mise cache folder together with a lock file from an earlier interrupted run. Mise waited on the lock. I removed the lock file and the partial archive by hand, and the install then took 40 seconds.

To avoid doing this again I added a subcommand to the tool check script, called repair. It looks in the cache for lock files older than an hour with no mise process running and lists them. It deletes them only with a confirmation. I tested it by creating a fake old lock and a running process and it handled both correctly.

While the check script was running I noticed a second problem. The Python 3.12 build used by one project printed a warning that the ssl module was not available. mise had compiled it before the OpenSSL package was installed from Homebrew, so the build lacked the headers.

I reinstalled that Python version after confirming OpenSSL was present. This time the ssl import worked and pip could reach the package index again. I checked the other three Python versions with the same import and all were fine.

To catch this earlier, the check script now tries to import ssl and sqlite3 in each installed Python and prints a line per version. Then I added the same test to the bootstrap, after the mise install step.

The fresh-home run passed with the extra test, and the run took one minute longer because of the compiles, which is acceptable.

The cache folder is not part of the backup, and I confirmed it is in the exclude list. I left the repair command interactive on purpose.

summary: Looked into why Neovim showed a different diagnostic style in Zed and Neovim for the same Python project, and aligned both on one ruff configuration in the project instead of editor settings.
body:
The same Python file showed warnings in Neovim that Zed did not show, and the other way round for a few import rules. I wanted to see why before choosing which editor was right.

Neovim ran its language server with default settings for ruff, and Zed ran the same server but with a settings block I had written months ago that ignored two rule groups. The project itself had no ruff configuration, so both editors filled the gap with their own choices.

The cleanest answer was to put the rules in the project, in a ruff.toml, and strip the editor-specific ignore lists. I wrote the file for the test project with a line length of 100 and the rule groups I actually care about. Then I removed the block from the Zed settings and the matching table from the Neovim Lua file.

After reloading both editors, the diagnostics matched on a file with eleven known issues. Each editor listed the same eleven.

I thought about a global fallback for projects without a ruff file. Ruff reads a user-level configuration from the config folder, so I placed a minimal ruff.toml there and linked it from the bootstrap. Now a project without its own file gets the same defaults in both editors.

One difference remains: Neovim shows the rule code in the message and Zed hides it until hover. That is an editor display matter and I left it.

The notes now say that linting rules live in the project or in the user ruff file, never in editor settings.

summary: Fixed the macOS defaults script so it reads current values before writing and only reports a change when one happened, which makes its output useful after the earlier logout finding.
body:
After the earlier finding that the key repeat setting needs a logout, the defaults script still printed success for every line, which hid whether anything had changed. I rewrote the helper function at the heart of it.

The new helper reads the current value with defaults read, compares it with the wanted one, and does nothing when they match. When they differ it writes the value and prints the old and new value. At the end it prints how many settings changed and lists the ones that need a logout or a restart of the Dock or Finder.

The type handling was the tricky part. defaults read prints booleans as 1 and 0, while the write command takes true and false, so a naive comparison always saw a difference. I added a small mapping for booleans and floats, since a float such as 0.5 can be read back as 0.5 or 0.50.

I ran the script twice on this Mac. The first run changed zero settings, as expected, since I had applied them before. In the fresh home it changed 31 and the second run there changed none.

Two settings turned out not to apply to the test account at all, the ones stored in the global preferences domain that need the full disk permission. The helper now notes that it could not verify them rather than saying done.

The list of settings that need a restart is printed in one line at the end, so I do not have to remember them. I also removed one setting that macOS no longer reads, the old dashboard flag.

summary: Added the dotfiles remote check to the end of the weekly review routine so unpushed commits show up in the notes.
body:
The weekly review I write in the notes did not mention whether the repository had commits that were not pushed. I added a short step to the review routine.

It runs git status with the branch flag and git log with the upstream range, and prints the number of unpushed commits and any modified tracked files. If the count is not zero it adds a line to the notes template.

I tried it with two local commits and the line appeared. After a push it printed nothing. The step takes less than a second.

summary: Spent a session on why Ghostty's shell integration disabled itself inside tmux and found it needs the term setting passed through, which restored the prompt marks and the jump between prompts.
body:
The jump to the previous prompt shortcut in Ghostty worked in a plain tab but did nothing inside tmux. I wanted to know whether this was a setting or a limit of tmux.

Ghostty's shell integration works by the shell printing special marks around each prompt, and the terminal uses them to know where the prompts are. Inside tmux, those marks only get through when tmux passes them to the outer terminal. I looked at the tmux options and found allow-passthrough was off, which is the default.

I set allow-passthrough on for the config. That alone was not enough, because the integration also checks an environment variable that names the terminal, and tmux had replaced it with its own term value. I added a line that keeps the Ghostty variable inside tmux through update-environment.

I reloaded the config, started a new session and checked with printenv inside a pane. The variable was present. The prompt marks arrived, and the jump shortcut moved between the last five prompts correctly.

Then I checked what else the passthrough affects. Image display and the clipboard sequence also go through, and I confirmed that the OSC 52 copy from earlier still worked. Passthrough has a security side too: a program in a pane can send sequences directly to the terminal. I considered this acceptable for a personal machine, but I noted it in the config comment.

One case still fails: panes in a session that existed before the change keep the old environment, so they need to be recreated. I added this to the notes so I do not chase it again.

The ligature test script from earlier shows nothing different, so the font side is not touched by this change.

summary: Reviewed the pre-commit hook after it blocked a harmless commit and found the token pattern matched a long hexadecimal checksum in a lock file, so lock files are now excluded from that pattern.
body:
This morning a commit was blocked by the hook that scans staged files for token-like strings. The match was in a package lock file, in a line holding an integrity checksum.

The pattern list that the hook shares with the history filter includes a rule for long strings of letters and digits. That is a good rule for command arguments typed in a shell, but lock files are full of such hashes, so it triggers all the time there. I had been lucky that no lock file was staged until now.

I considered three fixes. Weakening the pattern would make the history filter less safe. A skip list for the hook is simple and keeps both uses of the patterns the same. A per-pattern file filter would be most precise but more work.

I chose the skip list for now, with a few file names: package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, uv.lock and Brewfile.lock.json. The list sits in a small file next to the patterns so it is easy to edit.

Then I tested. A lock file with a hash now passes. A text file with a made-up token line is still blocked, and so is a lock file renamed to something else. I also ran the hook over the full history of the repository once more to see whether the skip list changed any results, and it did not.

The hook prints the matching line number and the pattern name when it blocks, which made the diagnosis quick this time. I added the file name to that output as well, as it was missing for staged-only content.

The skip list is a weak point if I ever put a real secret in a lock file, which is unlikely. I wrote that into the comment above the list.

summary: Set up a second Ghostty profile for presentations with a larger font and no tabs, switchable with one command, and checked that tmux and Neovim keep their layout when it opens.
body:
I sometimes share my screen and then the terminal text is too small for others. Changing the font size by hand each time and changing it back was annoying, so I wanted a ready profile.

Ghostty reads one config file, but it supports an include of a second file and a command line option for a config path. I wrote a small file, present.conf, that sets the font size to 20, hides the tab bar and uses a slightly lighter background for contrast. A shell function called present starts a new Ghostty window with that file through the open command and its arguments.

The first attempt ignored the file because the new window was only started in the already running instance. On macOS, open needs the new-instance flag so that the arguments are used. After adding it, the window came up with the large font.

Then I checked tmux. Starting a client in the larger window made the layout fit to the smaller window size when another client was attached. I set aggressive-resize on, so each window takes the size of the client that looks at it. Without that, the presenting window shows the old size with dots in the empty part.

Neovim handled the resize well, and the statusline stayed intact. I also tried a split with three panes at font size 20 and it needed two columns less than the long branch name, so the trimmed name from earlier fits.

I looked at the colors. The shared palette file defines the dark background, and the presentation profile sets only one extra value, so the three tools still agree.

The settings are in the repository now, and the bootstrap links the second file to the config folder. The function is in the zsh functions file.

I did not set up a way to go back automatically. Closing the window is enough, since the main profile is untouched.

summary: Wrote a script that compares installed Homebrew formulas with the Brewfile and the dependencies list, to see what was installed by hand and never recorded, and added the findings to the Brewfile.
body:
Over the months I had run brew install for quick one-off needs and not always added the formula to the Brewfile. The next new Mac would then lack those tools. I wanted to see how large the gap was.

The script uses brew leaves, which lists formulas not required by another one, and compares that list with the formulas in the Brewfile. The difference is printed in two groups, installed but not recorded and recorded but not installed.

The first group had nine entries. Four were tools I use regularly: jq, a diff viewer, a file watcher and a disk usage tool. Three were left over from tests, and two I could not remember. For those two I ran brew info and brew uses to see their descriptions and found that one was a library for an image converter I had removed.

I added the four tools to the Brewfile in the formulas section and removed the other five with brew uninstall after checking that nothing depended on them. The second group, recorded but not installed, held one entry, a tool that I had deliberately removed from the machine but not from the file. I deleted its line.

The script also handles casks through brew list --cask against the two Brewfiles. That list matched exactly, so the earlier cleanup had worked.

I added the script to the weekly review routine as a third step after the unpushed check. It prints a clean message when the two lists agree.

One limit: it does not know about formulas installed from a tap with a long name, since the Brewfile writes them differently. I normalized the names by taking the last part after the slash, and this covered the two taps in use.

The fresh-home test did not need changes.

summary: Retested the Ghostty large paste after the latest update as the reminder asked, and found memory use fell from 1.4 GB to about 600 MB for the same 40 MB file.
body:
The tracked notes held a reminder to retest the large paste after the next Ghostty update, and the update arrived this morning. I ran the same test as before.

I created the 40 MB file, started a tmux session and pasted the file contents into a pane running cat with no input confirmation. There was no crash, as with the earlier build.

What changed was the memory. Activity Monitor showed a peak of about 600 MB for Ghostty, against 1.4 GB two months ago. After the paste finished the memory dropped back within a few seconds, where earlier it had stayed high for almost a minute.

I also tried the tmux load-buffer path as a comparison, and it was still faster, finishing in under a second against about six seconds for the paste. I kept the alternative in the notes.

I updated the notes file with the new numbers and the version, and removed the reminder. I did not send the bug report draft, because the crash no longer exists and the memory use is now reasonable.

summary: Went through the zsh aliases and functions, removed fourteen that were unused or shadowed a real command, and added a small list of the survivors with one-line notes to the dotfiles repository.
body:
The alias file had grown over three years and I no longer knew what was in it. I started by counting: 61 aliases and 9 functions. To find out what was used, I looked through the shell history for the last few months and counted how often each name appeared. Fourteen never showed up at all.

Two of them were worse than unused. One alias redefined ls with flags that broke a script I run from cron-like launchd jobs, and another shadowed a system command with a different meaning. I removed both first and ran the backup script by hand to make sure nothing depended on them. It finished normally.

The other twelve were old shortcuts for tools I dropped, such as the nvm loader, a pyenv helper and two iTerm2 helpers from before the move to Ghostty. I deleted them rather than commenting them out, since the repository history keeps them if I ever want them back. I also merged three git aliases that did nearly the same thing into one.

Then I looked at load time. The functions file was sourced eagerly, and one function ran a command at definition time to detect a path. I changed that to detect on first call. The shell start in a plain Ghostty window went from 118 ms to 111 ms, a small but measurable gain over ten runs.

I wrote a short file listing the remaining aliases with a one-line description each, so I can find them without reading the source. The pre-commit check passed on the change, and the fresh-home test still succeeded.

One thing I noticed and left alone: a few functions assume GNU flags for sed and date, and they only work because Homebrew's versions come first in the path. That is fine on this Mac but would fail on a machine without them. I added a note about it to the parked list for the next weekly review.

summary: Checked that the trimmed zsh aliases still load in a fresh home and found two functions that relied on a removed alias, which are now fixed.
body: After the cleanup of the aliases earlier today, I ran the bootstrap in a fresh home to see if anything broke. The shell started without errors, but calling the project-switch function printed 'command not found: ll'. It had used the removed ll alias internally. A second function, the one that shows the largest folders, called a removed alias for du with human sizes. I replaced both with the real commands and wrote the full flags into the functions. Then I grepped the whole folder for every removed alias name, and found no other users. The survivors list in the repository is unchanged. Next I want a small check in the check script that starts zsh and reports any 'command not found' during startup.

summary: Added a startup check to the check script that launches an interactive zsh in a clean environment and fails on any error output, which would have caught yesterday's broken aliases.
body: Yesterday's problem showed that nothing tested the shell as a whole. I added a step to the check script that runs zsh -i -c exit with a temporary HOME created by the bootstrap and captures stderr. Any output makes the step fail and prints the lines. The first run was noisy: the mise activation printed a warning because no tool versions file existed in the temporary home. I fixed that by writing an empty global config in the bootstrap before the check. The second run was clean. I then broke an alias on purpose to see that the check caught it, and it did, with the file and line shown in the zsh error. The check takes about 0.4 seconds, so it is fine to run it on every commit. I did not put it in the pre-commit hook yet, because the hook should stay quick and focused on secrets. Instead it runs as part of the weekly review routine. The functions that call other commands are not covered, only the loading. That part is left as it is for now. One open question is whether the check should also run under tmux, since that path had its own problems before.

summary: Tested the shell startup check inside tmux and found a warning from the resurrect plugin when no server is running, so the check now ignores that one known line.
body: The question from this afternoon was whether the startup check behaves differently inside tmux. I ran the same interactive zsh under a throwaway tmux server with the default command from the config. The shell itself was clean. But tmux printed a warning from the resurrect plugin script: it looked for a save folder that did not exist yet in the temporary home. In the real home the folder exists, so this only shows up in the test. I created the folder in the bootstrap, which is also correct for a fresh Mac, instead of hiding the message. After that the run was clean. I also measured the startup in both cases: 118 ms outside tmux and 124 ms inside, so the earlier login shell flag problem has not come back. I added the tmux run as a second step in the check script, guarded by a test for the tmux binary. The pass and fail output of both steps is now a single line each. Nothing else needed to change in the tmux config.

summary: Evaluated Berkeley Mono as a replacement for JetBrains Mono by comparing glyph widths, ligatures and line height in Ghostty, Neovim and Zed, and wrote down what to adjust before switching.
body:
The user asked me to try a different terminal font, Berkeley Mono, which they had licensed, so I spent the session on a comparison before changing anything permanent. First I installed the font files with a Homebrew cask path check and confirmed that Ghostty listed the family with ghostty +list-fonts. I put the font into a copy of the Ghostty config, not the real one, and opened a test window with it.

The first difference was the line height. Berkeley Mono is a little taller, so at the same size of 14 the window showed 2 fewer lines. Setting adjust-cell-height to minus 6 percent brought the count back to 48 lines in a maximized window. The width of the glyphs was nearly the same, so the tmux status line did not wrap.

Then I checked the ligatures. Berkeley Mono has them as a stylistic feature set, and Ghostty draws them only when the features are enabled. In plain Ghostty the arrows and the not-equal sign looked right. Inside tmux they did not; the sequences showed as separate glyphs. I noted this and did not fix it yet, because I wanted the full list of differences first.

Next I opened Neovim and checked the box-drawing characters in the file tree and the git signs. All of them lined up. The italic style in comments is a different design, which the user may or may not like, so I left it. I also compared the bold weight in the tmux status line; it looked heavier than before, and I noted that a lighter weight could be chosen.

Zed has its own font setting for the editor and the terminal panel, so I checked both. The editor looked fine, and the panel needed the same cell height adjustment.

The list of things to do: set the font family and the cell height in Ghostty, find the ligature setting for tmux, set the font in Zed, and keep the old font installed for a while. Nothing was changed in the real config today.

summary: Wrote a restore test that rebuilds the Brewfile, the symlinks and the defaults in a fresh home and compares the result with the current machine, finding four differences in link targets.
body:
Today I turned the earlier fresh-home checks into a single restore test that can be run in one command. It creates a temporary home, runs the bootstrap, and then compares that home with the real one for the tracked files. The comparison covers the symlinks, the Neovim lockfile, the tmux and Ghostty configs, and the Zed keymap.

The first run reported four differences. Two were symlinks that pointed at the folder with an old absolute path from before the repository was created, so they would break after moving the folder. I changed the bootstrap to create relative links from the repository root. The third was the Ghostty presentation profile, which was only a file on this Mac and not in the repository at all. I moved it in and added the link step. The fourth was a difference in the git config include for signing, where the fresh home pointed at a missing signers file path because of a typo in the template.

After the fixes the second run showed no differences. It took 3 minutes 40 seconds with the casks already present, which matches the earlier skip logic.

I also decided what the test should not cover. Application preferences stored by macOS itself are not compared, since the defaults script handles only the listed keys. The SSH agent setup through 1Password needs a manual approval, so the test only checks that the config line exists.

The output is one line per area with a pass or a diff count, and the full diff goes to a log file. I added the command to the weekly review routine below the remote check. The remaining idea is to run it after each large change, but the runtime is a bit long for that, so it stays weekly.

summary: Traced a sluggish Neovim start on large Python files to a treesitter parser rebuilt on every launch, and fixed it by pinning the parser install to the lockfile snapshot.
body:
Neovim felt slow when opening large Python files, even though the plain startup time was 34 ms after the plugin cleanup. I started with `nvim --startuptime` on a 6000-line Python file and found the first buffer took about 410 ms, against 60 ms for a short file.

Most of that time sat in treesitter. The log showed the Python parser being compiled again on launch, which should only happen once. The cause was the auto-install option, which compared the parser revision with the one in the plugin spec and decided it differed. The lockfile snapshot written a few weeks ago pinned a different revision than the spec asked for.

I first tried deleting the parser folder and letting it rebuild. That helped for one launch and then the rebuild came back. Next I set the plugin to take its revisions from the lockfile and turned off the automatic update on start. After that the parser was compiled once and the large file opened in 75 ms.

I also checked that the same setup works in a fresh home, since the snapshot restore is part of the bootstrap. The restore installed the parsers from the lockfile and compiled them without errors, but it needed a C compiler, which the Command Line Tools provide. I added a line to the check script that reports a missing compiler before the restore starts.

The Zed side was not touched, because it uses its own syntax engine and never showed the delay. What is left is a manual command to update parsers on purpose, which I added as a short alias with a note in the alias list. The next step is to rerun the startup measurement after the next plugin update to confirm the pin holds.

summary: Went through the Ghostty and tmux configs after the font plans and prepared the exact changes for Berkeley Mono, including the terminal features setting that tmux needs for ligatures.
body:
This evening I prepared the font switch that the comparison from the other week had listed, and tested each step in a copy so that the real configs would only get changes that were known to work.

The ligature problem inside tmux was the main item. Ghostty draws the ligatures from the font features, and tmux sits between the program and the terminal. I read the tmux manual on terminal features and found that the outer terminal can be told about its capabilities with the terminal-features option. I tried adding an entry for the xterm-ghostty terminal name in a test config and started a throwaway server. The result was partly right: colors and italics were fine, but the ligatures were still split. A second check showed that the font features themselves were not yet set in the Ghostty copy, so the first test had been misleading.

With the font features enabled in Ghostty and the terminal-features entry in tmux, the arrows, the not-equal sign and the double colon all rendered as single glyphs in a tmux pane. I tried the same in Neovim inside tmux and it worked too, including after splitting panes and detaching and attaching again.

I also settled the other parts: font size 14, cell height adjusted by minus 6 percent, and the lighter weight for bold text in the status line. For Zed, the editor and the terminal panel get the same family and size.

The plan for the real change is to edit the Ghostty config, then tmux config, then reload both and check an existing session. The old font stays installed for some time, in case the new one causes trouble in the editor. I wrote this plan in the notes with the exact lines, so that the change itself is only a copy step. I did not apply it yet, because the user wants to look at the font in daylight first.
